meta.booktitle: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)

paper.title: Towards Probabilistic Question Answering Over Tabular Data
paper.abstract: Progress in question answering (QA) over tabular data has enabled reliable factual retrieval from relational tables. However, many real-world questions are probabilistic, requiring reasoning under uncertainty and latent conditional dependencies that are not directly stored in individual cells. We introduce LUCARIO, a large-scale benchmark for probabilistic QA over real-world tabular datasets, covering diverse domains, dependency patterns, and natural language variations. We propose Auto-BN, a fully automatic neuro-symbolic framework that induces a Bayesian Network from raw tables, translates natural-language questions into formal probabilistic queries, and performs exact inference. Experiments across multiple LLM backbones show that Auto-BN consistently outperforms NL2SQL, retrieval-based, and premise-based baselines, while maintaining a near-zero error rate. LUCARIO fills a relevant gap and provides a practical and scalable testbed for advancing probabilistic reasoning over structured data.

paper.title: Generating Linguistically Diverse and Semantically Faithful Patient Reports

author.affiliation: Université de Lorraine and University of Lorraine

paper.abstract: To protect patient privacy, medical models are frequently trained on synthetic datasets. Focusing on 13 clinical attributes commonly found in breast cancer records, we propose a synthetic data generation framework in which each generated sample is a data–report pair: the structured data capture the 13 attributes of interest, while the accompanying (French) text simulates a corresponding breast cancer pathology report. Data privacy and coverage are obtained by generating the structured data using a tabular data synthesiser. In this work, we focus on enhancing the diversity and quality of the generated texts through a combination of data-driven knowledge distillation, data filtering and data combination. Our findings suggest that the quality of the training data used for the student model outweighs its quantity; that combining data from multiple teachers helps improve performance; and that a compact model (Mistral 7B) can match the zero-shot Information Extraction performance of a significantly larger model (MedGemma 27B) when fine-tuned on high-quality synthetic data.

paper.title: Relational Priors as Convergence Pressure in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
paper.abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) are designed through roles, debate protocols, and aggregation rules. These choices create implicit expectations of trust, skepticism, deference, or collaboration. We make inter-agent relations explicit as signed pairwise priors, rendered in natural language and added to system prompts while keeping the task protocol fixed. Across commons governance and multi-agent debate, these priors change how readily agents coordinate or agree, a pattern we call convergence pressure. More positive relations generally improve sustainability within the GovSim relational-prior sweep and increase consensus on subjective questions. These improvements over negative relations differ from gains over no-prior prompting. On objective QA, fully positive priors usually yield lower final-answer accuracy than the no-prior baseline, and some conditions produce more frequent but less accurate consensus. Effects depend on model backbone, relation type, and topology; explicitly neutral relations also produce different outcomes from omitting relational framing. Relational priors are therefore task-specific interventions and diagnostic probes of sensitivity to social framing. Evaluate them against a no-prior baseline using the task’s primary metric, report accuracy and consensus correctness alongside agreement on objective tasks, and keep no-prior prompting as the default for accuracy-centric tasks unless validation supports a relational prior.

paper.title: Dynamics of Meaning: Towards the Evaluation of Diachronic Semantic Change in Sinhala
paper.abstract: Tracking semantic change in low-resource languages across extensive historical timelines presents significant challenges due to data scarcity and the limitations of static embedding alignments. This study investigates the diachronic evolution of the Sinhala language from the 13th to the 20th century using a multi-stage computational framework. We first align century-specific Word2Vec and FastText embeddings using Similarity Matrix Based Alignment (SMA) and Orthogonal Procrustes (OP) techniques, finding that OP alignment provides more stable neighbourhood tracking for identifying temporal similarity dips. To move beyond aggregate measures, we introduce a Bidirectional Semantic Impact Pruning approach using contextualised embeddings from a fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B. By applying Leave-One-Out (LOO) diagnostics, we attempt to isolate influential sentences to distinguish between systemic semantic shifts and transient polysemic expansion. Our results show that semantic drift in the fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B is not evenly distributed across all usages. Instead, a significant part of the change is driven by a smaller set of high-impact contextual instances, rather than gradual and uniform change across all occurrences. This work provides a preliminary framework for low-resource Sinhala diachronic analysis, highlighting the trade-offs between model sensitivity and data availability.

paper.title: ChartTableViVQA: A Vietnamese Benchmark Dataset for Visual Question Answering with Reasoning Instruction over Charts and Tables Images

author.affiliation: University of Information Technology, Vietnam National University Hochiminh City

paper.abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) over charts and tables requires joint reasoning over language, visual structure, and numerical information, yet no standard benchmark currently exists for Vietnamese. We introduce ChartTableViVQA, a Vietnamese VQA dataset with 13,003 question–answer–instruction triplets over 868 chart and table images. Questions cover multiple reasoning types, ranging from simple value lookup to multi-step aggregation, comparison, and trend analysis, and are accompanied by concise instructions that explicitly guide the reasoning process. The dataset is built via a semi-automatic human-in-the-loop pipeline, combining large language model generation with manual verification by Vietnamese annotators. We evaluate several vision-language models in zero-shot and instruction-based settings. Results show strong performance on simple questions but clear weaknesses in complex reasoning, particularly on charts, while instruction-based prompting consistently improves accuracy.

paper.title: Navigating the Reality Gap: On-Device Continual Adaptation of ASR for Clinical Telephony

author.affiliation: BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science
BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science
BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science

paper.abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) can ease clinical documentation in resource-constrained regions, but deployment is hindered by a "Reality Gap" between laboratory performance and noisy, real-world clinical telephony, compounded by strict data residency and compute constraints. We study this gap using Gram Vaani, a telephonic Hindi corpus spanning rural healthcare and agricultural helplines, as the closest publicly available proxy for clinical telephony speech, and show that a robust multilingual model (IndicWav2Vec) degrades from 11.60% WER on clean read Hindi to 41.72% WER on this data. We evaluate a progression of adaptation regimes, from full fine-tuning and offline Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) upper bounds to an on-device, stream-based continual adaptation framework in which raw audio never leaves the local device, and characterize the trade-offs between data-driven and parameter-driven stabilization strategies. Our evaluation covers both lexical accuracy (WER and CER) and semantic fidelity (BERTScore) on the target domain, alongside the retention of general-domain knowledge. Multi-domain Experience Replay (ER) yields the primary gains, improving target WER by 18.2% relative and reducing catastrophic forgetting by 54% compared to naive adaptation, with BERTScore reflecting consistent gains in semantic fidelity. Combining replay with Elastic Weight Consolidation based on a stabilized importance estimate (Absolute Fisher) yields the strongest retention at a small cost in plasticity. Finally, a language model spot check empirically verifies that the core mismatch lies at the acoustic level and cannot be resolved by language models alone.

paper.title: SPECI: Fine-grained Evaluation of Specificity for Image Captioning

author.affiliation: University of Information Technology, Vietnam National University Hochiminh City
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Image Captioning lies at the center of synthetic data generation in computer vision. The quality of the caption defines the behavior of the resulting model trained on image-caption pairs generated by Image Captioning. Measuring the specificity of image captioning plays an important role in supplying high-quality captions for the downstream tasks. To address the challenge of automatically assessing the quality of the caption, we propose SPECI, an automatic metric that decomposes dense captions into atomic facts and evaluates specificity across visual criteria such as granularity, spatial detail, color, and linguistic focus using WordNet-based hyponym levels. Empirical results on the benchmark datasets demonstrate significant correlation with human judgments, and its application in image captioning and image reconstruction tasks highlights the practical utility of SPECI. The source code of SPECI is available at https://github.com/sonlam1102/SPECI.

paper.title: Are Linguistic and Arithmetic Circuits Dissociated in LLMs?

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit both knowledge of language, rendered by, for example, grammatical judgment ability, and abilities to perform tasks through language, such as math-word problem solving. Motivated by neurolinguistic studies of their neural dissociation in human brains, in this study, we investigate the overlap of their circuits in large language models (LLMs). Specifically, we examine the overlap and causal effects between the circuits extracted for linguistic and arithmetic tasks, using controlled materials and circuit discovery methods from the mechanistic interpretability field. Our experiments with five LLMs show that circuit similarity is mostly explained by task domains (linguistic vs. arithmetic), rather than by their input and output vocabularies or by the syntactic similarities between natural-language sentences and arithmetic expressions. This finding suggests that LLMs may process linguistic and arithmetic information using largely separate neural circuits, highlighting an ability-based modular organization of circuits within these models.

paper.title: Steering with Multilingual Lexicons for Sentiment Control in Low-Resource Languages

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Activation steering offers a lightweight mechanism for controlling model behavior, but existing methods depend on sentence-level contrastive data that is unavailable for most of the world’s languages. We show that multilingual sentiment lexicons are a viable substitute across three model families: aggregated multilingual lexicons outperform English-derived steering vectors for mid- and low-resource languages, while monolingual lexicons remain stronger for languages a model has specialized in during pre-training. The steering efficacy is mechanistically dictated by both representational density and pre-training priors. Large-magnitude English vectors overwhelm the compact representations of low-resource languages, causing "linguistic collapse." This fragility is mitigated by the norm-dampening of multilingual aggregation. Architectural biases, including bilingual specialization penalty and latent numerical rigidity, also heavily constrain cross-lingual steering responsiveness. Ultimately, our work establishes lexicons as a practical steering signal and offers a comprehensive mechanistic account of cross-lingual steering dynamics.

paper.title: PRC: An Efficient and Unified Framework for Evaluating Robustness and Controllability of Large Language Models on Few-shot Prompt Variations
paper.abstract: Understanding the impact of prompt variations on large language model (LLM) outputs is critical. Despite extensive research, two challenges persist: conflated terminology stemming from loosely defined concepts, and inefficient evaluations reliant on output generation. To address these, we first formalize prompt categorization to clearly define prompt robustness and controllability. We then introduce the prompt vector (PV), a compact internal representation that reformulates these properties at the representation level. Building on PV, we propose PRC, an efficient and unified framework to systematically evaluate LLMs under few-shot prompt variations without requiring costly autoregressive decoding. Experiments across diverse instruction-tuned LLMs demonstrate that PRC tightly correlates with traditional output-based metrics while substantially reducing computational overhead. Overall, PRC offers a principled and highly efficient tool for diagnosing LLM behavior.

paper.title: JUMPSTARTER: Human-AI Planning with Task-Structured Context Curation
paper.abstract: Human-AI collaboration on complex planning goals is bottlenecked by how LLM interfaces handle context: users must manually curate and re-surface relevant information across long and unstructured chat histories. Despite advances in long-context prompting and memory-augmented retrieval, this burden remains unresolved: users still have to identify and supply the right context at each decision point, regardless of how much the model can store or surface. We propose JumpStarter, a system that enables LLMs to collaborate with humans on complex goals by dynamically decomposing tasks to help users manage context. We specifically introduce task-structured context curation, a framework that breaks down a user’s goal into a hierarchy of actionable subtasks and scopes context to localized decision points, enabling finer-grained personalization and reuse. The framework is realized through three core mechanisms: context elicitation, selection, and reuse. In a within-subjects user study, plans produced with JumpStarter were rated substantially higher in quality than those produced with ChatGPT. A complementary automatic simulation study shows that JumpStarter consistently outperforms ChatGPT baselines, planning and memory agents, and workflow ablations. These findings show that effective human-AI planning depends not on the volume of context provided, but on attaching the right context to the right subtask at the right time.

paper.title: Decomposing LLM Advice Sycophancy: Content, Style, and Framing Drive Distinct Response Dimensions
paper.abstract: Large language models are widely used for personal advice (relationship conflicts, financial decisions, mental-health support, etc.), but they often align their response with the user’s position rather than offering independent judgment, even when users need pushback rather than validation. Mitigating this, whether through training objectives, system-level guardrails, or evaluation design, requires knowing what triggers it. But what in the user’s message triggers this behavior is unknown. Natural advice-seeking messages vary simultaneously in semantic content (what is disclosed), linguistic style (how it is written), and narrative framing (whose side is told), but existing benchmarks cannot attribute model behavior to any single cue. Without this attribution, mitigations cannot be targeted, for example, suppressing warmth may harm users with genuine distress but might not fix the model’s tendency to endorse whichever side of a conflict speaks. In this work, we isolate which of these cues drive which aspect of sycophantic behavior across 787 advice-seeking scenarios and observe three patterns emerge: emotional warmth is content-driven; stance endorsement is framing-driven: endorsement drops by {\sim}50% when the same conflict is retold from the opposing perspective; and recommendation directness is style-driven. We also find that hedging reduces rather than increases model endorsement; models do not simply validate vulnerable-sounding users.

paper.title: HybridScholar: Personalized Paper Recommendation with Cross Attention-Gated Fusion and Verified Explanation Generation
paper.abstract: The exponential growth of scientific literature has made personalized, factually grounded paper discovery increasingly difficult. Existing systems suffer from limited personalization, cold-start fragility, or hallucinated explanations. We introduce HybridScholar, an integrated architecture combining a CrossAttention-gated fusion of collaborative filtering and RAG learning candidate-specific gate weights per candidate with a Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) pipeline for factually grounded explanations. Evaluated on the Scholar Inbox dataset, HybridScholar substantially outperforms (NDCG@10=0.2991) strong baselines including LightGCN and Scholar-Inbox. Cold-start analysis shows the RAG fallback prevents hard failure for sparse users (NDCG@10=0.283), with cold NDCG rising monotonically as interactions grow. The CoVe pipeline reduces hallucination rate by 23.8%, confirmed by a human evaluation study showing CoVe-revised explanations are preferred by experts on factual accuracy (76.7% vs. 36.0%) and by end-users on helpfulness (78.8%, p{<}0.0001). Overall, HybridScholar improves ranking quality, cold-start robustness, and factual reliability for large-scale scholarly research discovery, demonstrated on 15,881 users across 239,618 papers.

paper.title: How Robust Is Multimodal Claim Verification to LLM Rewriting?

author.affiliation: The Graduate University for Advanced Studies and National Institute of Informatics (NII)
Georg-August Universität Göttingen and NII, Tokyo Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: LLMs are known to introduce stylistic changes into generated text, yet how these stylistic shifts affect model decisions on scientific tasks remains underexplored. In this paper, we focus on multimodal claim verification, where the goal is to determine whether a textual claim is grounded in a given piece of evidence. We apply two rewriting strategies: natural rewriting, which simulates how researchers routinely use LLMs to polish academic text, and controlled injection, which inserts a single LLM-associated word to isolate the effect of vocabulary choice. We evaluate 11 open-weight models spanning five VLM families and ranging from 2B to 38B parameters. We find that models are robust to these modifications: most show no significant drop in accuracy, and compared to prior work on review-score manipulation, verification appears far more stable. However, consistent probability shifts do occur. Hedging-oriented conditions produce significant shifts across nearly all models, while boosting conditions show a weaker effect and general polishing conditions (e.g., grammar correction, fluency improvement) have little effect.

paper.title: Argument Summarization: A Unified Task Definition, Taxonomy, and Survey

author.affiliation: King's College London, University of London

paper.abstract: Argument summarization seeks to generate concise representations of argumentative content while preserving argumentative meaning, yet the field remains conceptually fragmented. In this survey, we provide a unified task definition of argument summarization that encompasses both argumentative text summarization and key point analysis, and introduce a taxonomy along input structure, output representation, and the role of argumentative structure. Using this framework, we analyze the evolution of the field and systematically review existing datasets, methods, and evaluation practices, revealing misalignment that hinders comparability and progress. We further situate argument summarization within the broader context of generic text summarization, identifying practical limitations and intrinsic challenges. Finally, we outline promising future research directions.

paper.title: Escaping the Tokenizer Trap: Probabilistic Semantic Routing for Dense Retrieval in Specialized Domains
paper.abstract: Dense retrievers can blur the distinctions between short, jargon-heavy records that share most of their vocabulary. We study Lex-TM, a training-free layer that interpolates dense cosine similarity with the Jensen–Shannon similarity of topic distributions from an LDA model whose topic–word prior is scaled by a Herfindahl–Hirschman (HHI) exclusivity score. On NTCIR-13 MedWeb, cast as retrieving tweets that share a query’s exact symptom-label set, Lex-TM reaches an English MRR of 0.8151 against 0.7081 for BM25+dense reciprocal rank fusion, a significant paired difference; in Japanese and Chinese the differences from fusion are not significant. With Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, routing improves on dense retrieval significantly in English and Chinese. Three findings bound these gains. SPLADE++ and BGE-M3’s multi-vector mode match or exceed Lex-TM. In English and Chinese the gain depends on the label strings in the indexed tweets: without them, routing no longer improves on dense retrieval. The HHI prior brings no benefit: on short texts it becomes a rarity weight, and a symmetric prior performs as well across five Gibbs seeds. Outside MedWeb, routing matches dense retrieval on Chinese medical QA and lowers nDCG@10 on ChatDoctor, FiQA and long biomedical abstracts. Code, seeds and a changelog of fixed bugs are released.

paper.title: ARR-Dv2: New Data from ACL Rolling Review and its Potential to Improve Reviewing in the ACL Community

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University College London
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and University of Houston
Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology, Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Technische Universität Darmstadt

paper.abstract: We present a new dataset to support AI-assisted and human studies of the peer reviewing process, based on the ARR Open Review Platform. Unlike previous similar data collections, ours, ARR-Dv2, not only contains the reviews but also author-reviewer discussions (aka rebuttal phase) and meta-reviews. We present statistical analyses of the data with respect to the overall score and the correlations among the overall score, confidence, and soundness scores. Additionally, we extend the task of Review Score Prediction also to include rebuttal data and analyze its effect on score prediction. Finally, we introduce a new task, Meta Review Score Prediction, based on a set of up to three reviews rather than a single review. Our initial results in a zero-shot setting indicate that the rebuttal data adds valuable information to the score prediction and enables reliable predictions.

paper.title: Attention-Guided Layer Selection for Contrastive Decoding in Large Language Models

author.affiliation: Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Contrastive decoding methods such as DoLa improve the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs) by contrasting the output distributions of mature and premature layers. However, DoLa’s dynamic layer selection relies solely on divergences in output vocabulary distributions. In this work, we propose three attention-guided strategies—Attention-JSD, Attention-Entropy-Max, and Attention-Entropy-Min—that leverage structural information carried by internal self-attention mechanisms as a signal for layer selection. Experimental results on TruthfulQA demonstrate that our strategies, particularly Attention-JSD and Attention-Entropy-Min, consistently outperform the original DoLa. We observe significant gains on multi-answer metrics (MC2 and MC3), suggesting that attention distributions can provide a more sensitive signal for resolving factual knowledge than output vocabulary distributions.

paper.title: Episodic Memory from Compression Boundaries in Latent Representation Space
paper.abstract: Long-term memory in Large Language Model (LLM) agents requires selective persistence: only a subset of interactions should be consolidated beyond the current context window. Existing memory systems rely on heuristic importance rules or similarity-based novelty, which remain external to the model’s internal computation. We propose a geometric principle for memory formation: episodic memory can emerge from compression failure in latent representation space. We approximate the manifold of routine LLM activations using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and define representational surprise as reconstruction error relative to this learned manifold. Deviations from routine structure yield elevated residuals, providing an unsupervised, model-internal signal for memory writing. We demonstrate this principle through ReSuME, a surprise-gated memory mechanism that commits turns to memory only when normalized reconstruction error exceeds a calibrated threshold. In long-horizon multi-turn dialogue settings, representational surprise separates routine, critical, and out-of-distribution states, and achieves a superior performance–memory trade-off against established memory-agent systems (MemGPT, EM-LLM) and unsupervised anomaly detectors, while operating without labels and at substantially lower inference cost than LLM-judge controllers. Covariance-aware normalization further enables robust cross-domain calibration. These results suggest that episodic memory gating in neural agents can be grounded in intrinsic latent geometry rather than externally engineered rules.

paper.title: Protocode: Prototype-Driven Interpretability for Code Generation in LLMs
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now widely used for tasks such as summarization, question answering, and speech-to-text translation, and increasingly for code generation, with tools such as Cursor and Windsurf analyzing massive code repositories and recommending changes. Big tech companies have acknowledged growing reliance on LLM-generated code. Although this improves developer productivity, it also raises the risk of suboptimal and insecure code. We introduce a retrieval framework for code generation that connects geometry-aware prototype sampling with syntax-grounded interpretability analysis. By conditioning AST-based explanations on retrieved demonstrations, our method evaluates retrieval quality through both functional correctness and interpretability alignment. In our experiments, high-quality in-context learning (ICL) demonstrations make outputs easier to interpret and improve P@10, whereas poorly chosen demonstrations reduce P@10 relative to the base model. Overall, our approach highlights the importance of efficient sampling strategies for ICL, which can affect model performance on any given task.

paper.title: North or South? Diagnosing LLMs’ Understanding of North Korean Language, Society, and Knowledge

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Google and Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in multilingual question answering, yet their ability to understand low-resource sociolinguistic contexts remains underexplored. We study North Korea as a unique testbed where decades of division have produced distinct differences from South Korea in vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse. We introduce LENS (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society), a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions evaluating LLMs across three dimensions: linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge. Evaluating diverse recent LLMs, we find a modest performance drop on North Korean language inputs, a larger gap in sociocultural perspective alignment, and severe limitations on domain-specific knowledge. Qualitative analysis reveals that models often conflate formal institutions with lived realities, project liberal-democratic assumptions, or rely on coarse stereotypes. Our results demonstrate that linguistic similarity alone does not guarantee sociocultural or domain-specific understanding, highlighting the critical need for grounded evaluation resources for underrepresented cultural and political contexts.

paper.title: HALF: Harm-Aware LLM Fairness Evaluation Aligned with Deployment

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across high-impact domains, from clinical decision support and legal analysis to hiring and education, making fairness and bias evaluation before deployment critical. However, existing evaluations lack grounding in real-world scenarios and do not account for differences in harm severity, e.g., a biased decision in surgery should not be weighed the same as a stylistic bias in text summarization. To address this gap, we introduce HALF (Harm-Aware LLM Fairness), a deployment-aligned framework that assesses model bias in realistic applications and weighs the outcomes by harm severity. HALF organizes evaluation datasets into harm tiers (Severe, Moderate, Mild) based on the specific task and bias type they measure. Harm severity is assigned according to deployment-relevant criteria grounded in regulatory and risk assessment frameworks. Our evaluation results across eight LLMs show that (1) LLMs are not consistently fair across datasets, (2) model size or performance do not guarantee fairness, and (3) reasoning models perform better in medical decision support but worse in education. We conclude that HALF exposes a clear gap between previous benchmarking success and model fairness. All data and code are available at https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/HALF

paper.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Capture Language-Specific Concepts Across Diverse Languages

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Understanding the multilingual mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) provides insight into how they process different languages, yet this remains challenging. Existing studies often focus on individual neurons, but their polysemantic nature makes it difficult to isolate language-specific units from cross-lingual representations. To address this, we explore sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for their ability to learn monosemantic features that represent concrete and abstract concepts across languages in LLMs. While some of these features are language-independent, the presence of language-specific features remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce \textit{SAE-LAPE}, a method based on feature activation probability, to identify language-specific features within the feed-forward network. We find that many such features predominantly appear in the middle to late layers of the model and are interpretable. These features influence the model’s multilingual performance and language output, and can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText, along with more interpretability. Our code and complete figures are available [here](https://github.com/LyzanderAndrylie/language-specific-features).

paper.title: Ask Twice: Bidirectional Cross-Encoder Scoring for Faithfulness Evaluation
paper.abstract: Current LLM-based question answering systems provide cited evidence for their claims. However, determining whether each claim within the generated responses is fully supported by its cited evidence is still an ongoing research problem. The task of evaluating attribution quality, or faithfulness to the source text, goes beyond the traditional idea of lexical matching used for relevance in early QA tasks, and the use of lexical models based on semantic distance or word-overlap has declined in favor of NLI-based models and large fine-tuned models. The larger fine-tuned models tend to perform best on current special-purpose benchmarks such as AttributionBench despite struggling with OOD data. Still, exactly why human judgments of faithfulness should align better with LLM evaluators than those based on lexical entailment has never been fully explained. We address the problem with current entailment models by introducing bidirectionality and codifying that idea into a new evaluation modeling approach. We show that this approach is both lightweight and extensible yet competitive with SOTA LLM-based methods, avoiding the pitfalls of both standard NLI and word-overlap approaches. We further show that our model architecture is motivated by a deeper understanding of the gap between lexical distance and faithful claim attribution, exposing the conceptual mechanism behind attribution quality evaluation.

paper.title: Multi-Perspective LLM Annotations for Valid Analyses in Subjective Tasks
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to annotate texts, but their outputs reflect some human perspectives better than others. Existing methods for correcting LLM annotation error assume a single ground truth. However, this assumption fails in subjective tasks where disagreement across demographic groups is meaningful. Here we introduce Perspective-Driven Inference, a method that treats the distribution of annotations across groups as the quantity of interest, and estimates it using a small human annotation budget. We contribute an adaptive sampling strategy that concentrates human annotation effort on groups where LLM proxies are least accurate. We evaluate on politeness and offensiveness rating tasks, showing targeted improvements for harder-to-model demographic groups relative to uniform sampling baselines, while maintaining coverage.

paper.title: Agent+P: Guiding UI Agents via Symbolic Planning
paper.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based UI agents show great promise for UI automation but of- ten hallucinate in long-horizon tasks due to their lack of understanding of the global UI transition structure. To address this, we in- troduce AGENT+P, a novel framework that leverages symbolic planning to guide LLM- based UI agents. Specifically, we model an app’s UI transition structure as a UI Transi- tion Graph (UTG), which allows us to refor- mulate the UI automation task as a pathfinding problem on the UTG. This further enables an off-the-shelf symbolic planner to generate a provably correct and optimal high-level plan, preventing the agent from redundant explo- ration and guiding the agent to achieve the au- tomation goals. AGENT+P is designed as a plug-and-play framework to enhance existing UI agents. Evaluation on the AndroidWorld benchmark demonstrates that AGENT+P im- proves the success rates of state-of-the-art UI agents by up to 14.32% and reduces the ac- tion steps by 37.70%. Our code is available at: https://github.com/KiteFlyKid/agentp.

paper.title: Twenty-Five Years of Inter-Annotator Agreement in NLP: A Systematic Survey of Trends, Metrics, and Reporting Practices
paper.abstract: Large language models are now deployed as annotators across NLP, generating training labels and evaluation scores, yet the field has no established standard for verifying whether LLM-generated labels are reliable, internally consistent, or comparable across studies. This methodological gap does not begin with LLMs: a systematic corpus study of 665 ACL Anthology papers from 1999 to 2026 reveals that even classical human annotation in NLP suffers from systematic measurement and reporting failures that have left a growing body of work scientifically incomparable. Papers were identified through keyword search and organised via topic modelling into a thematic taxonomy spanning eight annotation domains from named entity recognition to disagreement modelling. Full-text analysis of 549 papers yields three principal findings. First, Cohen’s kappa dominates across all task types (259 papers, 38.9%), regardless of whether its assumptions are satisfied; ICC, appropriate for continuous-scale tasks such as MT evaluation, appears in only 16 full-text papers (2.4%). Second, 226 of the 665 papers (34.0%) name no inter-annotator agreement (IAA) coefficient anywhere in the full text, which is a methodology-reporting concern; a further 50.1% of papers name a coefficient in the body but not in the title or abstract, so 84.1% of papers omit the metric from the abstract layer. We frame the body-only gap as a discoverability concern (the methodology is reported but is not visible at the abstract layer readers and reviewers encounter first), distinct from the full-text omission. Third, annotator disagreement modelling and LLM-as-annotator constitute the fastest-growing area of the corpus (124 papers, 18.6%): 26 of these appeared between 1999 and 2022 and 98 between 2023 and 2026, the only dimension whose volume rises in that window. Fewer than 5% of papers report confidence intervals. We provide a large-scale empirical analysis of metric reporting practice within the ACL Anthology and a seven-point agenda for standardised reporting, complementing prior normative guidance with field-scale descriptive evidence.

paper.title: Auto-AdvER: Disentangling Condition, History, and Commercial Offers in Automotive Advertisements
paper.abstract: This paper presents a case study on the development of Auto-AdvER, a specialised span-labelling schema, along with its corresponding dataset for the textual car advertisement domain. Developed with industry needs in mind, Auto-AdvER is designed to enhance text mining analytics in this domain and contributes a linguistically unique sequence-labelling dataset. We introduce a schema consisting of three labels: ’Condition’, ’Historic’, and ’Sales Options’. We outline the guiding principles for annotation, describe the methodology for schema development, and present the results of an annotation study demonstrating an inter-annotator agreement of 78%. Furthermore, we compare the performance of various models, including transformer encoder models (BERT, DeBERTaV3) and transformer decoder-based open- and closed-source large language models: Llama, Qwen, GPT, and Gemini, as well as conditional random fields. Our results show that a fine-tuned DeBERTaV3 encoder achieves the highest F1-score, followed closely by conditional random fields, while the large language models reach the highest precision but lower recall. We present this work as a stepping stone towards more fine-grained analysis and discuss Auto-AdvER’s potential impact on advertisement analytics, pricing, and customer insights. Potential applications include the analysis of market dynamics and data-driven predictive maintenance.

paper.title: Paying for Too Many Tokens? Valid and Cost-Efficient Multimodal LLM Annotation with Simple Heuristics
paper.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable video annotation at scale, but costs accumulate quickly: processing a typical 60-second short-form video at one frame per second requires millions of tokens. To reduce costs, researchers rely on heuristics such as sampling a subset of frames, compressing videos into image grids, or using only a single modality. However, it remains unclear which heuristics save cost, and whether they preserve the downstream conclusions these annotations enable. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic evaluation of these heuristics using short-form videos, on two computational social science (CSS) tasks: sentiment and topic classification. We evaluate each configuration along three axes the literature typically treats separately: classification accuracy, validity of downstream inference, and per-video token cost. First, we find that accuracy and validity diverge: the highest-accuracy configuration can produce wrong conclusions. Second, modality value is not guaranteed: text alone can yield strong performance, indicating that adding modalities can add cost without adding signal. Finally, we find that cost can be decoupled from video length when annotating short-form videos: a single 2x8 image grid built via simple shot-transition detection approaches full-video understanding (kappa within .05), at ~15% of the token cost. Based on these findings, we derive guidelines that can enable cost-aware VLM annotation in CSS.

paper.title: DBRAG: Multi-Table Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Complex Database Queries
paper.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models have introduced new capabilities for reasoning over structured data, particularly through program-aided tools that can analyze tables. However, many existing methods address single-table scenarios or assume that the relevant tables are already provided. In practice, users often issue complex data exploration queries over entire databases, where relevant information may be distributed across multiple relations. In this work, we introduce DBRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework tailored for multi-table question answering. DBRAG first retrieves candidate tables using an offline table index, enriches their summaries with query-relevant rows, and uses an LLM to rerank the candidates. A program-aided reasoner then selects the required tables and executes operations over their full contents, keeping the initial prompt context compact. Experiments on the Spider, GeoQuery, and ATIS datasets used in this study demonstrate improvements in table retrieval and multi-table question answering.

paper.title: BusMA: A Bus Communication Substrate for Multi-Agent Systems

author.affiliation: University of Sheffield and University of Sheffield

paper.abstract: Multi-Agent (MA) systems are effective at solving complex tasks that demand planning, tool use, and the synthesis of evidence from multiple sources. Existing systems typically adopt Hierarchical Manager-Worker (HMW) or Router-based Message Passing (RMP) structures as their communication protocol. However, these designs restrict agent autonomy: Worker agents cannot directly consult specific “peers”, and misrouted messages can propagate errors. Inspired by bus architectures in computer systems, we propose BusMA, a communication framework that allows any agent to address other agents through a shared channel, i.e., the Bus. It consists of agent registration, message routing, and shared memory management components. Worker agents, each equipped with tools, have their own local memory and can reason, act (tool usage), and communicate by posting shared messages with specific intents. We introduce four intents: discussion, challenge, guidance, and request for explanation, which support fine-grained communication among agents. A Chair agent monitors the shared memory to coordinate interactions and facilitate convergence among Workers. To evaluate the effectiveness of BusMA, we conduct extensive experiments with two frontier LLMs across 13 tasks spanning visual reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and knowledge retrieval. The results demonstrate that BusMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HMW and RMP methods.

paper.title: DOSA: A Tree-Guided, Self-Regressive Framework for Long Document Structure Analysis
paper.abstract: In visually-rich documents, information is encoded not only in individual page objects such as tables, headers, and text blocks, but also in the structural relations among them, making document structure analysis fundamental to information retrieval and document understanding. However, accurately inferring such relations remains challenging in multi-page documents with long-range dependencies and heterogeneous layouts. To address this, we propose a tree-guided and self-regressive framework, termed \textbf{DOcument Structure Analyzer (DOSA)}, for inferring relations among page objects and reconstructing document-level semantic trees. DOSA processes documents chunk-by-chunk, fusing visual, textual, and layout features for each page object and predicting hierarchical and ordering relations. The predicted relations are used to incrementally construct a semantic tree, which is then leveraged as structural context to guide inference on subsequent chunks. Experimental results on five benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of DOSA, with improvements of up to 4 F1 points and 19 TEDS points on DocHieNet, the most challenging multi-page hierarchy benchmark.

paper.title: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding
paper.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

paper.title: Token-Level On-Policy Contrastive Learning for Black-box Distillation Without Full Rollouts
paper.abstract: Black-box distillation trains student models using only teacher-generated outputs, making it practical when teacher models are accessible only through APIs. However, existing methods either rely mainly on positive imitation or require costly full-response rollouts to obtain corrective signals. We show that such corrective signals can be obtained locally from teacher trajectories alone. At each position, the teacher token provides a positive anchor, while a high-probability alternative sampled from the student provides an informative negative. Based on this insight, we propose Token-level On-policy contrastive Learning for blackbox Distillation (TOLD), which samples a single negative token from the student’s distribution and optimizes a Bradley-Terry objective anchored by negative log-likelihood. This enables the student to reinforce teacher tokens while suppressing its own likely mistakes, without teacher logits, reward models, or full-response rollouts. Experiments on reasoning and instruction-following tasks show that TOLD outperforms or matches strong black-box distillation baselines and achieves up to 1.88 times training speedup over rollout-based on-policy baselines.

paper.title: A Survey of the Training Process of LLM-Based Agents
paper.abstract: Autonomous agents based on large language models (LLMs) are becoming an increasingly prevalent paradigm for tackling complex and real-world tasks. Despite the remarkable zero-shot capabilities of modern LLMs, specialized agent training is often essential to obtain reliable and improved performance for specific target tasks. In this survey, we provide a process-centric review of the training of LLM-based agents, with a primary focus on methods that update the parameters of the main agent policy. Rather than organizing prior work only by application domain, agent capability, or learning algorithm, we examine the end-to-end pipeline through which LLM-based agents are trained: environment setup, data and trajectory construction, learning-signal design, and optimization objectives and schemes. This perspective highlights how design choices at different stages interact with one another. Finally, we conclude with a discussion on potential future directions.

paper.title: CHASE: Adversarial Red-Blue Teaming for Improving LLM Safety using Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Despite advances in safety alignment, prompt-rewriting attacks such as persona modulation, fictional framing and persuasion-based reformulation, can bypass safety filters even on frontier models. Existing defenses either rely on non-scalable human curation or white-box optimisation that overfits to specific model internals, leaving aligned models brittle against the very class of adaptive black-box adversaries they will face in deployment. To address this gap, we introduce CHASE (Co-evolutionary Hardening through Adversarial Safety-Escalation), a closed-loop red-blue teaming framework in which a black-box attacker and a safety-aligned defender co-evolve. The attacker is trained via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) under a multiplicative reward that jointly enforces bypass effectiveness and intent fidelity, while the defender is hardened on the harvested adversarial rewrites through a two-stage GRPO + rejection-sampled SFT pipeline balanced with benign data. Evaluated on BeaverTails and JailbreakBench against five held-out attack families (PAIR, TAP, AutoDAN, PAP, Translation), CHASE cuts mean StrongREJECT score by 43.2% on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 0% false refusal on benign (Alpaca) prompts, at a measured helpfulness cost of a 55.6% refusal rate on XSTest safe prompts and a 1.92-point MT-Bench reduction. A controlled ablation that varies only the training attack distribution shows that this generalisation comes from the template-free attack distribution rather than the pipeline, and the result replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Across the two similarly sized open models we study, these results suggest that template-free RL exploration recovers latent attack primitives that transfer across mechanistically distinct attack families.

paper.title: Iterative Critique-Refine Framework for Enhancing LLM Personalization

author.affiliation: University of Georgia and Vanderbilt University

paper.abstract: Personalized text generation requires models not only to produce coherent text but also to align with a target user’s style, tone, and topical focus. Existing retrieval-augmented approaches such as LaMP and PGraphRAG enrich profiles with user and neighbor histories, but they stop at generation and often yield outputs that drift in tone, topic, or style. We present \textbf{PerFine}, a unified, training-free critique–refine framework that enhances personalization through iterative, profile-grounded feedback. In each iteration, an LLM generator produces a draft conditioned on the retrieved profile, and a critic LLM - also conditioned on the same profile - provides structured feedback on tone, vocabulary, sentence structure, and topicality. The generator then revises, while a novel knockout strategy retains the stronger draft across iterations. We further study additional inference-time strategies such as Best-of-N and Topic Extraction to balance quality and efficiency. Across Yelp, Goodreads, and Amazon datasets, PerFine consistently improves personalization over PGraphRAG, with G-Eval gains of +8.5–12%, steady improvements over 3–5 refinement iterations, and scalability with increasing critic size. These results highlight that post-hoc, profile-aware feedback offers a powerful paradigm for personalized LLM generation that is both training-free and model-agnostic.

paper.title: The Curious Case of Curiosity across Cultures: Evaluating Cross-Cultural Information-Seeking Questions in Humans and LLMs

author.affiliation: EuroSafeAI and University of Toronto & Vector Institute

paper.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have expanded their role in human interaction, yet information-seeking behavior, particularly across cultural contexts, remains underexplored in these systems. In this work, we study cross-cultural variation in information-seeking using question-asking as a mechanism. We introduce IQUEST (Information-seeking QUestion Evaluation across SocieTies), an evaluation framework that measures human-model alignment in information-seeking question behavior through linguistic (style), topic preference (content) analysis and grounding insights in social science constructs. Across open- and closed-source models, we find that LLMs flatten cross-cultural diversity, aligning more closely with question-asking patterns expressed in Western countries. We also explore fine-tuning strategies, which narrow the human-model alignment gap by 43% overall. Finally, we demonstrate that stronger information-seeking question behavior improves downstream cultural adaptability, highlighting its importance for inclusive NLP research.

paper.title: EnComp: Lightweight Encoder-Only Context Compression for Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Efficient context compression is critical for retrieval-augmented question answering in resource-constrained settings, where long retrieved contexts increase latency, memory use, and LLM reader cost. We propose a lightweight encoder-only framework for query-driven sentence pruning that preserves answer-critical evidence while aggressively reducing irrelevant context. Our method learns marginal contribution scores for sentences using counterfactual training signals and optimizes a contrastive ranking objective that separates critical evidence from noncritical context. Our approach scores all sentences from a single full-context encoding, enabling fast inference with low computational overhead. Experiments show that it maintains accuracy comparable to the strongest baseline while using 3.7\times less peak memory and achieving nearly 3\times lower compression latency, demonstrating an

paper.title: Learn To Say NO! Incorporating Model Abstention In Medical Vision-Language Models for Pharmacovigilance

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Patna, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology
Indian Institute of Technology Patna, India

paper.abstract: Abstention is the intentional refusal of models to provide an answer. Adverse drug reactions (ADRs), which range from mild to life-threatening, are often underreported by patients in hospitals and to doctors because patients assume these are unavoidable. With the growing adoption of LLMs and vision language models (VLMs) in healthcare, patients are increasingly reaching out to these models for solutions. In such high-risk scenarios, incorrect or overconfident responses can cause unnecessary anxiety, lead patients to discontinue essential medications, or encourage inappropriate self-medication. In this work, we propose the \textbf{\textit{MAD-MED}}, a \textbf{M}odel \textbf{A}bstention approach for \textbf{D}rug Adverse Reaction for \textbf{MED}ical-VLMs. It is a training strategy to encourage models to abstain when answering would contradict the available input, exceed the model’s knowledge, or violate model ethics. In addition, we release an augmented \textbf{A}dverse \textbf{D}rug \textbf{R}eaction \textbf{ABS}tention (\textit{ADR-ABS}) dataset comprising image-answerable, text-answerable, and unanswerable questions to support systematic evaluation of abstention behavior. Quantitative and human evaluations confirm that our proposed \textit{MAD-MED} approach improved the abstention capabilities of models considerably while keeping the generative capabilities intact in cases where the model is expected to answer.

paper.title: CLFEC: A New Task for Unified Linguistic and Factual Error Correction in paragraph-level Chinese Professional Writing

author.affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Chinese text correction has traditionally focused on spelling and grammar, while factual error correction is usually treated separately. In paragraph-level Chinese professional writing, linguistic (word/grammar/punctuation) and factual errors can co-occur and interact. Moreover, editorial review leaves few observable errors in published professional texts, making controlled benchmark construction important. This paper introduces **CLFEC (Chinese Linguistic & Factual Error Correction)**, a new task for joint linguistic and factual correction. We construct a mixed, multi-domain Chinese professional writing dataset spanning current affairs, finance, law, and medicine. We then conduct a systematic study of LLM-based correction paradigms, from prompting to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic workflows. The analysis reveals practical challenges, including limited transfer of a specialized corrector, the need for evidence grounding for factual repair, the difficulty of mixed-error paragraphs, and over-correction on clean inputs. Results further show that handling linguistic and factual errors within the same context outperforms decoupled pipelines, and that agentic workflows can be effective with suitable backbone models. Overall, CLFEC provides a new benchmark for Chinese text correction research and practical guidance for proofreading systems. The dataset is publicly available at [https://github.com/jiu2021/CLFEC-Dataset](https://github.com/jiu2021/CLFEC-Dataset).

paper.title: When the Correct Law Still Fails: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Law-in-Force Retrieval in Versioned Legal RAG
paper.abstract: Legal RAG systems often retrieve passages by semantic relevance, lexical score, or citation match. In versioned legal corpora, however, a passage can be topically relevant and citation-matched while being legally invalid for the operative date. We study law-in-force retrieval: retrieving evidence that matches the authority, is valid at the operative date, and supports the answer. We build LawInForce-eCFR from 805 human-validated eCFR/CFR amendment pairs and 3,220 controlled answer-flipping yes/no questions. We also present AuthorityFirst-RAG, a transparent diagnostic retriever that decomposes retrieval into authority identification, temporal scoping, and rule-support ranking. AuthorityFirst-RAG improves Recall@1 from 2.80% for BM25-date-filter to 30.90%, but generation remains difficult even with GoldOracle evidence. These results show a dual bottleneck in versioned legal RAG: retrieving the law in force and applying numeric legal rules.

paper.title: EvidenceRL: Reinforcing Evidence Consistency for Trustworthy Language Models
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fluent but prone to hallucinations, producing answers that appear plausible yet are unsupported by available evidence. This failure is especially problematic in high-stakes domains where decisions must be justified by verifiable information. We introduce EvidenceRL, a reinforcement learning framework that enforces evidence adherence during training. EvidenceRL scores candidate responses for grounding (entailment with retrieved evidence and context) and correctness (agreement with reference answers) and optimizes the generator using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). We evaluate across two high-stakes domains, cardiac diagnosis and legal reasoning, where EvidenceRL consistently improves evidence grounding and faithfulness without sacrificing task accuracy. On cardiac diagnosis, F1@3 increases from 37.0 to 54.5 on Llama-3.2-3B while grounding (G_{max}@3) rises from 47.6 to 78.2; hallucinations drop nearly 5x and evidence-supported diagnoses increase from 31.8% to 61.6%. On legal reasoning, EvidenceRL raises Faithfulness from 32.8% to 67.6% on Llama-3.1-8B, demonstrating consistent behavioral change across domains.

paper.title: AgentArch: A Benchmark for Evaluating Agent Architectures in Enterprise Workflows
paper.abstract: While individual components of agentic architectures have been studied in isolation, we lack empirical evidence on how design dimensions interact in realistic multi-agent systems. This study aims to address these gaps by providing a comprehensive enterprise-specific benchmark. We introduce AgentArch: a benchmark that evaluates 18 agentic configurations across state-of-the-art large language models. The study spans four dimensions: orchestration strategy, agent style (ReAct versus function calling), memory architecture, and thinking tool integration. Results reveal strong model-specific architectural preferences that challenge one-size-fits-all assumptions in agentic AI. They also expose notable performance gaps on enterprise tasks: the best models reach only 35.3% success on the complex task and 70.8% on the simpler task. We aim to inform architecting choices for enterprise agents by grounding model selection and component design in systematic evidence.

paper.title: CROP: Token-Efficient Reasoning in Large Language Models via Regularized Prompt Optimization
paper.abstract: Large Language Models utilizing reasoning techniques improve task performance but incur significant latency and token costs due to verbose generation. Existing automatic prompt optimization(APO) frameworks target task accuracy exclusively at the expense of generating long reasoning traces. We propose Cost-Regularized Optimization of Prompts (CROP), an APO method that introduces regularization on response length by generating textual feedback in addition to standard accuracy feedback. This forces the optimization process to produce prompts that elicit concise responses containing only critical information and reasoning. We evaluate our approach on complex reasoning datasets, specifically GSM8K, LogiQA and BIG-Bench Hard. We achieved an average 68% reduction in token consumption across diverse reasoning benchmarks (and up to 80.6% on algorithmic tasks) while maintaining competitive accuracy, seeing only a nominal decline in performance. This presents a pragmatic solution for deploying token-efficient and cost-effective agentic AI systems in production pipelines.

paper.title: J-ToRL: Tool-Integrated LLM-as-a-Judge via Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge frameworks offer scalable alternatives to human evaluation but inherit the limitations of text-only reasoning, particularly in tasks requiring precise computations. We introduce J-ToRL, a framework that trains LLM judges to leverage computational tools via code generation through end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL). Unlike prior approaches relying on inference-time integration, J-ToRL internalizes tool-use strategies as part of its policy, enabling exploration of diverse reasoning pathways. We identify a key challenge in applying RL with verifiable rewards to judgment: the coarse reward signals inherent in multiple-choice verdicts can incentivize shortcut learning. J-ToRL mitigates this via an auxiliary verifiable reward mechanism based on reference-answers, that enforces stricter criteria beyond simple verdict accuracy alone. With a sophisticated pairwise comparison dataset across five domains, J-ToRL-trained LLMs improve the base models, outperform prior judges, and close the gap to frontier LLMs. Further, J-ToRL-trained models exhibit beneficial cognitive behaviors such as self-error-recovery and self-refinement of tool use strategies.

paper.title: Comparative Personalization for Multi-document Summarization

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

paper.abstract: Personalized multi-document summarization (MDS) is essential for meeting individual user preferences of writing style and content focus for summaries. In this paper, we propose that for effective personalization, it is important to identify fine-grained differences between users’ preferences by comparing preferences of different users. Motivated by this, we propose ComPSum, a personalized MDS framework. It first generates a structured analysis of a user by comparison between users. The generated structured analysis is then used to guide the generation of personalized summaries. To evaluate ComPSum, we propose AuthorMap, a fine-grained reference-free evaluation framework for personalized MDS. It evaluates the personalization of a system based on the authorship attribution between two personalized summaries generated for different users. For robust evaluation of personalized MDS, we construct PerMSum, a personalized MDS dataset in the review and news domain. We evaluate the performance of ComPSum, showing that it outperforms strong baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/leehaoyuan/comparative_personalize_sum.

paper.title: Thinking with Deltas: Incentivizing Reinforcement Learning via Differential Visual Reasoning Policy
paper.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced reasoning capabilities in Large Language Models. However, adapting RLVR to multimodal domains suffers from a critical perception-reasoning decoupling. Existing paradigms, driven by text-centric outcome rewards, reasoning in language medium, inadvertently encourage models to bypass visual perception. We empirically validate this through blind experiments: paradoxically, state-of-the-art policies maintain or even improve performance even when visual inputs are entirely removed. This reveals that these models degenerate into blind reasoners, exploiting linguistic priors to generate plausible answers instead of attending to visual evidence. In response, we propose Thinking with Deltas, a framework driven by a Differential Visual Reasoning Policy (DVRP). DVRP introduces intrinsic supervision via visual triplets, comprising original, masked, and perturbed inputs. It optimizes the model to maximize reasoning divergence from masked inputs (enforcing visual sensitivity) while minimizing divergence from perturbed inputs (ensuring visual robustness). By aligning reasoning variations strictly with the Delta of visual information, DVRP inherently bolsters visual understanding capabilities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both general and medical benchmarks, without requiring external annotations or auxiliary tools.

paper.title: JudgeMoE: Distributional Aggregation for LLM-as-a-Judge

author.affiliation: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

paper.abstract: When an LLM judge scores an output, its score distribution retains uncertainty and disagreement information that is lost after scalar compression. We introduce JudgeMoE, a lightweight aggregator that assigns example-specific weights to cached judge score distributions and fuses them before computing a final score. A protocol study shows that score-range choice is unstable across judge–dataset settings and that soft scoring usually outperforms hard decoding. On the original 10-cell benchmark, JudgeMoE improves mean Spearman over uniform log pooling by +0.079. Applying the same configuration to six additional cells yields a +0.0393 mean gain over the strongest local single judge across 16 cells, with positive differences in 12/16 cells and a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank p=0.0091. Validation-based analyses further show that the preferred aggregation method depends on the task and judge pool.

paper.title: Method Ranking Inverts Across Targets: A Matched-Grid Evaluation of Jailbreak Attacks on Open-Weight Vision-Language Models

author.affiliation: BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science
Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology (KIIT) Bhubaneswar India
Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology and BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science
BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science

paper.abstract: Jailbreak attacks are usually compared by their attack success rate (ASR), with a higher ASR read as a stronger attack. But an ASR mixes an attack’s general strength with its fit to the particular model it was measured on, and it also depends on the judge that scored it. We separate these factors with a matched evaluation grid: five attacks on eight open-weight vision–language models, 200 HarmBench behaviours per cell, every turn scored by three judges (Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-72B and Llama-Guard-3), and each ASR decomposed into general strength, target susceptibility and target-specific fit. Attack rankings invert across targets: FigStep leads PAIR on InternVL2.5-8B (13.0% vs. 3.5%, paired p{=}4{\times}10^{-10}) and trails it on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, in the same direction under all three judges. Across the grid, the target-specific component is statistically significant under every judge (p{<}10^{-12}). The judge matters as well: agreement between judges is low (Cohen’s \kappa between 0.03 and 0.29), and a larger judge with the same rubric changes which attack ranks first on three of eight targets. A higher ASR therefore shows that an attack succeeded more often on a given model under a given judge, but not whether its advantage is general or specific to that model. We release the protocol and {\sim}20{,}400 trajectories with per-turn scores under all three judges

paper.title: The Language of Bargaining: Linguistic Effects in LLM Negotiations

author.affiliation: BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science

paper.abstract: Negotiation is a core component of social intelligence, requiring agents to balance strategic reasoning, cooperation, and social norms. Recent work shows that LLMs can engage in multi-turn negotiation, yet nearly all evaluations occur exclusively in English. We systematically isolate language effects across English and three Indic framings (Hindi, Punjabi, Gujarati) by holding game rules, model parameters, and incentives constant for multi-agent simulations for Ultimatum, Buy-Sell, and Resource Exchange games. Our results indicate that language choice is correlated to agreement and process dynamics, while final payoffs are statistically unchanged, and that this correlation persists across model architectures. Crucially, effects are task-contingent: Indic languages lower acceptance and longer negotiations in the Ultimatum Game, and higher trade volume in Resource Exchange. Further, they suggest that findings obtained under English-only conditions may not generalize to other linguistic settings. Even within one related language family, we observe task-contingent divergence from English, which cautions against treating English-only evaluation as representative. Whether this extends to typologically distant languages remains open.

paper.title: Exploring Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey for AIScientists

author.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are reshaping scientific discovery. They do more than answer questions: they read multimodal evidence, reason over scientific constraints, use tools, and close parts of the research loop. This survey explains how such systems are built for scientific discovery, moving from multimodal perception to training, inference, evaluation, and human-AI collaboration. Across this pipeline, scientific agents face bottlenecks that generic assistants often hide, including scarce expert annotations, evolving domain structures, complex reasoning, immature tool interfaces, safety and toxicity risks, and unfaithful results. We highlight design choices for turning agentic MLLMs into trustworthy, evidence-grounded collaborators. Curated resources are available at https://github.com/JianJinglin/awesome-agentic-AIScientists.

paper.title: Conversational Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Evolution, Taxonomy, and Pedagogical Frontiers

author.affiliation: A*STAR Centre for Frontier AI Research (A*STAR CFAR) and Nanyang Technological University

paper.abstract: Conversational Intelligent Tutoring Systems (CITS) represent a convergence of artificial intelligence, learning sciences, and human-computer interaction, aiming to provide the adaptive and dialogic learning as expert teachers. In the past decades, the advancement of machine learning and natural language processing reshaped CITS’s design, implementation, and evaluation. In this survey, we analyze the evolution of computational paradigms in shifting pedagogical affordances, interaction styles, and methodological development. We frame CITS not merely as dialogue systems, but as proactive agents that reason about learner cognition, affect, and context while enacting pedagogical strategies grounded in educational theories. From domains, populations, and instructional goals, we identify key components, evaluation approaches, and unresolved challenges. Our paper highlights the promise and limitations of conversational tutoring in the generative AI era, offering a foundation for future research that seeks to maximize their pedagogical value.

paper.title: Reference-Grounded Data Curation for Instruction-Following Thai-English Machine Translation
paper.abstract: Instruction-following machine translation (IF-MT) requires respecting prompt-level rules on terminology, formatting, and register. Rule compliance typically trades off against translation quality, a tension that general-purpose IF data augmentation methods do not address. We propose Reference-Grounded Data Curation, a two-phase pipeline that extracts every supervised constraint from a reference translation that already satisfies it, ensuring feasibility by construction. Phase 1 applies Instruction-Following Difficulty (IFD) scoring to retain the hardest-but-learnable instances from an English-Thai parallel pool. Phase 2 extracts constraints from each reference target and keeps only generations satisfying every constraint, yielding the 1.97M-record Grounded dataset. We fine-tune open-weight bases on Grounded to produce ChindaMT, a Thai-English translation family at 4B, 2B, and 0.8B parameters. Under length-controlled pairwise judging, ChindaMT outperforms or matches every same-size baseline at every tier on both plain translation and under explicit rules, reaching up to a 68.4% win rate against the strongest baseline. The recipe transfers cleanly across Qwen generations. We release model weights, the Grounded dataset, and evaluation suites.

paper.title: Are Many Tasks Necessary for General LLM Evaluation? A Matrix Completion View of Benchmark Redundancy

author.affiliation: Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
CyberAgent, Inc. and Nara Institute of Science and Technology
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan

paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluation usually averages scores across many benchmark tasks, implicitly assuming broad task coverage is necessary for reliable general evaluation. This practice also implicitly treats all benchmark tasks as equally important for general evaluation. We revisit this assumption by treating benchmark results as a model-task score matrix under the performance prediction task. We find that a broad range of benchmarks are redundant with scores for 100 LLMs on 13 aggregate tasks and 523 subtasks. Specifically, we recovered model rankings with high rank correlation with the ALS matrix completion method after masking out several task scores. This means that no tasks dominated the recovery process, and both low-scoring and high-scoring tasks shared the same trends. Further analyses show that multiple-choice scores allow us to recover model rankings on free-form generation tasks. For general model ranking, free-form generation evaluation is not necessarily more informative than multiple-choice evaluation. These findings suggest that evaluating general-purpose LLMs can be accomplished with fewer tasks than the current common practice. Our analysis also estimates the number of models required to capture the overall trends in the benchmarks.

paper.title: Investigating LLM Capabilities on Long Context Comprehension for Clinical Question Answering
paper.abstract: Despite the impressive reported performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on medical Question-Answering (QA), evaluation still overrelies on multiple-choice and extractive settings primarily assessing textbook knowledge, with limited work on open-ended QA over patient records. We present a comprehensive study investigating LLM long-context (LC) comprehension on longitudinal, patient-centric Electronic Health Records (EHRs) across multiple datasets, models and metrics, covering extractive, multiple-choice, and open-ended generative QA under different context formulation and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) settings. We show that medically fine-tuned models offer no measurable benefit over base counterparts, smaller models exhibit stronger memorization, and longitudinal supplementary notes aid generative QA. Reasoning models gain on complex multi-note QA under LLM Correctness but not stricter reference-aligned metrics, while hybrid RAG with reranking outperforms Full-Context (FC) prompting. A question-category analysis and multi-faceted metric evaluation further reveal where RAG and FC excel and struggle, with RAG falling behind in longitudinal reasoning, thus uncovering systematic failures pointing to the need for reasoning-appropriate metrics.

paper.title: Video-guided Machine Translation for Indic Languages

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay

Department of Computer Science, Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, Indian Institute of Technology, Madras and National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT), National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology

paper.abstract: Video-guided machine translation (VMT) translates text by leveraging the context provided by the accompanying video. This additional contextual information helps improve translation quality by disambiguating ambiguous words or explicitly indicating attributes such as the colour or gender of objects and people. Prior works have extensively explored VMT; however, most approaches train models from scratch, which requires large amounts of data.
