Additionally, the majority of VMT research has focused on the English–Chinese language pair. In this paper, we explore training strategies for VMT using only a limited amount of data and extend the task to Indic languages, specifically Hindi, Marathi and Odia. We also propose a synthetic data framework that is effective for training VMT models in low-resource language settings. Our results demonstrate an improvement of +1.75 BLEU compared to baseline models.

paper.title: Lexically Stable but Semantically Improvable: On the Editability of Machine Translation Drafts for LLM Post-Editing
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly in machine translation, but their effectiveness as translation refiners depends on the draft source. We compare direct translation, self-refinement, and cross-system refinement on English-to-Chinese WMT test sets. Sockeye drafts obtain higher lexical-overlap scores but lower COMET than the stronger Qwen3 drafts, and receive larger gains after Qwen3 refinement. Additional controls qualify this pattern. Qwen3-0.6B drafts obtain the largest raw gain but lower final quality, while Qwen3-1.7B drafts start near Sockeye in COMET yet benefit less. Cross-family GLM-4-9B-Chat drafts also improve with Qwen3-8B, but achieve smaller gains and lower final quality than refined Sockeye drafts. Descriptive bucket, common-support, and regression analyses suggest that initial quality alone is an incomplete account of these differences. xCOMET-XL score and span diagnostics further characterize the contrast with Qwen3-8B self-refinement. We frame translation editability as a property of the evaluated draft–editor pairing, assessed jointly through quality gain, improvement probability, degradation risk, and final quality.

paper.title: Bahnar–Vietnamese Parallel-Sentence Retrieval: A Low-Resource Case Study with Lexical, Neural, and Hybrid Methods

author.affiliation: Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology
Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology

paper.abstract: For very low-resource language pairs such as Bahnar-Vietnamese, the relative effectiveness of generic multilingual, language-pair-specific lexical, and task-adapted retrieval remains unclear. We study Bahnar-Vietnamese parallel-sentence retrieval (bitext retrieval) as a controlled candidate-ranking task and compare lexical, alignment-based, neural, and hybrid methods under a development-based selection protocol. The strongest off-the-shelf encoder, LaBSE, reaches 24.24% Recall@1, while symmetric IBM1 reaches 49.33%. Among four in-domain modern dense retrievers, development selection chooses DPR-XM, which reaches 47.43% Recall@1 and 72.21% Recall@10. XLM-R LoRA reaches 64.02% Recall@10, and the development-selected XLM-R-first IBM1 reranker gives the highest Recall@1 point estimate, at 51.62%, with an MRR of 0.5579. Paired tests do not establish a significant difference between the hybrid and IBM1 at the 0.05 level, although reranking substantially improves over its neural first stage. Under pair-specific training, LoRA projection with CSLS also performs strongly on Khmer-Vietnamese and Lao-Vietnamese, reaching 80.14% and 84.58% Recall@1. Overall, the results show complementary strengths between lexical alignment and lightweight neural adaptation in low-resource bitext retrieval. Data and code are available at https://github.com/NgThTy/translation-vn-bahna.

paper.title: Atomic and Holistic LLM Judges for Reference-Grounded Support Labels: A Prompt-Controlled Comparison
paper.abstract: When an LLM judge only has to assign a three-way support label to a candidate answer given a reference, does asking it to decompose the answer into atomic claims help, and at what cost? We compare four single-call designs that share the judge model, the inputs, and the level of instruction detail: candidate-side atomic decomposition, a matched holistic rubric, reference-side decomposition that checks whether each reference claim is covered, and a bidirectional combination. Support labels are constructed from TruthfulQA, ASQA, and QAMPARI references (200 questions and 400 rows per dataset). All four designs are run with Opus-4.6, GPT-4.1, and Gemini Flash Lite; Sonnet-4.6 is added for the candidate-side and holistic designs. Candidate-side decomposition is weak where the label depends on completeness: the holistic rubric is more accurate on ASQA and QAMPARI for every judge while using fewer tokens. Reference-side decomposition is 12.5-21.3 points more accurate than holistic on ASQA for 28-29% more tokens, and stays near the holistic ceiling on QAMPARI at 63-69% more. On TruthfulQA misconceptions, candidate-side decomposition is competitive and significantly better for two judges. On a 60-row single-author subset whose labels are looser than strict reference completeness, candidate-side decomposition edges ahead of holistic for every judge, reversing the construction-label order. What a judge decomposes should follow what the label measures.

paper.title: Learning What Is Said, Not How: Stance-Contrastive Learning for Generalizable Hate Speech Detection
paper.abstract: Hate speech classifiers often misclassify counter speech, including condemnation and quotation of hateful content, as hateful because they fail to distinguish propositional content from speaker stance. We identify this issue as content stance conflation and address it as a representation learning problem. We learn stance invariant representations of the same proposition by constructing contrastive pairs that share content but differ in stance. We implement this idea through factorized annotation, stance controlled augmentation, and Stance Contrastive Learning (SCL). On the Implicit Hate Corpus, stance variant augmentation reduces counter speech false positives by 60%, and SCL further improves cross domain F1 by up to 6.5 points on top of the augmented signal. On SBIC, where use mention conflation is less prominent in the training labels, SCL maintains a low counter speech false positive rate. Semantic similarity pairing on the same augmented data yields no cross domain gain over the model trained without contrastive learning (0.623 vs. 0.625), which identifies the pair construction signal rather than contrastive learning itself as the determining factor.

paper.title: Cleaner Speech, Weaker Generalization: Revisiting Pitt-Derived Benchmarks for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection
paper.abstract: Speech-based Alzheimer’s disease (AD) detection increasingly relies on speech-enhanced and curated versions of the Pitt Corpus, where speech enhancement, sample selection, and demographic balancing are often treated as beneficial preprocessing steps. However, whether these transformations improve real-world AD detection or instead affect model generalization and prediction behavior remains unclear. In this work, we revisit the role of speech preprocessing and dataset curation across widely used benchmarks for speech-based AD detection. We evaluated the speech quality of different datasets, the cross-dataset generalization of multiple deep learning models under matched and mismatched enhancement settings, and the behavior of several recent large audio-language models (LALMs). Experimental results show that across multiple supervised speech models, speech-enhanced datasets often improve in-domain performance while reducing robustness in cross-domain evaluation. Matched enhancement between training and test data alleviates, but does not eliminate, this degradation. LALMs show a similar sensitivity: enhanced datasets induce stronger class imbalance and prediction shifts than unprocessed data. These results suggest that speech preprocessing and dataset curation can substantially influence downstream AD detection behavior, indicating that "cleaner" speech datasets are not necessarily more reliable for real-world AD detection.

paper.title: CARE-Bench: Benchmarking Patient-Facing LLM Triage
paper.abstract: Patient-facing medical LLMs and agents increasingly answer symptom questions before clinician contact, where the key safety question is what action the user should take next. We introduce CARE-Bench, a source-grounded benchmark that evaluates sequential patient-facing triage as a four-label per-turn current-action task. CARE-Bench contains 500 cases and 1,059 evaluated patient-disclosure prefixes reconstructed from medical dialogue, consultation, and follow-up-question sources. We evaluate 11 models on 269 held-out rounds under unprompted and minimally prompted open-ended protocols, using a fixed gpt-5.5 mapper to code each response into the four-label action space. Unprompted macro-F1 remains low, ranging from 31.2 to 50.4. Prompting improves 10 of 11 models, with prompted macro-F1 ranging from 46.9 to 63.4, but substantial threshold errors remain. Prompted models often recommend care before needed clarification is obtained; when the correct action was to ask for more information, only 33.5% of prompted outputs preserved the step. The persistence of these errors after prompting suggests that patient-facing triage is not a simple prompting problem and supports explicit evaluation of action timing before deployment.

paper.title: OpenQTS: A Metadata-Rich Open Dataset for Tang Dynasty Poetry
paper.abstract: Tang Dynasty poetry (618–907 CE) represents one of the most significant corpora in Chinese literature, yet no openly accessible, computationally-suitable resource exists with comprehensive author metadata. We present OpenQTS, a complete machine-readable edition of the Quan Tang Shi (全唐詩), containing 48,300 poems from 2,602 authors across 900 volumes. Unlike existing resources, OpenQTS provides systematic biographical metadata through algorithmic inference and authority file integration. Each poem receives a unique identifier, with proper handling of multi-part poems (15.5% of corpus) and collaborative works. All metadata includes provenance tracking, documenting whether information derives from Wikidata, biographical text inference, or historical markers.

paper.title: Geo-spatial and Geo-temporal Reasoning in Vision-Language and Large Language Models : A Review

author.affiliation: Computational Intelligence and Operations Laboratory, Cognitive Agents and Interaction Lab (CAIL), University of Dhaka and North South University
University of Surrey and Computational Intelligence and Operations Laboratory

paper.abstract: Geo-spatial and geo-temporal reasoning require models to determine not only what information is present but also where and when it applies, which is critical for applications such as crisis response, environmental monitoring, and urban planning. This review surveys recent advances in vision–language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) that address geographically and temporally grounded reasoning across tasks including image geolocation, spatiotemporal question answering, language-guided navigation, and Earth observation. We organize the literature through a structured analysis covering task families, input modalities, model architectures, and reasoning paradigms, highlighting how perception, retrieval, tool use, and intermediate reasoning steps contribute to system performance. The survey further synthesizes existing datasets and benchmarks, identifying common evaluation pitfalls such as spatial granularity mismatch, temporal drift, geographic bias, and potential data leakage. Finally, we outline key research challenges and opportunities for developing robust, verifiable, and time-aware geo-spatial AI systems while addressing broader concerns related to fairness, bias, and location privacy.

paper.title: Knowing When to Critique: Task-Adaptive Metacognitive Regulation for Reliable LLM Reasoning

author.affiliation: Nankai University and National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reason fluently but do not regulate their reasoning: they apply uniform scrutiny to every input, which leaves them vulnerable to adversarial and counterfactual prompts, while indiscriminate critique over-corrects answers that were already sound. We propose MetaCrit, a multi-agent framework grounded in Nelson and Narens’ metacognitive regulation theory that calibrates how much critique each task receives. MetaCrit separates regulation into four agents: an object-level generator, a monitoring agent that assesses response validity, a control agent that critiques logical soundness, and a meta-level synthesizer that reconciles their signals into a regulated response. Adaptivity here is input-conditioned intervention strength within a fixed pipeline: all four agents run on every input and what varies is the direction and magnitude of the correction they produce, not which stages execute. Across reasoning, safety, and bias benchmarks, MetaCrit improves truthfulness and logical soundness and reaches zero toxicity on BOLD and HONEST without a reasoning trade-off, whereas the same critique applied indiscriminately degrades performance. The cost is four calls per query, about one sixth of the cost of a dedicated reasoning model of similar accuracy. A writing study shows that MetaCrit is preferred for critical-thinking support, and its agents transfer to existing frameworks without architectural change. Code is available at https://github.com/Paparare/EduThink4AI.

paper.title: Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Foundation Models: A Survey of Spatial Understanding in LLMs and VLMs

author.affiliation: University of Surrey and Computational Intelligence and Operations Laboratory
Shahjalal University of Science and Technology
Shahjalal University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Spatial reasoning, the ability to represent and reason about spatial relations, geometry, topology, and embodied environments, is increasingly vital for evaluating and deploying large language models (LLMs) and vision–language models (VLMs). While multimodal foundation models show strong performance on spatial benchmarks, navigation, and embodied planning, much of this stems from shallow pattern matching rather than grounded spatial understanding. This review offers a comprehensive, framework-driven analysis of spatial reasoning in LLMs and VLMs, covering tasks, representations, datasets, benchmarks, architectures, training, and failure modes. We also link spatial reasoning to embodied AI, emphasizing challenges in generalization, compositionality, and grounding. Our survey unifies diverse fields, NLP, vision, robotics, and cognitive science, to guide the development of truly spatially grounded foundation models.

paper.title: Agent-Environment Alignment via Automated Interface Generation
paper.abstract: Large language model agents have shown impressive capabilities in interactive decision-making tasks. These agents interact with environment through intermediate interfaces, such as predefined action spaces and interaction rules, which mediate the perception and action. However, mismatches often happen between the internal expectations of the agent regarding the influence of its issued actions and the actual state transitions in the environment, a phenomenon referred to as **agent-environment misalignment**. While prior work has invested substantially in improving agent strategies and environment design, the critical role of the interface still remains underexplored. In this work, we empirically demonstrate that agent-environment misalignment poses a significant bottleneck to agent performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose **ALIGN**, an Auto-Aligned Interface Generation framework that alleviates the misalignment by enriching the interface. Implemented as a lightweight wrapper, ALIGN-generated interface achieves the alignment without modifying either the agent logic or the environment code. Experiments across multiple domains including embodied tasks, web navigation and tool-use, achieve consistent performance improvements, with a 45.67% success rate improvement in ALFWorld.

paper.title: ToneCL:Contrastive Learning for Few-Shot Syllable-Level Tone Classification
paper.abstract: Tone languages constitute over 50-70% of the world’s languages, but the vast majority are low-resource, lacking the large transcribed corpora needed for automatic tone classification. Existing datasets are typically collected at the sentence level, whereas field linguists require fine-grained syllable-level annotations. We propose ToneCL, a lightweight contrastive learning framework for few-shot syllable-level tone classification. We simulate low-resource conditions on Mandarin and Vietnamese, limiting labeled data to tens of examples per tone class. ToneCL is pretrained on unlabeled speech with augmentations that preserve tonal identity, then fine-tuned on few-shot examples. Experiments show our method consistently outperforms baselines, achieving 91.6% on six-speaker Mandarin at 10 shots. Cross-lingual transfer is also effective: pretraining on Vietnamese and fine-tuning on Mandarin reaches 91.0% accuracy at 10 shots. Ablation confirms that frequency band rejection is the most critical augmentation.

paper.title: Less Random, More Incoherent: Greedy Hadamard Alignment for LLM Quantization
paper.abstract: Hadamard preprocessing is widely used in large language model (LLM) quantization to reduce activation coherence and suppress peaks. Existing methods typically rely on random sign flips before the Hadamard transform, which do not use information from the target data distribution. We propose Greedy Hadamard Alignment (GHA), a simple training-free method to build a signed-permutation preconditioner from calibration data. GHA uses a pooled representative activation, a greedy search over flat targets, and an efficient alignment step that is analytically optimal once the target is fixed. We also study when one shared GHA preconditioner can transfer across LLM activations. GHA works best when activations are directionally aligned and stable across calibration sources. Overall, GHA improves post-quantization model quality over randomized Hadamard baselines, with the strongest gains in KV-cache quantization, more moderate gains for hidden states, and little compute overhead during inference.

paper.title: DAMG-RAG: Document-Aware Multi-Granularity RAG for Visually Rich Document Understanding
paper.abstract: Real-world documents are visually rich and structurally organized, with text, tables, figures, and captions interleaved across pages. Although retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used for document question answering, existing pipelines often treat such documents as fixed page- or chunk-level collections. This document-agnostic construction either dilutes evidence in dense pages or fragments semantically related layout elements. Moreover, cross-page questions often require iterative evidence exploration, but existing systems typically follow fixed retrieval paths that do not adapt to the evidence already found.We propose DAMG-RAG, a Document-Aware Multi-Granularity RAG framework for visually rich document understanding. During ingestion, DAMG-RAG constructs layout-aware atomic retrieval units and links them to page- and section-level nodes, forming a multi-granularity document tree. During inference, a state-aware agentic workflow maintains explored regions and validated evidence, dynamically selecting exploration and navigation tools over this tree. On MMLongBench, DAMG-RAG obtains 64.7% accuracy with Claude Sonnet 4.6, yielding a 3.6-point gain over the best-performing agentic baseline in our experiments while using 18.8% of its token budget.

paper.title: AstroAgentBench: Evaluating Agentic Planning on Space Mission Planning Tasks

author.affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institution and Fudan University

paper.abstract: Recent LLM-for-Space systems address mission planning, scheduling, operations support, simulator control, and autonomy, but their evaluations use different task contracts, control settings, simulators, and success criteria. We introduce AstroAgentBench, a seven-family benchmark for executable space mission planning in the domains of scheduling, observation planning, constellation design, and relay support. For each case, an agent submits a planning artifact that is checked by an external verifier for schema, timing, geometry, resources, and mission value. Results report validity and normalized scores, with comparisons to task-specific solver references. Across five LLM agent systems and 35 held-out cases, the strongest systems approach or exceed solver-reference scores on several families, while weaker systems often fail to produce high-value valid plans and even strong systems lose quality on geometric, product-level, or design-heavy tasks. Trace analyses separate two failure points: task-contract misformulation and weak solution construction. Successful runs instead calibrate agent-written implementations against verifier feedback and adapt search to case-specific structure. Ablations show that procedure injection and memory accumulation help selectively, when they supply the missing formulation, calibration, or search support.

paper.title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the **Scenario-Actor**, which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.

paper.title: Bait-and-Recover: Poisoning Internal Refusal Signals to Defend LLMs against White-Box Editing Jailbreaks

author.affiliation: Anhui Laboratory for Safe Artificial Intelligence in the Yangtze River Delta and IFLYTEK CO.LTD.

paper.abstract: Open-weight large language models face a low-cost white-box threat from representation engineering attacks. Attackers can estimate refusal directions and search for projection-matrix edits that suppress safety alignment while preserving general capabilities, within minutes on a single GPU and without gradient-based training. We propose Bait-and-Recover, a weight-level defense that places a bait adapter where attackers read activations and a paired recovery adapter at the subsequent layer. Trained via gradient routing, this decouples the observation path from the behavior path. By actively poisoning the residual signal used for measurement, Bait-and-Recover disrupts the attacker’s edit search, while the recovery layer restores clean downstream computation. Across four open-weight models, our defense raises the minimum refusal rate against white-box edit searches from 16.25% to 71.75% under a strict behavior-preservation budget (KL ≤ 0.10), with negligible impact on general benchmarks. By invalidating the core measurement assumption of these attacks, observation-path poisoning offers a practical complement to behavior-level safety training.

paper.title: T2MBench: Evaluating Text-to-Motion Generation under Diverse Language Instructions

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and University of Oxford
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

paper.abstract: As text-to-motion (T2M) models move beyond short action captions toward real-world applications, they are increasingly expected to follow diverse instructions. However, existing evaluation protocols remain insufficient for systematically assessing instruction following, physical plausibility, and fine-grained controllability under such diverse language instructions. To address this gap, we introduce T2MBench, a benchmark with 1,025 prompts across four categories—Dynamics, Complexity, Interaction, and Accuracy—covering 14 representative T2M models and three evaluation dimensions: LLM-Based Evaluation, Multi-Factor Motion Evaluation, and Fine-grained Accuracy Evaluation. Our results reveal substantial gaps in current T2M models’ ability to consistently follow diverse language instructions while maintaining motion plausibility and fine-grained control.T2MBench establishes a reusable diagnostic benchmark for advancing research toward more reliable T2M generation under diverse language instructions. Data and materials are available at https://github.com/Courteous121/T2MBench-release.

paper.title: State-Anchored Complete-View Distillation for Robust Conversational Multimodal Emotion Recognition
paper.abstract: Conversational multimodal emotion recognition MER requires reliable prediction when language acoustic or visual observations are missing or unreliable. Many missing-modality methods reconstruct absent inputs yet such recovery can be non-unique in dialogue context and nonverbal cues may conflict with the target utterance. To this end we propose CoRe-KD Complete-view Reference-guided Knowledge Distillation a state-anchored conflict-regularized complete-view distillation framework for robust conversational MER. A complete-view teacher provides structured references including prediction-level references fused states and modality-specific states. Complete-view State Anchoring CSA aligns incomplete-view student predictions and states with these references while Nonverbal Conflict Exposure NCE trains on target-preserving nonverbal conflict views to reduce donor-label bias. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD with CMU-MOSEI as a supplementary utterance-level check show consistent gains under fixed- and random-missing protocols. Comprehensive ablation studies and further analyses support the role of CSA and the complementary effect of NCE.

paper.title: Can LLMs Follow the Pulse of a Crisis? Evaluating Crisis Sentiment in Bangladesh’s July Uprising

author.affiliation: Computational Intelligence and Operations Laboratory, Cognitive Agents and Interaction Lab (CAIL), University of Dhaka and North South University
Charles Sturt University and The University of Queensland

paper.abstract: Sentiment analysis during political crises is difficult because language, context, and public reaction can change rapidly. This challenge is especially underexplored for low-resource languages such as Bangla. We introduce **UnrestSent200K**, a Bangla crisis sentiment dataset containing approximately 200K Facebook and YouTube comments from the July–August 2024 Bangladesh uprising. The dataset covers five event-aligned phases, ranging from early escalation and internet blackout to regime transition and a later flood crisis. Each comment is linked to its parent post, allowing evaluation both with and without discourse context. All comments are annotated through a fully human process involving 14 native Bangla-speaking annotators and senior validation. The annotation process achieves substantial agreement, with Cohen’s kappa of 0.73, Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.71, and 94.2% blind-audit agreement. We benchmark fine-tuned encoders, prompted LLMs, and LoRA-tuned LLMs. Results show that adding parent-post context consistently improves performance, while temporal shifts across crisis phases cause large performance drops. Strong LLMs perform well, but they still struggle with sarcasm, implicit political references, and meanings that depend on the event phase. UnrestSent200K provides a benchmark for studying context-aware and temporally robust sentiment analysis in low-resource crisis discourse.

paper.title: Hierarchy Aware Preference Optimization for the Safety of Korean Small Language Models
paper.abstract: Safety alignment of small language models (SLMs) typically incurs an alignment tax: benign prompts are refused along with truly harmful ones. The problem is sharper for Korean SLMs, where limited capacity meets a language whose intent signal is blurred by honorifics. We propose KoSCoPe, which combines a Hierarchical Safety Curriculum, a level-conditional adaptive margin (HARM-DPO), and Counterfactual Consistency Regularization, with a reasoning internalization schedule that recovers 1.5 to 3.2× inference speed. Across five Korean SLMs of 1.7B to 4B, KoSCoPe achieves the strongest Safety/Over-refusal trade-off among the baselines under our matched protocol and remains competitive with general-purpose models several times larger. Under paired-bootstrap tests, its Safety gains over the matched preference-optimization baselines survive multiple-comparison correction for all but the closest competitor, Cat-DPO, where the gain is smaller but directionally consistent. Preliminary cross-lingual validation on Japanese, Mandarin Chinese, and English suggests the same design can transfer beyond Korean, with larger gains where surface politeness markers are more salient.

paper.title: CCD-CBT: Multi-Agent Therapeutic Interaction for CBT Guided by Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram

author.affiliation: Beijing Institute of Technology and Lanzhou University

paper.abstract: Large language models show potential for scalable mental-health support by simulating Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) counselors. However, existing methods often rely on static cognitive profiles and omniscient single-agent simulation, failing to capture the dynamic, information-asymmetric nature of real therapy. We introduce CCD-CBT, a multi-agent framework that shifts CBT simulation along two axes: 1) from a static to a dynamically reconstructed Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram (CCD), updated by a dedicated Control Agent, and 2) from omniscient to information-asymmetric interaction, where the Therapist Agent must reason from inferred client states. We release CCDChat, a synthetic multi-turn CBT dataset generated under this framework. Evaluations with clinical scales and expert therapists show that models fine-tuned on CCDChat outperform strong baselines in both counseling fidelity and positive-affect enhancement, with ablations validating dynamic CCD guidance and diagnostic analysis supporting asymmetric interaction design. Our work offers a new paradigm for building theory-grounded, clinically-plausible conversational agents.

paper.title: SG-LegalCite: A Principle-Augmented Benchmark for Legal Citation Retrieval in Singapore Law

author.affiliation: Singapore University of Technology and Design
Singapore University of Technology and Design

paper.abstract: Legal citation in common-law systems depends not only on factual similarity, but also on the legal principle for which a precedent is invoked. However, existing benchmarks for legal citation retrieval use case facts, citation context or full judgments as inputs, where the governing legal principle is often missing or only implicitly expressed and entangled with broader context. As a result, models may retrieve precedents that are factually similar yet doctrinally irrelevant. This limitation is particularly consequential in Singapore, where the legal system has evolved independently: only domestic precedents are binding, while foreign authorities serve merely as persuasive references. Thus, we propose a new retrieval paradigm that ranks cited cases based on queries integrating case facts and explicit legal principle, inspired by the real-world legal reasoning workflows. To support this paradigm, we further introduce SG-LegalCite, a dataset of 100,890 case–principle pairs extracted from 8,523 Singapore Supreme Court judgments spanning 2000–2025. Experiments across 11 baselines demonstrate the effectiveness of our principle-augmented retrieval paradigm, showing that explicit legal principles provide strong discriminative signals for legal citation retrieval. Our dataset and code is at https://github.com/ShannonLeeYuehErn/SG-LegalCite

paper.title: Decoupling Internal Representational Changes and Causal Importance in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Fine-tuning has emerged as a widely adopted approach for adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to a variety of downstream tasks. However, how it reshapes their internal mechanisms remains poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how fine-tuning alters internal representations in LLMs, including attention patterns and layer-wise activations, and examine whether these changes are linked to task-relevant components identified by Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) (e.g., attention heads and logit-level activations) that drive task performance. We find that EAP-identified components are concentrated within specific layers, indicating a degree of functional localisation in how models internalise task-specific behaviour. Notably, the distribution of these components across layers is largely uncorrelated with the layers undergoing the most substantial representational changes during fine-tuning. Furthermore, we observe that overlap in EAP-identified components across tasks does not translate into cross-task performance transfer if the tasks are different in nature (e.g., classification vs. generative tasks). More specifically, fine-tuning on one task can lead to a degradation of performance on another when the two tasks exhibit a high degree of overlap in their EAP-identified components.

paper.title: DeBERTa-ConPara: Attack-Aware and Deployment-Realistic Detection of AI-Generated Text

author.affiliation: Technical University of Munich and Ostbayerische Technische Hochschule Regensburg
Technische Universität München and Imperial College London

paper.abstract: Robust detection of AI-generated text under deployment conditions is challenging: distribution shifts across domains and generators, adversarial perturbations of the input surface, and the absence of target-domain labels for threshold calibration all degrade detectors that perform well in-domain. We present DeBERTa-ConPara, a deployment-oriented detector combining attack-aware Unicode preprocessing with a contextual transformer encoder trained over HC3 Plus, M4, MAGE and RAID. Our central finding is that preprocessing acts in opposite directions depending on where it is applied: normalising the training corpus deduplicates it, collapsing 35.4% of RAID rows into copies of their clean siblings and deleting the adversarial supervision, whereas normalising at inference is an effective defence. A factorial varying the two placements independently identifies raw training with normalised inference as the best configuration, reaching 99.61% AUROC, 99.01% TPR@5% FPR and 96.57% TPR@1% FPR on the official RAID hidden test, alongside 93.14% average balanced accuracy across HC3 Plus and MAGE under a fixed threshold. The gain is confined to two of twelve attack classes: homoglyph and zero-width-space insertion rise from 11.05% and 1.12% to 96.98%. The same signature reproduces in a zero-shot detector of different architecture, showing the effect belongs to the attacks rather than to our model. We additionally report two negative results: semantic-invariance augmentation through paraphrasing and supervised contrastive learning (ConPara) does not improve the best configuration, and the handcrafted feature-fusion branch is inert in distribution and harmful outside it.

paper.title: Cantus: Toward Pedagogical Feedback Generation for Sight-Singing Learning
paper.abstract: Sight-singing is a fundamental yet challenging task in music education, where timely and fine-grained feedback is crucial for helping learners identify mistakes and improve their performance efficiently. However, existing automatic methods mainly focus on isolated subtasks such as alignment or scoring, and are unable to provide end-to-end diagnostic feedback with explicit identification of pitch, rhythm, and musical fluency errors. In this paper, we propose Cantus, a novel multimodal large language model framework for sight-singing assessment and exercise recommendation generation. Cantus jointly models vocal audio and symbolic musical representations, and leverages a pedagogically grounded error representation module together with a large language model to diagnose performance errors, generate structured assessment comments, and provide personalized exercise recommendations. To support this task, we construct a new dataset MIVO (MIDI-Voice) containing 1,003 real-world sight-singing samples with aligned MIDI notes and vocal recordings collected from authentic teaching scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Cantus in sight-singing assessment, achieving strong performance across multiple metrics. Human evaluation of feedback quality shows the potential of Cantus in supporting student-centered sight-singing learning.

paper.title: CoSelector: Multi-Agent Collaboration for Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.abstract: General Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems would suffer from performance degradation in multilingual scenarios due to the complexity of integrating different retrieval results from multilingual collections. In this paper, we propose CoSelector, a multi-agent collaborative framework for multilingual retrieval selection, which is optimized by the centralized training with decentralized execution. Under this paradigm, agents share the same goal but execute decisions using only local observations. CoSelector consists of a Selector agent and a Generator agent. The Selector dynamically filters and composes the most pertinent multilingual documents into a coherent context, while the Generator processes this context to understand and integrate information for answer generation. Across the 15 languages evaluated on MKQA and XOR-TyDi QA, CoSelector achieves competitive improvement in response language consistency, demonstrating its effectiveness in both linguistic alignment and the selection of retrieved results.

paper.title: MMA: Multimodal Memory Agent
paper.abstract: Long-horizon multimodal agents depend on external memory. However, similarity-based retrieval often surfaces stale, low-credibility, or conflicting items, which can trigger overconfident errors. We propose Multimodal Memory Agent (MMA), which assigns each retrieved memory item a dynamic reliability score by combining source credibility, temporal decay, and conflict-aware network consensus, and uses this signal to reweight evidence and abstain when support is insufficient. We also introduce MMA-Bench, a programmatically generated benchmark for belief dynamics with controlled speaker reliability and structured text–vision contradictions. Using this framework, we uncover the "Visual Placebo Effect," revealing how RAG-based agents inherit latent visual biases from foundation models. On FEVER, MMA matches baseline accuracy while reducing accuracy standard deviation by 35.2% and improving selective prediction utility; on LoCoMo, a safety-oriented configuration improves actionable accuracy and reduces wrong answers; on MMA-Bench, MMA reaches 41.18% Type-B accuracy in Vision mode, while the baseline collapses to 0.0% under the same protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/MMA.

paper.title: Empathy Is Not the Scapegoat for Declines in Factuality and Reliability

author.affiliation: Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology
Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology
Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology

paper.abstract: Language models are increasingly expected to support users in stressful or uncertain situations, where warmth and empathy are desirable. While recent work links warmer models to lower factuality and reliability, we show that this conclusion is incomplete: prior studies often use warmth as a global persona and conflate tone effects with SFT data distribution shift. We revisit this issue through prompting, fine-tuning, factual robustness, and empathy evaluation, using an 11-dataset benchmark suite and EmoFact, a benchmark for factual accuracy under emotional context. Across three large language models, we find that warmth effects are task- and model-dependent, and that task-aligned adaptive tone can improve empathy while preserving reliability. We further train human-validated empathy evaluators to evaluate the output of our finetuned model. Our results suggest that models can be made more supportive in human relationships and social interactions without compromising overall reliability.

paper.title: RouterKGQA: Specialized–General Model Routing for Constraint-Aware Knowledge Graph Question Answering

author.affiliation: Shenzhen Farben Information Technology Co., Ltd.
Shenzhen Farben Information Technology Co., Ltd.
Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen and Harbin Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) is a promising approach for mitigating LLM hallucination by grounding reasoning in structured and verifiable knowledge graphs. Existing approaches fall into two paradigms: retrieval-based methods utilize small specialized models, which are efficient but often produce unreachable paths and miss implicit constraints, while agent-based methods utilize large general models, which achieve stronger structural grounding at substantially higher cost. We propose RouterKGQA, a framework for specialized–general model collaboration, in which a specialized model generates reasoning paths and a general model performs KG-guided repair only when needed, improving performance at minimal cost. We further equip the specialized model with constraint-aware answer filtering, which reduces redundant answers. In addition, we design a more efficient general agent workflow, further lowering inference cost. Experimental results show that RouterKGQA outperforms the previous best by 3.57 points in F1 and 0.49 points in Hits@1 on average across benchmarks, while requiring only 1.15 LLM calls per question on WebQSP (1.23 on CWQ). Code and models are available at https://github.com/Oldcircle/RouterKGQA.

paper.title: CoMMA: Conflict-Aware Read-Time Control for Conversational Memory QA

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Memory-augmented assistants must answer questions from long-horizon conversations in which facts are not only missing, but also revised, corrected, or mutually inconsistent. Existing methods largely optimize retrieval, storage, or updating, and many controllers still treat failure primarily as insufficient evidence. We argue that conversational memory QA also requires an explicit model of inconsistency: when remembered claims disagree, a system should not simply retrieve more or guess, but may need to resolve versions, return a qualified answer, ask for clarification, or abstain. We introduce CoMMA, a transparent read-time controller with explicit conflict state for conversational memory QA. CoMMA extracts provenance-aware claims from retrieved memories, groups potentially incompatible claims into conflict clusters, infers lightweight question intent, and chooses among direct answer, qualified answer, clarification, and abstention. In an evaluation centered on the full LongMemEval-Oracle benchmark, a LongMemEval conflict-focused diagnostic slice, and FactConsolidation-20, CoMMA performs best on the main LongMemEval answer-quality comparison, is the only method with non-zero conflict F1 on the conflict-focused diagnostic slice, and ties the strongest write-time overwrite baseline on FactConsolidation-20. These results suggest that making conflict explicit at read time improves both decision quality and the auditability of memory-aware behavior.

paper.title: LogicLure: Toward Evidence-Grounded Safe Decision-Making under Hidden Risks
paper.abstract: Safety evaluations of large language models (LLMs) have largely focused on whether models refuse explicitly harmful requests. However, in high-stakes decision-support settings, seemingly legitimate requests may conceal missing information or hidden risk signals. We propose LogicLure, a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs avoid premature decisions and actively seek evidence under such plausible scenarios with hidden risks. The benchmark spans eight domains and pairs persuasive visible narratives with hidden evidence maps accessible only through verification. Our evaluation measures not only the decision of models, but also whether they ask verification questions and whether their final decision is grounded in the revealed evidence. In our evaluation, the strongest model reaches only 26.4% evidence-grounded refusal despite 94.7% overall refusal. Furthermore, we analyze how scenario surface cues, explicit scrutiny setting, and prompt-induced stance shape these decisions. Together, these analyses characterize the key behavioral factors underlying LLM performance on LogicLure. The benchmark and code will be made publicly available.

paper.title: Initialisation Determines the Basin: Efficient Codebook Optimisation for Extreme LLM Quantization
paper.abstract: Additive quantization enables extreme LLM compression while preserving lookup-table inference with free-form codebooks. At 2 bits per weight, however, greedy sequential initialisation can cause large quality losses that wider assignment search and PV-tuning do not fully erase. We show that this failure reflects an interaction between representational pressure and sequential codebook coupling. We use \rho=N/K^M as a structural pressure measure and propose OA-EM, a hard generalised-EM initialisation procedure using Hessian-weighted Mahalanobis distance to minimise output-aware reconstruction error. Across four models from 3B to 14B parameters, OA-EM consistently lowers matched post-PV perplexity. Controlled experiments at a fixed bitrate show that \rho alone does not explain sensitivity to initialisation; the number and size of the additive codebooks also matter. A Euclidean-EM ablation and curvature diagnostics show that the gain is not explained by EM refinement alone: OA-EM reduces error in high-curvature directions. On Llama 3.2 3B, OA-EM also improves the measured quality-compute trade-off. Overall, the final quantized solution remains persistently dependent on initial codebook geometry. Code: https://github.com/kenno94-IK/aqlm-oaem.

paper.title: FrenchNews-7: Benchmarking Cross-Publisher French News Editorial Desk Classification
paper.abstract: We present FrenchNews-7, a cross-publisher France-based French-language news editorial desk classification benchmark combining a large multi-outlet corpus, a URL-derived seven-class taxonomy, and a fine-tuned CamemBERT classifier. Labels are assigned via a hybrid pipeline combining publisher URL slugs with LLM annotation for structurally ambiguous cases, audited through an inter-rater study (2 humans + 2 LLMs; pairwise κ ≥ 0.766, human–human κ = 0.806). We evaluate lexical, multilingual, and French-specific trained classifiers under both in-distribution and held-out-publisher settings, with additional comparison against zero-shot LLM baselines (GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral Small 3.2, Llama-3.3-70B) on the held-out pool. The strongest model, CamemBERT-base on full article text, outperforms headline-only input, generalizes to unseen outlets, and exceeds all three zero-shot LLM baselines on overall recall (0.799), with the gap concentrated in the ambiguous editorial-boundary categories Économie and Société. Cross-publisher evaluation reveals uneven boundary stability: Sport, Culture Loisirs, and International transfer cleanly, while Économie (recall = 0.517) is statistically indistinguishable from blinded human agreement on the same articles (0.55, n = 40), and Société (precision = 0.577) absorbs boundary ambiguity, both suggesting editorial conventions rather than recoverable classifier headroom. The fine-tuned CamemBERT-base model is released on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/LeFrenchNewsLab/camembert-base-frenchnews7) and the labeled manifest on (https://huggingface.co/datasets/LeFrenchNewsLab/frenchnews-7), alongside reference collection scripts to assist re-fetching and a reliability-tier guidance table.

paper.title: SweSpecQA: A Swedish Benchmark for Specialized Document-Native Question Answering

author.affiliation: RISE Research Institutes of Sweden AB

paper.abstract: We introduce SweSpecQA, to our knowledge, the first Swedish benchmark for specialized institutional and professional QA with paired text and full-page PDF evaluation. It contains 1,500 questions from public Swedish examination and certification materials across six domains: EU aptitude, boating, antibiotic stewardship, interpreter licensing, physician licensing, and pharmacist licensing. Of these, 234 questions require an original visual or layout-dependent source element; the remaining 1,266 are text-eligible. All benchmark questions are drawn directly from Swedish-language source materials, avoiding translation artifacts in multilingual adaptations of English benchmarks. We evaluate 17 models under a closed-book protocol, reporting accuracy by domain, exam subtype, visual/layout dependence, modality, and prompting strategy, as well as whether models follow the requested answer format. On the text-eligible subset, every multimodal model performs worse with full source-page input than extracted text; PDF penalties range from 4.0 to 38.2 points under direct prompting and from 1.7 to 36.4 points under chain-of-thought prompting. Reasoning prompts often improve PDF performance for several open-weight VLMs, while sometimes reducing clean-text accuracy. These results show that document-native evaluation exposes failures hidden by text-only evaluation and that preprocessing remains important for reliable Swedish exam-style QA.

paper.title: DuDi: Dual-Signal Distillation with Cross-Lingual Verbalizer

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are efficient and scalable, but their multilingual capabilities degrade severely at sub-billion scales, especially for Southeast Asian (SEA) languages. We introduce DuDi, a dual-signal multilingual distillation framework that combines an online sequence-level signal with off-policy and on-policy token-level signals. DuDi further uses a cross-lingual verbalizer to refine teacher feedback and improve teacher-student transferability in multilingual settings. Experiments on SEA-HELM across multiple model families, scales, and teacher-student settings show that DuDi consistently outperforms competitive distillation baselines. Ablations and analyses confirm that sequence-level optimization, token-level supervision, and cross-lingual verbalization provide complementary and transferable learning signals for multilingual SLMs.

paper.title: SEA-NLI: Language Inference as a Lens into Southeast Asian Cultural Understanding

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Vidyasirimedhi Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Frontier LLMs perform well in Western contexts, but remain poorly tested on underrepresented cultures such as those in Southeast Asia (SEA). Existing NLI benchmarks are largely Western-centric, translation-derived, or monolingual, limiting their ability to measure culturally grounded reasoning. We introduce SEA-NLI, a native, culturally grounded NLI benchmark covering eight SEA countries in English and native regional languages, verified by native speakers. Across 17 encoder and decoder models, we observe a low performance from all models, especially for knowledge-intensive categories such as Languages and Science and Technology. Our analysis shows that failure cases mainly stem from missing SEA cultural knowledge: SEA-adapted models and culture-aware prompting improve performance, while CoT prompting offers limited gains.

paper.title: Grounding What Users Care About: Multi-Aspect Personalized Modeling from Implicit Preferences
paper.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) personalization is challenging because user preferences are rarely stated explicitly; instead, they emerge as implicit, multifaceted signals in users’ past interaction histories. Existing methods often compress user histories into a single representation or retrieve and inject past records without explicitly linking them to supporting evidence, which can lead to hallucinated or overly generic outputs. In this work, we propose Multi-Aspect PersonaLized Modeling with Evidence (MAPLE). MAPLE structures implicit user preferences through a MULTI-ASPECT PREFERENCE PROFILE and connects them to target-specific grounding evidence through a PERSONALIZED EVIDENCE PLAN. By selecting only generation points that are both relevant to the user and supported by available evidence, MAPLE improves personalization and grounding faithfulness simultaneously. Experiments on the Games and Books domains with two backbone LLMs show that MAPLE consistently outperforms strong baselines and generalizes robustly under limited-history and unseen-user settings.

paper.title: Incorporating Abstract Meaning Representation and Uniform Meaning Representation into In-Context Learning Strategies for Machine Translation
paper.abstract: While in-context machine translation approaches lead to notable progress for low-resource languages, it is not yet clear what kinds of linguistic information in prompts can consistently and reliably lead to performance gains. We evaluate whether English semantic representations, specifically Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) and its extension Uniform Meaning Representation (UMR), can improve LLM-based MT via prompting. Across 12 languages, 7 models from 5 families, and multiple prompting strategies, we find that conclusions about their effectiveness are highly sensitive to the setting. We further observe that prompts using UMR tend to outperform those using AMR, particularly in few-shot scenarios and for certain models. These results highlight the need for comprehensive evaluation for in-context learning work.

paper.title: Beyond Downstream Task Performances: A Set-Theoretic Evaluation of Sentence Embeddings
paper.abstract: Sentence encoders are foundational to a wide range of NLP applications, yet they are predominantly evaluated through performance on downstream tasks. Such task-specific evaluations provide limited insight into whether the resulting sentence representations capture fundamental compositional relationships in a task-independent manner. To address this gap, we introduce a set-theoretic framework for evaluating the compositional properties of sentence embeddings. Drawing on classical set theory, we define six evaluation criteria based on three core set-like text operations: TextOverlap, TextDifference, and TextUnion. We use these criteria to systematically evaluate 19 sentence encoders, including 7 classical models and 12 Large Language Model (LLM)-based encoders. Our results reveal substantial differences in their compositional behavior: notably, SBERT exhibits the strongest overall alignment with the proposed set-theoretic criteria, outperforming even recent LLM-based encoders. We further examine whether these intrinsic compositional properties are associated with downstream performance across five NLP tasks. Among them, summarization exhibits the strongest correlation with the TextOverlap and TextDifference criteria, suggesting that our framework may also provide useful signals about downstream capability without relying exclusively on task-specific evaluation. Finally, we release a benchmark comprising ~192K samples to support systematic evaluation and future research on the compositional properties of sentence embeddings.

paper.title: Are Reasoning Vision-Language Models Robust to Semantic Visual Distractions?
paper.abstract: Reasoning Vision-Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on complex multimodal tasks, but reliable real-world application requires handling visual inputs that are messier than clean, curated benchmarks. Existing works mainly evaluate such reliability of VLMs through input corruptions, such as noise, blur and weather effects, which make visual evidence harder to perceive. This leaves a critical reliability failure mode underexplored: a model may perceive the evidence correctly, yet reason from plausible but irrelevant and distracting evidence and propagate this mistake to its final answer. To address this gap, we introduce **Distract-Bench**, a benchmark for evaluating VLM robustness to **semantic visual distractions**, defined as meaningful but task-irrelevant visual cues added to inputs while preserving the ground-truth answer. We comprehensively evaluate eight leading open-source and two closed-source VLMs across conventional vision corruptions and Distract-Bench. Our results show that Distract-Bench exposes a robustness failure distinct from vision corruptions: reasoning VLMs largely track their non-reasoning base models under perceptual degradation, but show consistently lower robustness to semantic distractions. Further analysis shows that these distractions often enter the reasoning process of VLMs, are treated as evidence, and lead to incorrect answers. Together, these findings reframe robustness evaluation for reasoning VLMs, shifting the focus from degraded perception to distractions for reliable real-world visual reasoning. Our data and code are available at _https://github.com/Yizheng-Sun/Distract-Bench_.

paper.title: Routing-Based Continual Learning for Multimodal Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with continual learning, often suffering from catastrophic forgetting when adapting to sequential tasks. We introduce a routing-based architecture that integrates new capabilities while robustly preserving foundational knowledge. While Multi-Task Learning (MTL) is a strong performance reference, its training cost grows linearly with the number of tasks. In contrast, our method maintains fixed per-task training data and compute requirements regardless of the task sequence length. Across models ranging from 2B to 8B parameters, we demonstrate that our routing approach performs on par with MTL while retaining the training efficiency of sequential fine-tuning. Beyond merely mitigating forgetting, we observe that token-level routing facilitates cross-modal transfer, leveraging knowledge from one modality to bolster performance in another. We also show that routing remains robust even with large expert pools and effectively capitalizes on task relatedness. Finally, we show that our method scales favorably, with larger models exhibiting minimal degradation compared to fully specialized fine-tuning.

paper.title: Mechanistic Evidence Routing in Transformers: Margin-Gated Intervention for Retrieval-Conflict Hallucination
paper.abstract: When a language model ignores retrieved evidence and answers from memory instead, this is not a knowledge failure, the correct information is present. It is a routing failure; the model commits to its parametric answer despite the evidence signal. We show this distinction is mechanistically meaningful, localizable, and correctable at inference time without training data or weight modification.A single prefill-margin computation detects routing failures (AUC \geq 0.93 across five model dataset pairs) and gates a format-appropriate logit-bias correction. On MedQA multi-option conflicts, this achieves 77.5% restoration at zero harm, exceeding the strongest prompting baseline by 67.5 pp and matching domain-matched ITI without training data. On open-ended PopQA (3,141 items, three models), balanced alias promotion achieves 80-88% restoration at near-zero harm, Pareto-dominating prompt-only baselines in five of six cross-model conditions. The central mechanistic finding is that effective late-layer intervention sites are structurally distinct from the causal commitment locus (a five-head cluster, joint flip rate 88.6%, p < 10^{-9}), suggesting that steering can succeed through residual-stream write access without exactly identifying the full decision circuit.

paper.title: Prompting Underestimates LLM Capability for Time Series Classification

author.affiliation: University of Texas at San Antonio and University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio

paper.abstract: Prompt-based prediction pipelines suggest that large language models (LLMs) perform poorly on time-series classification, raising doubts about whether they encode meaningful temporal structure. We show that this conclusion reflects limitations of prompt-based generation rather than the model’s representational capacity by directly comparing prompt outputs with linear probes over the same internal representations while controlling for important confounding factors. While prompting performs near chance, linear probes improve average F1 from 0.15–0.26 to 0.61–0.67, often matching or exceeding specialized state-of-the-art (SoTA) time-series models. Layer-wise analyses further show that class-discriminative time-series information emerges in early transformer layers and is amplified with multimodal inputs and the presence of pretrained weights. Together, these results demonstrate a systematic mismatch between what LLMs internally represent and what prompt-based prediction pipelines reveal, leading current prompt-based prediction pipelines to underestimate the degree to which these models function as useful time-series feature extractors.

paper.title: Universal Boosts, Specific Suppressors: Sparse Autoencoder Steering of Medical Vision-Language Models

author.affiliation: ZHAW - Zürcher Hochschule für Angewandte Wissenschaften and University of Zurich
Kobe University, Graduate school of medicine
University Hospital Zurich and University of Zurich

paper.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) commit clinical errors when generating chest X-ray reports: they fabricate findings that are not present in the image, miss important ones, or locate them incorrectly. We steer the error composition of generated reports without weight updates by decoding-time residual steering on a per-token sparse autoencoder (SAE) basis: Top-K SAEs on late layers, per-error-type causal feature screening against clinical errors, then combined suppress/boost intervention at inference time. On the MIMIC-CXR test split, our inference-only method improves the quality of generated reports for three radiology VLMs (RadVLM, LLaVA-Rad, and CheXOne), with relative improvements of +5.4%, +7.2%, and +17.0% in the clinical composite metric, and statistically significant GREEN gains on all backbones. The gain is an explicit, controllable trade-off rather than uniform error reduction: steering shifts models toward more complete reporting, substantially fewer missing findings, at the cost of some additional false findings, and we analyse and quantify this redistribution per error type. A cross-model feature alignment shows that the quality-promoting (boost) directions have functionally similar error-type profiles across architectures, whereas hallucination-linkedm (suppress) directions are model-specific. Census-motivated steering should therefore treat suppression per-backbone, rather than sharing a universal suppress list. The same recipe applied zero-shot to IU-Xray (GREEN +7.7\% rel., on RadVLM) suggests that the identified features are properties of the model rather than of the training corpus. The causal feature sets and an interactive feature dashboard are shared.

paper.title: Language Models Should Be Used to Surface the Unwritten Code of Science
paper.abstract: This position paper argues that researchers should not only study how human biases enter large language models (LLMs), but actively leverage those biases as diagnostic tools to surface society’s "unwritten code"—the tacit norms and hidden heuristics that govern high-stakes decisions yet resist explicit articulation. We present a case study in peer review: a framework that iteratively pushes LLMs to generate self-consistent hypotheses explaining score differences across 26,731 submissions to 46 conferences. LLMs’ normative priors (cues extracted by self-talk) emphasizing theoretical rigor are systematically updated toward posteriors (cues actually used in the judgment) emphasizing storytelling and contextualization—a finding cross-validated by independent human survey evidence. Human reviewers explicitly reward prior-aligned aspects (r=0.49) but rarely articulate the storytelling posteriors (r=-0.14), despite implicitly rewarding them. These findings generalize to out-of-sample judgment and different models. We argue this framework applies to hiring, admissions, and criminal justice, offering a scalable path to making hidden evaluative codes visible for public scrutiny and equitable reform.

paper.title: Absolute Error Is Not Enough: Ranking Model Performance Without Labels to Estimate Disparities at Scale

author.affiliation: University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio

paper.abstract: Estimating model performance without labeled data is important for deploying NLP systems across diverse domains. Prior work has proposed proxy measures based on distribution shift or predicted correctness, but it remains unclear whether these methods reliably preserve the ranking of domains, which is critical for model selection and risk triage. We study this problem from an ordinal perspective using a two-step framework that pairs a base classifier with an error predictor to estimate instance-level failures and disparities and aggregate them into label-free performance estimates. Across multiple sample sizes from the GeoOLID and Amazon Reviews datasets, large language model–based error predictors substantially outperform drift-based baselines in \rho and \tau rank correlations. We further show that lower absolute estimation error (RMSE) does not necessarily imply better ranking, highlighting the importance of evaluating ordinal consistency directly.WARNING: This paper contains offensive and hateful speech in the appendix.

paper.title: Persona Non Grata: LLM Persona-Driven Generations in MCQA are Unstable in Distinct Dimensions
paper.abstract: Persona-driven generations (PDGs) have seen prolific use in research and industry applications, where a large language model (LLM) takes on a “persona” while completing some task. While persona expressed through free-form text (like dialogue) has substantial work investigating stability or consistency, relatively, persona expressed in non-text-heavy outputs (like in multiple-choice question answering, or MCQA) is often overlooked. We work to address this gap, seeking to understand the instability of LLM PDGs in MCQA tasks. We develop three metrics investigating the performance, outcome, and question correctness stability, evaluating three distinct dimensions. Using these metrics, we find that instability varies consistently between model families and model size, and across question domains, with math/commonsense questions leading to greater instability. We also find task prompt format introduces more prediction instability than other hyperparameters, like temperature. Finally, we find that instability is related to task accuracy, and using our instability metrics, find different experimental settings that result in different best and worst personas for tasks, despite their similarity. This reveals the importance of checking hyperparameter instability in PDGs.

paper.title: Large Language Models Approach Expert Pedagogical Quality in Math Tutoring but Differ in Instructional and Linguistic Profiles
paper.abstract: Recent work has explored the use of large language models (LLMs) to generate tutoring responses in mathematics, yet it remains unclear how closely their instructional behavior aligns with expert human practice. We analyze a dataset of math remediation dialogues in which expert tutors, novice tutors, and seven LLMs of varying sizes, comprising both open-weight and commercial models, respond to the same student errors. We examine instructional strategies and linguistic characteristics of tutoring responses, including uptake (restating and revoicing), pressing for accuracy and reasoning, lexical diversity, readability, politeness, and agency. We find that expert tutors produce higher-quality responses than novices, and that larger LLMs generally receive higher pedagogical quality ratings than smaller models, approaching expert performance on average. However, LLMs exhibit systematic differences in their instructional profiles: they underuse discursive strategies characteristic of expert tutors while generating longer, more lexically diverse, and more polite responses. Regression analyses show that pressing for accuracy and reasoning, restating and revoicing, and lexical diversity, are positively associated with perceived pedagogical quality, whereas higher levels of agentic and polite language are negatively associated. These findings highlight the importance of analyzing instructional strategies and linguistic characteristics when evaluating tutoring responses across human tutors and intelligent tutoring systems.

paper.title: Text-Preserving Lossy Text Compression: A Study of Strategic Deletion and LLM Reconstruction
paper.abstract: Traditional lossless text compression preserves every byte, but its gains on natural language are often modest. We study lossy semantic text compression, where the encoder strategically deletes parts of the text and a large language model (LLM) reconstructs the original from the retained skeleton. We benchmark a progression of deletion strategies, from character-level and word-level rules driven by word length or corpus frequency to surprisal-based and hybrid rules that require a neural encoder, and reach three findings. First, deletion by corpus word frequency is a strong low-cost baseline: a static frequency lookup remains competitive with far more expensive semantic methods. Second, semantic and hybrid methods gain most at mild-to-moderate compression, whereas at the lowest retention rate frequency-based deletion matches them and keeps more named entities. Third, QLoRA fine-tuning yields a compact local decoder that, once adapted, is competitive with zero-shot Gemini 2.0 Flash. Additional English and Chinese experiments show that the framework transfers across domains, while the best deletion rule remains dataset-dependent.

paper.title: INMS: Memory Sharing for Large Language Model based Agents
paper.abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) based agents excel at complex tasks, their performance in open-ended scenarios is often constrained by isolated operation and reliance on static databases, missing the dynamic knowledge exchange of human dialogue. To bridge this gap, we propose the INteractive Memory Sharing (INMS) framework, an asynchronous interaction paradigm for multi-agent systems. By integrating real-time memory filtering, storage, and retrieval, INMS establishes a shared conversational memory pool. This enables continuous, dialogue-like memory sharing among agents, promoting collective self-enhancement and dynamically refining the retrieval mediator based on interaction history. Extensive experiments across three datasets demonstrate that INMS improves agent performance by effectively modeling multi-agent interaction and collective knowledge sharing.

paper.title: ATOD: An Evaluation Framework and Benchmark for Agentic Task-Oriented Dialogue Systems

author.affiliation: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and IEEE

paper.abstract: Agentic task-oriented dialogue (TOD) requires systems to track concurrent goals, dependencies, and long-horizon state. We examine goal-lifecycle recovery from fixed dialogue trajectories. ATOD contains 1,000 synthetic dialogues annotated for six advanced-TOD properties, and ATOD-Eval defines metrics for dependency-sensitive completion, memory recall, and proactivity. We implement a symbolic–vector memory evaluator for ATOD-Eval. Among five prompt-only predictors and six matched-backbone memory baselines, our evaluator is the only configuration above 90% in both goal detection F1 and conditional status accuracy on medium dialogues. On complex dialogues, no baseline exceeds it on both metrics; it has the highest conditional status accuracy within the memory-based block and the lowest measured per-turn latency. These experiments assess lifecycle tracking rather than interactive agent task success. A cross-family judge swap and a manual audit with 94.0% agreement provide initial checks on measurement reliability. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/amazon-science/ATOD.

paper.title: Embarrassingly Simple Access Control for Large Language Models

author.affiliation: University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio

paper.abstract: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is fundamental in secure systems handling healthcare, financial, and government data. Prior work on LLM safety under role constraints has largely relied on fine-tuning or prompting-based enforcement. In contrast, we take a mechanistic view and probe internal representations to identify signals associated with roles, permissions, and refusal behavior. We evaluate this approach across three datasets, database- and department-separated splits, varying policy complexity levels, and adversarial prompts. On the structured Text-to-SQL datasets, simple probes achieve strong performance, reaching average macro-F1 scores of .913 on BIRD and .926 on Spider, while remaining more stable than prompting as policies grow longer. However, probing does not perform equally well in all settings: it underperforms prompting in most OrgAccess comparisons and can degrade substantially under adversarial instructions. Overall, our results show that access-control information can be strongly represented in LLM hidden states, but its usefulness depends on the model, domain, and prompt.

paper.title: A Unified Ambiguity Signal for Calibrated Multimodal Emotion Recognition
paper.abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition (MER) in conversation is inherently ambiguous, as linguistic, acoustic, and visual cues may support multiple plausible interpretations. Existing approaches often treat ambiguity as prediction uncertainty rather than modeling its structured sources. We propose UAF, an ambiguity-aware framework for MER built around a single unified ambiguity signal. UAF estimates a normalized per-sample Model-based Ambiguity Degree (MAD) from the predicted emotion distribution by measuring its proximity to the maximally ambiguous uniform distribution, and uses it as a shared control signal rather than a post-hoc uncertainty score. This single scalar coordinates three parts of learning: it aligns representation radius with ambiguity, emphasizes ambiguous samples during optimization, and scales OT-based perturbation consistency. The fused evidence is organized into context, speaker, temporal, cross-modal, and residual subspaces that serve as the substrate on which this signal operates. Experiments on IEMOCAP, CMU-MOSEI, and MELD show that UAF yields consistently better calibration and high-ambiguity reliability alongside competitive accuracy and weighted-F1, showing that a single ambiguity signal can be an effective shared training signal for reliable MER

paper.title: MisconceptDialogue: Evaluation Criteria Shape Measured Success in LLM Math Tutoring

author.affiliation: Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute and University of Science and Technology
University of Science and Technology and Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute
University of Science and Technology and Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute

paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as math tutors, raising two questions: can a single LLM detect a student’s error, diagnose the underlying misconception, and remediate it through multi-turn dialogue—and can we trust the numbers that report how well it does? We address both with MisconceptDialogue, a fully automated framework that runs the full pipeline on five open-weight LLM tutors (7B–14B) interacting with LLM-simulated students over 5,000+ dialogues—a deliberately simulated protocol (paired conditions, a wrong-diagnosis control unsafe with real learners, scale) whose results do not establish real-student learning. On measurement, our headline finding is uncomfortable for the field: benchmark-style exact-match scoring common in standard math NLP—a lower-bound stress test—reports 42.1% measured Remediation Success Rate on identical dialogues where a human-calibrated LLM-as-judge reports 81.3%, a 39.2 percentage-point spread larger than the combined effects of tutor model, teaching strategy, and supplied diagnostic information. This is not a single-judge artifact: four independent LLM judges and 200 human annotations converge to within a few points (κ up to 0.91). On capability, the verdict is equally striking: the score barely changes whether we tell the tutor the student’s actual misconception or a deliberately swapped one—under the tested diagnosis-presentation format, these tutors show little evidence of reliably conditioning on the diagnostic information they are handed. For LLM tutoring evaluation to mature, multi-criterion scoring with multi-judge convergence and human anchoring should become standard practice—and the measurement question deserves as much scrutiny as the capability question it claims to answer.

paper.title: Tracing the Genesis of Logic: Causal Data Attribution of Mechanistic Features via Counterfactual Poisoning

author.affiliation: Prentis AI, Incept Labs, Forta and Titan Holdings

paper.abstract: How do interpretable internal features that implement a learned capability emerge during training? We present a mechanistic interpretability study of 3-digit addition in a 19M-parameter transformer trained from scratch, using the grokking transition as a natural microscope for feature genesis. Our framework, Causal Genesis Attribution (CGA), combines checkpoint-resolved training dynamics, Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature analysis, and counterfactual training interventions to trace arithmetic and carry features from emergence to causal function. We find layer-4 SAE features that are silent on non-arithmetic text, selective for the arithmetic probes, and co-emerge with validation accuracy at step 500 (near-zero to 85%). Zero-ablating the top arithmetic features drops exact-match accuracy from 100% to 0%, showing that these directions are necessary for the learned addition algorithm.
