A four-arm intervention study reveals what sustains these features: removing arithmetic data collapses feature activation by 81%; matched numeric-noise replacement also fails, ruling out surface token statistics; and poisoning answers by +137 hyperactivates features by 27% while making the model produce systematically shifted outputs. Across four seeds, the genesis detector fires consistently, with detection accuracy stable at 85.6% ± 1.0%. Together, these results provide a mechanistic data–feature–capability chain for an emergent arithmetic reasoning ability.

paper.title: Three Numbers and a Precondition: Auditing Multi-Source LLM Benchmarks for Source-Identity Leakage
paper.abstract: LLM benchmarks often pool rows from several sources (judges, retrieval configurations, training frameworks) and report one headline score. When label rates differ by source, a detector can earn that score by recognizing a row’s source, not its quality, and such a score is no promise about a new source. Our audit reports three AUCs of one detector: given features plus source (\mathrm{AUC}_\text{full}, the headline), features alone, and source alone. Their ratio L=\mathrm{AUC}_\text{source}/\mathrm{AUC}_\text{full} shows how close the source alone comes to the headline. The precondition: L is read only above a default floor, \mathrm{AUC}_\text{full}\geq 0.65, because two near-chance AUCs give a ratio near 1 although nothing leaks. On four RAGBench configurations (adherence rates 40.2% to 94.2%) the headline is 0.843 and the configuration label alone reaches 0.811 (L=0.96), above every per-query feature. When five LLM judges grade the same hard-math answers, L=0.84 looks similar, but the headline (0.594) fails the floor: judge identity predicts nothing. The floor, not L, separates the two panels. Six further audits with the floor and a 0.90 band on L frozen add the other outcomes, including a floor-passing panel whose source carries nothing.

paper.title: PatchHolmes: Agentic Patch Retrieval via Listwise Selection
paper.abstract: Patch retrieval, the task of finding the commit that fixes a known vulnerability, is the foundation of vulnerability management workflows, yet 60% to 63% of CVEs in the major advisory databases lack a patch link. We present PatchHolmes, a two-phase patch retrieval system that pairs a hybrid first-stage retriever with an agentic second-stage inspection loop. Unlike pointwise prior work that scores each candidate independently, the Phase 2 agent reads the top-100 listwise: it sees the full candidate list at once and selectively reads 3 to 10 commits through four budgeted tools before submitting a single best commit. On GitHubAD, PatchHolmes beats the pointwise binary classifier Favia by 25.34% Recall@1 and the retrieve-and-CoT baseline IRCoT by 31.40%, at one agent conversation per CVE versus Favia’s ten; with the candidate set held identical, the agent adds 27.32% Recall@1 over taking the retriever’s top candidate, and the same agent, transferred unchanged to PatchFinder_top10, lifts Recall@1 from PatchFinder’s own top-1 pick (24.28%) to 39.86%. Swapping the LLM backbone within the Qwen family changes Recall@1 by under 1%, and a second model family (gpt-oss) stays far above the no-agent floor, so the gain comes from the listwise agent loop; the entire system runs on a frozen open-weight model over a local Git repository, without fine-tuning or external search APIs.

paper.title: Schema-Key Wording as an Instruction Channel in Structured Generation under Constrained Decoding
paper.abstract: Constrained decoding is widely used to make large language models produce structured outputs that satisfy schemas such as JSON. Existing work mainly treats schemas as structural constraints, overlooking that schema-key tokens also enter the autoregressive context and may guide generation. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first systematic study of schema keys as an implicit instruction channel under constrained decoding. We formulate structured generation as a multi-channel instruction problem, where task signals can be placed in prompts, schema keys, or both. We further provide a projection-aware analysis that gives a sufficient condition under which an unconstrained expected-score advantage of an instructional key is preserved after grammar projection. Experiments on GSM8K and Math500 across seven language models show that changing only schema-key wording can substantially affect accuracy, with both positive and negative effects across models. Prompt-level and schema-level instructions also interact non-additively. The evidence is substantially stronger on GSM8K than on Math500. Our findings show that schema design is not merely output formatting, but part of instruction specification in structured generation.

paper.title: Anchored Turns: A Length-Driven Gradient in Chain-of-Thought Causal Necessity Across Multi-Turn Conversations

author.affiliation: BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science
Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology (KIIT) Bhubaneswar India
BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science

paper.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness is measured almost exclusively in single-turn settings, leaving open how the reasoning-trace-to-answer relationship evolves as conversations lengthen. We introduce turn-level CoT counterfactual deletion: at every assistant turn we regenerate the answer at five truncation levels of the current-turn thinking block under greedy decoding, and label a turn anchored—a descriptive label for causal redundancy of the trace, not a mechanistic claim—when all five regenerations agree on the same answer. Across 67 multi-turn sharded-GSM8K conversations from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the anchored fraction grows 3.9× from short (< 10 turns, 7.2%) to long (> 20 turns, 28.4%). Strict early < mid < late monotone ordering holds in five of seven reasoning models from three base families and four post-training pipelines (binomial sign test, p=0.002). A supplementary pooled GEE across all seven models converges on this direction (β=1.12, p=5.1×10⁻⁸, n=2,838 turn-level rows). A surface-feature predictor flags anchored turns at AUC= 0.71 (+0.07 over a length-only baseline) without additional generation, providing a cheap online signal for CoT monitors calibrated on short conversations. Single-turn CoT benchmarks, by construction, cannot detect this gradient.

paper.title: LKValues: Aligning Large Language Models with Sri Lankan Societal Values

author.affiliation: Tianjin University and Kunming University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Value alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has been shown to be culturally biased toward Western norms. This results in the mishandling of local values in multilingual societies such as Sri Lanka that have their unique cultural dynamics. Existing benchmarks overlook Sri Lankan-contextualized values in its official language Sinhala, hindering culturally sensitive evaluation and fine-tuning. To bridge this gap, we propose LKValues, the first survey-grounded resource suite for Sri Lankan value alignment. From a trilingual survey of 205 respondents, blending adapted global frameworks and LLM-elicited local constructs, we derive 40 majority-endorsed societal values. Using these values, we construct LKvaluesIT, a Sinhala-English news-derived instruction corpus containing 150K scenario-based instances, and LKvaluesBench, a value-sensitive evaluation benchmark of 1,000 instances. We evaluate a set of proprietary and open-weight LLMs with LKvaluesBench. We fine-tune three open-weight base models (Qwen3.5-4B-Base, Qwen3.5-9B-Base, and Aya-Expanse-8B-Base). Our experiments show that newer and larger LLMs still exhibit low-resource and cultural value-alignment gaps. LKValues fine-tuning improves Qwen-family models in English and Sinhala, reducing invalid outputs and cross-lingual disparities, though gains remain model-family dependent. These highlight LKValues’ efficacy in embedding Sri Lankan values, offering a replicable pipeline for low-resource, country-specific pluralist value alignment. The datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NextME14/LKValues.

paper.title: EcoStatKG: A Domain-Specific Statistical Knowledge Graph and Benchmark for Evaluating Numerical Hallucination in LLMs

author.affiliation: International Institute of Information Technology, Bangalore

paper.abstract: Large language models routinely produce numerical hallucinations—plausible but incorrect quantities, percentages, and statistics—yet existing benchmarks focus almost exclusively on entity-level factuality. We introduce EcoStatKG, a knowledge graph (KG) of 50,746 statistical triples and 306,231 structural triples from 6,871 Wikipedia articles on environmental sustainability, and NumHallu, a 500-question numerical benchmark grounded in held-out KG topics. We use these resources to diagnose how knowledge-base coverage affects eight retrieval strategies across six LLMs. In the full-index, oracle-coverage condition, simple cosine retrieval reaches 0.989 Numerical Exact Match (NEM), statistically indistinguishable from Graph RAG (0.992; paired-bootstrap p=0.14). In the deliberately constructed held-out condition, which removes answer-bearing triples, retrieval methods fall below the zero-shot baseline (0.506 NEM), exposing the risk that topically related numerical distractors can override parametric knowledge. Similarity-threshold filtering restores KG Cosine to near-baseline performance (0.511), rather than establishing a new state-of-the-art. A bounded clinical-domain proof of concept reproduces the coverage and distractor patterns. The contribution is a diagnostic study and resource: its results clarify when numerical retrieval helps, when missing coverage can make it harmful, and why confidence gating is best viewed as damage control.

paper.title: Automatic Evaluation of Mental Health Stigma in Online Communication

author.affiliation: University of Melbourne, University of Melbourne and University of Melbourne

paper.abstract: Mental health stigma has profoundly harmful impacts but its complexity makes it difficult to evaluate. Stigma may involve explicit derogation, but also subtler forms of blame, fear, paternalistic pity, social distancing, structural exclusion, and discrimination. We introduce a theory-grounded benchmark for automatic evaluation of mental health stigma in online communication, consisting of naturally occurring online news and social media text annotated with a fine-grained taxonomy of stigma across multiple mental health conditions. Our annotation framework comprises a binary stigma-detection task and a multi-level taxonomy covering (i) stigma mode, (ii) domain, and (iii) specific components of certain forms of stigma. We apply this framework to texts mentioning six mental health conditions and evaluate large language models alongside stigma-related classifiers for detecting sentiment, toxicity, and hate speech. Results show that mental health stigma is not well captured by models trained to detect these neighboring constructs, and that LLMs often overpredict stigma unless given explicit operational rules - mirroring the importance of decision rules in human annotation

paper.title: Domain Knowledge Annealing: A Structured Local-to-Global Paradigm for Constructing Expert LLMs
paper.abstract: Expertise in vertical domains requires more than exposing LLMs to vast corpora; it demands the systematic learning of complex logic. Standard fine-tuning often treats data as an unstructured collection, failing to capture the dependencies needed for high-level reasoning. We propose Domain Knowledge Annealing (DKA), a curriculum learning paradigm designed to improve domain proficiency. Inspired by physical annealing, DKA organizes training from local to global: it starts by injecting discrete concepts via entity-centric samples and progressively advances to synthesizing complex, inter-document relationships. This progression allows the model to integrate isolated facts into a coherent knowledge system. Experiments on Linguistics and Law benchmarks show that DKA outperforms standard strategies, achieving state-of-the-art results among comparably sized models in domain-specific reasoning.

paper.title: The Geometry of Uncertainty in Language Model Representations
paper.abstract: Hidden-state probes have been used to predict factual errors in language-model outputs. We study whether the same representations also distinguish four types of prompt-model relationship: known, unknown, ambiguous, and misleading (built on a false premise). On a controlled 200-prompt dataset constructed to balance six surface features, all six pairwise type contrasts are linearly recoverable from hidden states at the position where generation begins, at AUROC \geq 0.986 on three open-weight instruction-tuned models spanning two families and a fourfold parameter range. The probe exceeds surface-feature, TF-IDF, and frozen sentence-embedding baselines on every pair. Under group-aware evaluation on paraphrased prompts with group-level shuffled controls, probe AUROC remains at least 0.949 on every pair while lexical baselines degrade. These findings frame hallucination as one downstream consequence of a four-type representational structure that also captures ambiguity and false premises.

paper.title: Language Models Detokenize, But Only for Themselves

author.affiliation: University of Washington and University of Washington, Seattle

paper.abstract: Language models often appear to become insensitive to how text is tokenized. Models trained with different tokenizers can reach similar language-modeling loss, and prior work shows that they recover word-level information from the raw subword segmentations (a phenomenon referred to as "detokenization"). This raises a natural question: once that information has been recovered, do the resulting hidden states become independent of the tokenizer that produced them? We study this using *tokenizer twins*, pairs of models matched in architecture, training data, and random seed but trained with different tokenizers. We learn small translators between their hidden states at positions where the two tokenizers agree, and then test the same mapping where their tokenization paths differ. Transfer works well at agreement positions, adding less than one nat of loss, but breaks sharply at disagreement positions, where the loss increases by more than seven nats. This gap appears from the first hidden layer and persists through the network. At the same time, word-identity probes can still recover much of the underlying content from these representations. In other words, language models can abstract beyond their individual subword tokens while still carrying a lasting imprint of how the text was tokenized.

paper.title: PAIRSAFE: Proxy-Resistant Paired Safety Evaluation for Refusal Boundaries
paper.abstract: Aggregate refusal scores on mixed safe and unsafe prompts can obscure local boundary failures and label-correlated metadata shortcuts. We present PAIRSAFE, Proxy-Resistant Paired Safety Evaluation, a score-agnostic diagnostic protocol built from 150 deterministic, matched XSTest-derived safe/unsafe pairs. PAIRSAFE distinguishes strict pair locks from audited residual fields, then asks whether nuisance proxies collapse, unsafe twins rank above safe twins, and one threshold yields pair-consistent decisions; generated behavior is evaluated separately. Strict source, normalized-type, and pair-ID controls collapse to PSA 0.50 and PCDA 0.00, as required by construction. Residual metadata remain informative: a leakage-safe combined probe obtains nested Cal-PCDA 0.397, yet residualizing model scores against measured metadata leaves substantial paired signal. Direct-logit margins for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct reach PSA/Cal-PCDA of 0.987/0.880 and 0.973/0.760, respectively. Qwen’s secondary generation check is lower again (PCGA 0.700). These disagreements show why local ranking, shared-threshold decisions, and generated responses should not be collapsed into one score. PAIRSAFE is a bounded diagnostic protocol, not a new classifier or deployment certificate.

paper.title: KaiToM: A Benchmark for Culturally Informed Theory-of-Mind in Thai Context
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show impressive reasoning capabilities, yet their understanding of culturally specific social dynamics remains limited. We present KaiToM, a Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmark for Thai cultural contexts, focusing on Kreng-Jai, a uniquely Thai concept of social reluctance and consideration. Extending TactfulToM, we construct 882 conversations (39.2K questions) spanning three Kreng-Jai dimensions: White Lies, Avoidance of Confrontation, and Fear-Based Respect. To disentangle language proficiency from cultural knowledge, the dataset includes Thai scenarios at varying cultural depths, general English scenarios, and English translations of Thai content. We evaluate Thai-specialized (Typhoonv2.1, SEA-LION-v3), open-weight (Gemma-3, DeepSeek-V3.2, Kimi-K2, Qwen), and proprietary models (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5.1, Gemini-3-Flash). Models achieve only moderate performance, struggle with Fear-Based Respect, and cannot reliably identify specific Kreng-Jai types, a failure shared by Thai-specialized models. Human evaluation shows that native speakers significantly outperform models on culturally loaded tasks. Performance also degrades in deep relative to surface-level cultural contexts, and generalist models often perform better on English translations than on the original Thai, suggesting that models capture surface cues but lack deeper cultural alignment. KaiToM supports the development of culturally aware systems for low-resource languages. Code is available at https://github.com/Augustus2011/KAI-ToM.

paper.title: Diagnosing Prompt Sensitivity and Interaction Instability in LLM-Based Humor Judgment
paper.abstract: Humor judgment is subjective and often depends on ambiguity, expectation violation, and contextual reinterpretation, so the reliability of an LLM judge cannot be assessed from final detection performance alone. Existing LLM-based humor research and LLM-as-a-Judge studies largely focus on final performance, generation quality, or agreement with human evaluation, leaving prompt sensitivity and rebuttal robustness in subjective judgment tasks relatively underexplored. This paper analyzes how prompt design, structured interpretation, and user rebuttals shape LLM-based humor judgment. In zero-shot sentence-only judgments, models with similar F1 scores show substantially different FPR–FNR values, shifting between over-accepting and under-predicting humor depending on prompt formulation. Few-shot examples partially reduce these directional fluctuations, but their effects remain model-dependent. We further propose the Incongruity-Resolution Judgment framework, which compares a humor-supporting interpretation with a counter interpretation before producing a final judgment. Rather than uniformly improving performance, this framework serves as a diagnostic structure for examining how competing interpretations reshape model judgment behavior. Finally, explicit user rebuttals show that high initial performance does not guarantee robustness, highlighting the need to evaluate judgment persistence, directional error patterns, and interaction-level judgment trajectories.

paper.title: WiC is Not WSD: A Study on LLMs and Lexical Ambiguity Resolution

author.affiliation: Cardiff University, TeIAS and University of Cambridge

paper.abstract: Word-in-Context (WiC) remains challenging for language models, despite recent progress on lexical-semantic tasks. We hypothesise that this difficulty arises not only from comparing two contextual uses of a word, but also from the absence of an explicit sense inventory that specifies the relevant level of semantic granularity. We evaluate open LLMs on WiC and traditional Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) under similar settings. We find that providing candidate senses, similar to what is done in traditional WSD, improves WiC performance in all settings. In general, explicit sense information helps models make more consistent and targeted judgements. Human evaluation further shows that many apparent WiC errors reflect label ambiguity or mismatches between model and annotator sense boundaries rather than simple failures of lexical understanding. In particular, results show that LLMs overthink the sense distinction often leading to errors based on overly fine-grained distinctions.

paper.title: MM-NeuroOnco: A Multimodal Benchmark and Instruction Dataset for MRI-Based Brain Tumor Diagnosis

author.affiliation: Guangdong Institute of Intelligence Science and Technology, Zhuhai, China

paper.abstract: Brain tumor MRI diagnosis requires models not only to identify lesions but also to perform fine-grained medical reasoning based on imaging modality, tumor location, and key imaging findings. However, existing medical multimodal datasets often lack structured diagnostic semantics, and closed-ended evaluations may overestimate model ability due to option cues or elimination shortcuts. To address this issue, we introduce MM-NeuroOnco, a large-scale multimodal instruction dataset and benchmark for brain tumor MRI diagnostic reasoning, containing 24,726 MRI slices from 20 public data sources and approximately 200,000 multimodal instructions grounded in imaging evidence. We develop a multi-model collaborative pipeline for semantic completion and quality control, which supplements original tumor labels and segmentation masks with key diagnostic attributes, and further construct MM-NeuroOnco-Bench with a no-LLM-inference policy for ground-truth labels. The benchmark adds a “None of the above” option to closed-ended questions to reduce evaluation bias caused by option shortcuts. Experiments show that existing general-purpose and medical-specialist multimodal large models remain limited on this task, with the strongest baseline achieving only 41.88% accuracy on diagnosis-related questions. Fine-tuning on MM-NeuroOnco yields NeuroOnco-GPT, achieving a 27% absolute accuracy improvement and demonstrating the effectiveness of our dataset in enhancing fine-grained multimodal medical reasoning. Code and dataset documentation are available at https://github.com/gfnnnb/MM-NeuroOnco.

paper.title: MGSM-Pro: A Simple Strategy for Robust Multilingual Mathematical Reasoning Evaluation

author.affiliation: McPherson University and University of Ibadan

paper.abstract: Large language models have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning. However, benchmark development for multilingual evaluation has lagged behind English in both difficulty and recency. Recently, GSM-Symbolic showed a strong evidence of high variance when models are evaluated on different instantiations of the same question; however, the evaluation was conducted only in English. In this paper, we introduce MGSM-Pro, an extension of MGSM dataset with GSM-Symbolic approach. Our dataset provides five instantiations per MGSM question by varying names, digits and irrelevant context. Evaluations across nine languages reveal that many low-resource languages suffer large performance drops when tested on digit instantiations different from those in the original test set. We further find that models robustness in HRL setting do not necessarily translate to LRL. Moreover, proprietary models, such as Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-4.1 are less robust to digit, whereas Gemini 3.0 Pro is more robust. Among open models, GPT-OSS 120B and DeepSeek v3 show stronger robustness. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating each problem using at least five digit-varying instantiations to obtain a more robust and realistic assessment of math reasoning.

paper.title: IndicIFEval: A Benchmark for Verifiable Instruction-Following Evaluation in 14 Indic Languages

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology, Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology and AI4Bharat

Department of Computer Science, Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, Indian Institute of Technology, Madras and National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT), National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Instruction-following benchmarks remain predominantly English-centric, leaving a critical evaluation gap for the hundreds of millions of Indic language speakers. We introduce IndicIFEval, a benchmark evaluating constrained generation of LLMs across 14 Indic languages using automatically verifiable, rule-based instructions. It comprises around 800 human-verified examples per language spread across two complementary subsets: IndicIFEval-Trans, translated prompts from IFEval carefully localized for Indic contexts, and IndicIFEval-Ground, synthetically generated instructions grounded in native Indic content. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of major open-weight and proprietary models spanning both reasoning and non-reasoning models. While models maintain strong adherence to formatting constraints, they struggle significantly with lexical and cross-lingual tasks – and despite progress in high-resource languages, instruction-following across the broader Indic family lags significantly behind English. We release IndicIFEval and its evaluation scripts to support progress on multilingual constrained generation.

paper.title: Rethinking Cross-Modal Attention for Visual Token Pruning in Multimodal LLMs
paper.abstract: Recent studies challenge the reliability of cross-modal attention mechanisms as an indicator for visual token pruning in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). In this work, we demonstrate that such negative conclusions can be substantially influenced by an overlooked phenomenon termed task-bound coupling, wherein cross-modal attention patterns become entangled with task-specific prompts. Through controlled configurations that decouple visual inputs from downstream queries, we observe that attention distributions can be relatively consistent across the evaluated settings. Concurrently, we identify an empirical scaling phenomenon which we term Attention Fidelity Decay, where the downstream effectiveness of attention maps exhibits semantic dilution in higher-capacity models or advanced architectures. Motivated by these insights, we introduce TAP-LLaVA, a simple training-free framework that leverages localized task-agnostic attention for efficient, reusable visual token pruning across multi-turn sessions. Our approach achieves competitive downstream performance while substantially lowering computational overhead. This suggests that attention can provide a reliable structural prior at moderate model scales when isolated from textual confounders.

paper.title: Corrective Feedback-Driven Humor Generation for Tiny Language Models
paper.abstract: Humor generation remains a challenging problem for language models due to its subjective, creative, and culturally sensitive nature. While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generative capabilities, their deployment is often constrained by computational cost. We propose a lightweight, corrective feedback-driven framework in which a compact generator (GPT-2, 140M parameters) produces punchlines under the guidance of an LLM acting as a critic. Unlike traditional knowledge distillation, our method leverages the LLM as a feedback provider rather than a teacher to be mimicked, enabling the student model to iteratively refine its outputs through corrective supervision. We systematically evaluate multiple LLMs (LLaMA3-8B, Qwen3-8B and Mistral-7B) as guides under different strategies, including frozen and learnable configurations, to study their impact on humor quality and diversity. To support responsible humor generation, we curate a high-quality setup–punchline dataset from Reddit and explicitly filter out harmful content. Experimental results show that corrective feedback-guided training substantially improves humor quality, fluency, and diversity over standard fine-tuning and knowledge distillation baselines, while preserving the efficiency of compact models. We observe that, among the evaluated guides, Mistral-7B consistently provides particularly strong guidance on the curated joke dataset. Our code and resources are available at: https://github.com/Ramakrishna176420/Corrective-Feedback-Driven-Humor-Generation-for-Tiny-Language-Models.

paper.title: REMIND: Enhancing CoT Reliability with Self-Supervised Introspection
paper.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, CoT can also produce fluent but logically flawed reasoning chains that make incorrect answers appear more reliable. In this work, we introduce REMIND (Reliability Enhancement via Metacognitive INtrospection and Debiasing), a framework that enables LLMs to learn from their own failures via episodic memory. Unlike standard error-correction methods that rely on external feedback or extensive fine-tuning, REMIND leverages a self-supervised introspection cycle. We first isolate epistemic failure—instances where CoT decreases model confidence despite yielding incorrect results. The model then performs structured introspection to diagnose the root cause and synthesizes a reusable natural language lesson. These lessons are stored in a vector database and retrieved during future inference steps to correct similar future errors. Experiments on eight diverse reasoning benchmarks spanning mathematical, scientific, multi-hop, truthfulness, and commonsense reasoning demonstrate that REMIND significantly improves reliability by effectively converting past CoT failures into actionable insights for unseen problems. Codes are available in https://github.com/newcodevelop/REMIND.

paper.title: DeepVision-103K: A Visually Diverse, Broad-Coverage, and Verifiable Mathematical Dataset for Multimodal Reasoning

author.affiliation: Alibaba Group US and University of California, Los Angeles

paper.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been shown effective in enhancing the visual reflection and reasoning capabilities of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). However, existing datasets are predominantly derived from either small-scale manual construction or recombination of prior resources, which limits data diversity and coverage, thereby constraining further gains in model performance. To this end, we introduce DeepVision-103K, a comprehensive dataset for RLVR training that covers diverse K12 mathematical topics, extensive knowledge points, and rich visual elements. Models trained on DeepVision achieve strong performance on multimodal mathematical benchmarks, and generalize effectively to general multimodal reasoning tasks. Further analysis reveals enhanced visual perception, reflection and reasoning capabilities in trained models, validating DeepVision’s effectiveness for advancing multimodal reasoning.

paper.title: SurgAgents: A Multi-agent Framework for Embodied Cataract Surgical Intent Prediction
paper.abstract: Predicting next surgical phase, viewed as a form of surgical procedural intent, with high accuracy is essential for robotic real-time surgical systems. Previous approaches struggle with short-term dynamics, occlusions, and phase persistence; end-to-end large vision-language models (LVLMs) can reason from visual inputs but often fail to exploit structured temporal observations. Thus, we introduce SurgAgents, a multi-agent framework for embodied surgical intent prediction. SurgAgents decomposes prediction into specialized agents: (1) a ResNet-based single-frame classifier agent extracts per-frame phase information; (2) a YOLO-based instrument specialist agent extracts per-frame instrument sets; (3) a history descriptor agent composes these facts into frame-level descriptions; (4) a history summarizer agent compresses long histories into a compact temporal narrative; (5) a phase predictor agent assembles the narrative and the current frame into a formatted LVLM prompt; (6) a retrieval agent with a confidence-gated Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module selectively retrieves similar case patterns when prediction confidence is low. On Cataract-1K, SurgAgents attains 46.54% macro-F1 with GPT-4o, outperforming the baseline, with systematic ablation studies showing that each agent materially contributes to performance. Latency measurements demonstrate feasibility for robotic real-time surgical support during surgery procedures.

paper.title: GROWTHEVAL: Evaluating Stage-Conditioned Developmental Realism in Role-Playing LLMs
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as role-playing dialogue agents in long-horizon applications such as tutoring, companionship, and narrative interaction, where users may expect stable persona consistency as well as plausible stage-conditioned change. Existing evaluations emphasize static persona fidelity, temporal factuality, or isolated social skills, but rarely test whether role-playing models produce coherent developmental differentiation across ordered stages. We introduce GROWTHEVAL, a psychology-inspired diagnostic framework for assessing stage-conditioned developmental realism in single-turn, stage-isolated role-playing responses. Using stage-conditioned scenarios and multi-axis scoring, GrowthEval evaluates cross-stage patterns in developmental appropriateness, role-play coherence, and canon fidelity across five socio-emotional dimensions. Across the evaluated LLMs, we observe a model-tiered empirical pattern: higher-capacity models respond more consistently to stage conditioning but can over-mature at early stages, whereas lower-capacity models exhibit flatter and weakly differentiated profiles. Reliability and robustness analyses provide evidence for the stability of these findings. Overall, the evaluated LLMs only partially realize coherent, stage-appropriate developmental change. GROWTHEVAL provides an extensible diagnostic framework for analyzing stage-conditioned behavioral differentiation and associated failure modes in single-turn role-playing responses.

paper.title: S^4R: Selective Sampling, Subspaces, and Sparse Reconstruction for Compressed Long-Context KV Caching
paper.abstract: The growth of context window lengths in Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly enhances their long-context capabilities but incurs prohibitive memory costs due to the Key-Value (KV) cache. Although low-rank compression of KV cache is a promising remedy, existing methods face a dilemma: offline approaches depend on external calibration data, whereas online approaches incur substantial compute for full-prompt decomposition and reconstruction. In this paper, we propose **S^4R**, which builds low-rank subspaces from selectively sampled tokens and computes attention over a sparsely reconstructed KV representation. S^4R uses prompt-aware initialization to build initial key/value bases from a representative prompt subset, trading off calibration-data dependence against prefilling cost. Because fully reconstructing the cache at every decoding step is prohibitively expensive and hurts throughput, we further adopt sparse reconstruction to retain only informative positions during decoding. Extensive experiments on LongBench and RULER with Llama and Qwen model families show that S^4R achieves up to 5x KV compression with near full-cache accuracy, combining the efficiency of fixed compression with the adaptability of prompt-dependent methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Draconis98/S4R

paper.title: QUILT: Query–User Interaction Linguistic Taxonomy
paper.abstract: Large language models are used by people with very different expertise levels, but existing work studies what users ask more than who is asking. We introduce QUILT (Query User Interaction Linguistic Taxonomy) , a two-dimensional framework that jointly characterizes LLM conversations by task type and user expertise level. Applying QUILT to 3,000 WildChat dialogues, we construct the first large-scale corpus linking expertise level to task-level interaction patterns in open-ended LLM conversations. Corpus analysis reveals clear expertise-dependent asymmetries: debugging queries are strongly associated with expert users, novice users rarely engage in reasoning-intensive tasks, and expert queries are substantially longer across all task types. These patterns are statistically significant and recoverable by automatic classifiers, indicating that expertise differences are systematically reflected in conversational language. Together, QUILT and the QUILT Corpus provide an empirical foundation for studying user heterogeneity in LLM interaction and for developing expertise-aware response strategies.

paper.title: VERGE: Verification-Enhanced Generation of Multi-Hop Evaluation Datasets for Task-Specific RAG
paper.abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on custom knowledge bases requires task-specific benchmarks of multi-chunk evidence synthesis, yet most existing generation pipelines apply quality control only after the full question set has been solved. We present VERGE, which moves quality control inside the generation loop: a verification agent targets, per item and without an external solver pass, an operational multi-chunk criterion and a QA-integrity criterion, refining items that fail and discarding those it cannot repair. From 11,052 candidates across six domains, VERGE yields 2,854 verified multiple-choice items targeting aggregation- and comparison-style synthesis over topically coherent evidence. We contribute a method-agnostic validation protocol — exhaustive strict-subset ablation, chunk-removal ablation, format-unconfounded open-ended re-evaluation, and inter-chunk-similarity stratification — and use it to localise where the multi-chunk dependence holds. On a stratified sample (n = 250), 69.8% of items not answerable closed-book cannot be answered from any strict subset of their supporting chunks (strict-necessity violation rate 15.2%). A human annotation study finds the verifier reliable (Cohen’s \kappa = 0.903) and VERGE items higher in QA integrity and distractor quality than the closest prior method (p < 0.001).

paper.title: Encoded but Not Decoded: Layer-Localized Evidence for a Three-Level Gap in LLM Syntax
paper.abstract: A language model can fail a syntactic test in two distinct ways: by not encoding the relevant structure, or by encoding it but failing to use it at the output. Behavioral evaluation alone cannot tell these apart. We propose a three-level evaluation framework (behavioral deployment, LM-head readout, and probe recoverability) measured on the same items under the same binary decision. Using a compact trilingual (English, Chinese, German) control-dependency benchmark, we find that probe recoverability exceeds or equals LM-head readout, which in turn exceeds or equals behavioral deployment, across seven models and all three languages in the aggregate. The recoverability surplus is never negative across all 14 (model, task) conditions. The disconnect concentrates in subject-control, where a nearest-noun heuristic gives the wrong answer. The single largest gap (0.653) appears on Qwen3-0.6B Instruct in question answering. The gap persists at Qwen3-14B Instruct. Instruction tuning degrades deployment more than encoding in percentage terms. We rule out option-position bias, late-layer erasure, output-formatting artifacts, and probe-training variance. The pattern is consistent with decoding that favors surface shortcuts, and the behavior-probe gap measures the strength of that preference. Activation patching shows the gap is layer-localized. Under instruction tuning, the LM-head-decoded layer shifts approximately ten layers later than the probe-decoded layer. These findings argue that behavioral evaluation understates what models encode, while probing alone overstates what they deploy.

paper.title: Memorization or Extraction? Auditing LLM-Based Recovery of Scientific Assumptions
paper.abstract: We audit whether benchmarks for LLM-based recovery of scientific assumptions measure corpus-grounded extraction or pretraining memorization. Using author-defined targets for 10 historical AI breakthroughs (frozen 4-case protocol plus 6 post-hoc stress cases) and a "field-wide paradigmatic assumption" prompt, GPT-4o’s top-10 extractions cover the target in 6/10 cases under a generous any-of-top-K criterion—an upper bound that a 10-rater study corroborates for only {\sim}0.19 of sampled top-ranked pairs (human–rule \kappa{=}0.70, \alpha{=}0.634). Controlled stress tests structure the diagnosis: a no-corpus control (field name only) still scores 4/4 on the primary shifts (memorization dominates), while a wrong-corpus control collapses to 0/12 across all 4{\times}3 cross-pairings (corpus can be causally read); a five-LLM canonical sweep (GPT-4o 4/4, Qwen 2/4, Claude 1/4, Llama-3.1 1/4, Mistral 0/4) shows the gap is model-specific rather than closed-vs-open, with format compliance a major but not fully isolable contributor; a Min-K% Prob cross-check actually mis-ranks synthetic non-members as more contaminated than real pre-shift papers, motivating the behavioral framing; and synthetic/niche controls are mixed (causal in 1 of 3 synthetic scenarios, one shows corpus harm). We release an audit kit — five factorable controls (no-corpus, wrong-corpus, pair-level precision, {\geq}2-LLM, multi-seed; {\sim}\$15) — as a reusable benchmark-validity probe, with all artifacts released.

paper.title: CAFE: Caption-Anchored Feature Enrichment and Evidence Routing for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
paper.abstract: Multimodal sarcasm detection aims to identify sarcasm in image-text posts by capturing how visual content changes the interpretation of short informal text. Existing methods have advanced the task through multimodal fusion, caption-based cues, and fact/sentiment incongruity modeling, but their evidence use is often controlled inside latent feature channels or reduced discrepancy scores. This makes it difficult to decide which visual information should be selectively weighted for a particular post. We propose CAFE, a caption-anchored feature enrichment and evidence routing framework that decides how to use visual evidence for each sample under ambiguity. CAFE enriches each image with two generated descriptions, one for visible facts and one for the image-text relation, then estimates how useful each description is for the current post and fuses caption-calibrated contrast evidence with direct cross-modal evidence for prediction. Experiments show that CAFE achieves state-of-the-art performance on the primary MMSD2.0 benchmark with 87.81+/-0.33% F1 (mean over 5 seeds). Component ablations on the original MMSD provide an additional evaluation.

paper.title: How Far Do Auto-Interpretation Labels Generalize: A Controlled Study Across Languages, Scripts, and Rewordings
paper.abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are increasingly used to interpret language models, with auto-generated natural-language labels serving as the primary interface for understanding what each feature represents. We ask whether these labels generalize: does a feature labeled for a concept actually track that concept across languages and scripts? Using Serbian digraphia as a controlled testbed—the same language written in both Latin and Cyrillic via deterministic transliteration—we first find that SAE feature sets activated by the same content in different languages, scripts, and wordings share substantial overlap (mean Jaccard 0.39 vs. 0.13 random baseline, peaking at 0.57), suggesting genuine cross-lingual semantic features. We then test whether auto-interpretation labels keep pace. They often do not: features whose labels describe semantic content miss the same meaning in Serbian up to 4\times more often than within English, and miss Serbian Cyrillic more than Serbian Latin—two scripts that are deterministic transliterations of each other. The gap grows with network depth, yet the labels give no indication that they fail. These results suggest that auto-interpretation labels reflect a feature’s behavior on the languages and scripts a model has seen most in training, rather than the concept itself.

paper.title: The Limits of Simulated Societies: How LLM Alignment Erases Cross-Cultural Variance
paper.abstract: Using large language models (LLMs) to simulate diverse human populations promises to transform computational social science. However, the accuracy of these simulations remains unclear because current evaluations prioritize predicting an average response over capturing the rich diversity of opinions within real human groups. Here, we develop a diagnostic framework measuring both accuracy and viewpoint retention across 10,000 respondent-question pairs from the World Values Survey, spanning twelve countries and six continents. By evaluating nine LLMs across four alignment paradigms (zero-shot, SFT, DPO, GRPO) against ground-truth human responses, we identify a failure mode we term consensus collapse. While training alignment improves point accuracy, we find that it compresses the range of outputs toward a single demographic stereotype. The highest-performing model (Tulu 3 70B DPO, 57.9% accuracy) retains only 50% of real human variance (σr = 0.50). We demonstrate this collapse is within the models’ underlying parameters rather than decoding procedures; temperature scaling up to T = 1.0 alters fewer than 3.7% of predictions. Furthermore, this diversity loss is inequitable, erasing significantly more variation for Global South populations like Nigeria (σr = 0.11) and Ethiopia (σr = 0.16) compared to Western democracies (σr = 0.70–0.87), with accuracy-rewarded GRPO unable to reverse this effect. While mixing an aligned model with an unaligned prior partially mitigates the collapse (reducing W1 from 0.55 to 0.52), substantial gaps remain (Nigeria recovering from σr = 0.14 to 0.47). Ultimately, we find that modern AI alignment methods trade distributional diversity for point accuracy, challenging existing assumptions for using LLMs as substitutes for human populations. Yet, by exposing the mechanics of this collapse, our work provides insight for future methods designed to value and preserve diverse human viewpoints.

paper.title: LLM-Ideoplasticity: Measuring Ideological Plasticity in the Political Behavior of LLMs as a Context-Conditioned Distribution
paper.abstract: We argue, with systematic empirical evidence, that a large language model’s political ideology is not a fixed point, but a *conditional distribution* \mathbb{P}(position\midcontext) over a real political space. We evaluate nine current LLMs using a unified measurement framework anchored by VAA–CHES projection models, which map responses onto three validated dimensions (*lrgen*, *lrecon*, *galtan*) across six contextual axes. Our findings reveal high sensitivity to context: persuasive framing and under-represented languages displace coordinates by up to 0.57 and 0.52 units, respectively, while chain-of-thought reasoning often amplifies rather than dampens paraphrase instability. Despite this local plasticity, the model cohort occupies a remarkably narrow Overton envelope overall, occupying roughly one-third the spread of major European parties. Supported by a multi-trait multi-method (MTMM) analysis, we conclude that a single point cannot summarize LLM political behavior; it must be characterized as a shape. Our code and data are publicly available.

paper.title: ProMoral-Bench: Comparing Prompting Strategies for Moral Judgment and Jailbreak Robustness in LLMs

author.affiliation: Algoverse AI Research and Algoverse AI Research

paper.abstract: Prompt design affects the moral judgments and refusal behavior produced by large language models (LLMs), yet controlled comparisons remain fragmented across datasets and models. We introduce ProMoral-Bench, a benchmark-style comparison of 10 prompting paradigms across four LLM families. Using ETHICS, Scruples, WildJailbreak, and our 200-pair ETHICS-Contrast set, we report task-level metrics together with Moral Competence Score (MCS), jailbreak/over-refusal Safety Robustness Score (SRS), and Unified Moral Safety Score (UMSS). UMSS is a study-specific relative summary of MCS and SRS, not an absolute measure of model safety or moral grounding. In this fixed-template evaluation, compact exemplar-guided scaffolds attain stronger competence-robustness trade-offs at lower token cost than the particular multi-stage variants tested, although multi-stage prompting occasionally improves jailbreak refusal. The few-shot demonstrations are non-overlapping but drawn from the evaluation distributions, so their advantage should not be read as out-of-distribution robustness. Code and data are available at https://github.com/rohanthomas334-sketch/ProMoral_Bench.

paper.title: Enhancing Safety Alignment by Universal Adversarial Prompts
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities but remain susceptible to adversarial attacks aimed at eliciting harmful responses. Current defense mechanisms, while partially effective, often compromise the models’ performance on benign tasks. To address this issue, we propose a novel two-stage framework to enhance LLM robustness against adversarial attacks. Initially, we train a universal adversarial prompt designed to align the hidden representations of harmful inputs with benign ones, effectively emulating adversarial attack patterns. Subsequently, we utilize this soft prompt to augment training data, strengthening the model’s capability to reject harmful content. We conduct extensive evaluations to empirically demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods such as Circuit Breaker (CB) and Deliberative Alignment SFT (DSFT), achieving average defense rate of 96.4% on llama3-8b-instruct model, compared to CB (90.6%) and DSFT (87.9%).

paper.title: Effects of Theory of Mind and Prosocial Beliefs on Steering Human-Aligned Behaviors of LLMs in Ultimatum Games

author.affiliation: Australian National University and Singapore Management University

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in simulating human behaviors and performing theory-of-mind (ToM) reasoning, crucial for complex social interactions. We investigate ToM reasoning’s role in aligning agentic behaviors with human norms in negotiation tasks, using the ultimatum game as our referenced task. We initialized LLM agents with different prosocial beliefs (Greedy, Fair, Selfless) and reasoning methods (chain of thought and ToM reasoning of varying levels), examining their decision-making processes and outcomes across multiple LLMs, including reasoning models like o3-mini and DeepSeek-R1 Distilled Qwen 32B. We perform 2,700 simulations to show that ToM reasoning enhances behavioral alignment with human norms, decision-making consistency, and negotiation outcomes. Consistent with prior findings, reasoning LLMs exhibit limited capability compared to ToM-enhanced LLMs, with different game roles benefiting from different ToM orders.Fair proposers and responders accepting offers were the most consistent with their strategic reasonings, whereas all agents showed strong consistencies with human beliefs when rejecting offers, except when the offer was fair. Human verification further revealed that Llama 3.3 70B produces reasoning most consistent with its actions and beliefs. Our findings advance understanding of ToM’s role in human-AI interaction and cooperative decision-making. The code used for our experiments can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/UltimatumToM.

paper.title: From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models
paper.abstract: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.

paper.title: Edit Policy-Aligned Text Simplification

author.affiliation: Osaka University, Tokyo Institute of Technology
RIKEN, Institute of Science Tokyo and AIST, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Text simplification aims to modify documents and sentences to make them easier to read and understand while preserving their meanings. Different applications require distinct simplification policies, e.g., lexical-oriented simplification and overall rewriting while trading off detail for simplicity. However, achieving such policy-driven control remains an open challenge. In this work, we introduce a simple yet powerful approach that leverages Large Language Model-as-a-Judge (LLM-Judge) to automatically construct policy-aligned training data, removing the need for costly human annotation or parallel corpora. Our method enables the construction of simplification models that adapt to diverse simplification policies at both the sentence and document levels. Remarkably, small-scale open-source LLMs match or surpass GPT-5, as verified by both automatic metrics and edit analysis. The consistent improvements across model families and sizes demonstrate the robustness of our approach.

paper.title: Do LLM Embedding Spaces Recover Expert Structure? Evidence from Mental-Health Language
paper.abstract: Pretrained text embeddings are increasingly used as representational maps, yet high category separability does not imply that their geometry recovers expert-defined structure. We study this problem in mental-health-related language, where symptom relations provide an external reference and online communities introduce strong domain, affective, stylistic, and discourse confounds. Using 28 Reddit communities, we compare pretrained and supervised fine-tuned Qwen3 embedding spaces at two scales (0.6B and 4B). We construct category prototypes, evaluate their representational dissimilarity matrices against an expert symptom matrix with representational similarity analysis, and complement this global test with prototype-based typicality and multi-baseline confound controls. Pretrained embeddings show measurable alignment with expert structure within the mental-health subset; fine-tuning strengthens this alignment most at the finest category level; and larger scale improves both zero-shot alignment and supervision-induced gains. Residual alignment remains substantial after controlling for VAD, LIWC, lexical style, and topic-distribution structure. These results suggest that LLM embeddings can recover expert-relevant category geometry, but this recovery is level-dependent and should be tested against explicit confounds rather than inferred from classification alone.

paper.title: The Model Knows Where to Look: Visual-Grounding-Guided Head Suppression for Mitigating Hallucination in LVLMs
paper.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) achieve strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, yet are still prone to object hallucination - often generating content that is not grounded by the visual input. Existing attention-based training-free mitigating methods rely on visual attention heads identified by high attention weights or sensitivity to visual token perturbations. However, we show that these identified visual attention heads are not necessarily responsible for visual grounding, and using this as guidance is suboptimal. Motivated by this observation, we propose a novel training-free decoding method that identifies visually sensitive heads by counterfactual region masking. We find that these heads provide a clear signal when visual grounding is required and can therefore be used to mitigate hallucination by guiding the suppression of hallucination heads. Across multiple LVLMs and benchmark image captioning and VQA datasets, our method achieves best or near-best performance in reducing hallucination while preserving generation quality.

paper.title: Prompt-Based Abstention Fails Under Misleading Context: A Controlled Study of Small Frozen RAG Models
paper.abstract: Missing and misleading evidence are not the same problem in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but prompt-based abstention treats them alike. Small frozen models abstain when context is absent, not when it is misleading. We introduce GRAB-RAG (Graded Abstention Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a paired benchmark that tests the same questions across four context conditions (supportive, degraded, missing, and misleading) in Natural Questions and HotpotQA. In the misleading condition, we edit a gold passage to support a wrong answer and place it among other retrieved passages. We test five abstention policies on three small frozen models (3.8B–8B) across two English QA benchmarks. Models abstain reliably when evidence is missing, but under explicit abstention prompting still answer 41.6% of misleading questions, with 63% of those answers echoing the planted wrong entity. Chain-of-thought provides little additional benefit. A generator-side conflict check cuts the rate to 13.3% but discards many correct answers, while a natural language inference (NLI) verifier recovers that coverage but fails when parametric memory and the misleading passage agree on the same wrong answer. Prompt-based abstention asks whether context is sufficient, not whether it is correct. The two-pass checks are diagnostic baselines, not deployable mitigations.

paper.title: PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning

author.affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen and Harbin Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Adaptive learning systems commonly formulate learning path planning as Exercise-Centric (EC) recommendation, where the next step is inferred from item-level interaction logs. Evaluating goal-oriented guidance additionally requires explicit learner goals and curriculum-scale prerequisites: learners with similar exercise records may need different paths toward their targets. We therefore study Knowledge-Centric (KC) personalized learning path planning, where a planner must reason over learner profiles, mastery states, and prerequisite knowledge structures to decide which textbook, unit, and concept should be studied next. To support this setting, we introduce PersonaPath, a benchmark that pairs 2,000 fine-grained learner personas with a hierarchical knowledge graph of 347 textbooks, 1,751 units, and 4,092 concepts across 77 subjects. We evaluate representative LLMs on PersonaPath. Results show that even the strongest LLM reaches only a 29.5% final pass rate in Basic Education, and that the main bottleneck lies in adaptivity, where no model exceeds 44.7% in tailoring paths to individual learners.

paper.title: Multicultural Spyfall: Assessing LLMs through a Dynamic Multilingual Social Deduction Game

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has necessitated more robust evaluation methods that go beyond static benchmarks, which are increasingly prone to data saturation and leakage. In this paper, we propose a dynamic benchmarking framework for evaluating multilingual and multicultural capabilities through the social deduction game Spyfall. In our setup, models must engage in strategic dialogue to either identify a secret agent or avoid detection, utilizing culturally relevant locations or local foods. Our results show that our game-based rankings are consistent with Chatbot Arena rankings on the overlapping model. However, we find a significant performance gap in non-English contexts: models are generally less proficient when handling locally specific entities and often struggle with rule-following or strategic integrity in non-English languages. We demonstrate that this game-based approach provides a scalable, leakage-resistant, and culturally nuanced alternative to traditional NLP benchmarks. The dataset (game history) and source code can be accessed here.

paper.title: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Readability Explanations for Arabic

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and New York University, Abu Dhabi

paper.abstract: In this work, we introduce BAREC-X, the first explanation-annotated Arabic readability dataset, comprising 1,793 sentences drawn from the Balanced Arabic Readability Evaluation Corpus (BAREC) and labeled by expert annotators with linguistic justifications aligned with the BAREC guidelines. Annotators reached an average inter-annotator agreement of 93.3% under the At-Least-1 metric (73.9% Exact Match at the Category+Reason level, and 81.9% at the Category level). We frame readability explanation as a gold-level-conditioned classification task: given a sentence and its gold readability level, a system must return the linguistic reasons that justify the label. We present the first systematic benchmark for this task on Arabic. We evaluate two contrasting paradigms: (i) eight LLMs under zero- and few-shot prompting, and (ii) a fully interpretable, training-free rule-based system grounded in 67 linguistic features spanning morphology, syntax, vocabulary, and syllabic structure. Gemini 3 and GPT-5.5 achieve the highest exact-match agreement on fine-grained reason prediction (55.8% and 56.4% Category+Reason), while the rule-based system achieves the strongest exact-match performance at the Category level (65.9%). Together, BAREC-X and our benchmark establish a transparent foundation for interpretable Arabic readability explanation.

paper.title: Multi-Task Instruction Tuning via Data Scheduling for Low-Resource Arabic SpeechLLMs

author.affiliation: Hamad Bin Khalifa University and Qatar Computing Research Institute

paper.abstract: Audio large language models (LLMs) enable unified speech understanding and generation, but adapting them to linguistically complex and dialect-rich settings such as Arabic-English remains challenging. We present a controlled study of multi-task instruction tuning for an Arabic-centric audio LLM across generative tasks including ASR and speech and text summarization, and discriminative tasks including dialect and emotion recognition, in a resource-constrained setting. To support end-to-end Arabic speech summarization, we introduce AraMega-SSum, a first speech summarization resource for training and benchmarking Arabic-centric Audio-LLMs. We compare four training strategies (i) Uniform Mixing (UM), (ii) Task-Progressive Curriculum (TPC), (iii) Aligner-Based Diverse Sampling (ADS) for training-time batch construction, and (iv) A two-stage TPC→ADS strategy. Our results show a clear task-dependent trade-off: TPC and uniform mixing favor generative tasks, while ADS is strongest for SER. The two-stage TPC→ADS strategy achieves the best DID performance across both backbones while preserving competitive generative quality. The adapted models also outperform zero-shot proprietary baselines, including Gemini-2.5-Pro, on discriminative tasks. We made AraMega-SSum and all experimental resources available to the community (https://huggingface.co/datasets/QCRI/AraMega-SSum).

paper.title: ROCOB: Dual-Manifold Alignment with Optimal Budgeting for Training-Free PTQ Recovery
paper.abstract: Post-training quantization facilitates efficient LLM deployment, yet it disproportionately erodes reasoning and mathematical performance. To recover fidelity without costly fine-tuning, we identify a critical vulnerability in existing output-space methods: the tendency to overfit the limited calibration manifold, which necessitates structural regularization for unseen data. We propose **ROCOB** (**R**esilient **O**utput **C**ompensation with **O**ptimal **B**udgeting), a training-free framework based on *Dual-Manifold Alignment*. ROCOB couples a Principal Activation Component (PAC), which minimizes error on the calibration manifold, with an Orthogonal Geometric Component (OGC), which recovers residual weight-space structure without fitting a second calibration objective. To compare methods fairly under the same added-parameter budget, ROCOB uses Global Spectral Energy Maximization (GSEM) to allocate ranks according to recovered spectral energy and module cost. Across Qwen3 and Llama-3 models, quantizers, and reasoning benchmarks, ROCOB improves average post-quantization recovery in most evaluated model–quantizer settings while preserving a training-free construction pipeline.

paper.title: Synergizing Large Language Models and Theory for Human-like Causal Reasoning

author.affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
National Engineering Research Center of New Electronic Publishing Technologies and Peking University

paper.abstract: Performing causal reasoning akin to humans is fundamental to achieving strong artificial intelligence. However, existing studies on causal reasoning and large language models (LLMs) often underestimate the role of human causal cognition. Human causal reasoning is far more than recognizing causes and effects. Humans often factor in many other considerations when establishing a causal link between two events, such as norm violations, intentionality, morality, counterfactual scenarios, etc. To simulate such reasoning, it is intuitive to identify cause-effect pairs using token causality formalisms while modeling the factors that influence human causal judgment using findings from cognitive science experiments. To support the evaluation and modeling of human-like causal reasoning in LLMs, we introduce HCR-Bench, a challenging benchmark with 1,093 instances and detailed human causal reasoning step annotations, and HCR-Reasoner, an approach that systematically integrates theories of token causality and cognitive science into LLMs for human-like causal reasoning. Results suggest that HCR-Reasoner consistently improves LLMs’ causal alignment with humans, and that theory-guided reasoning is highly effective.

paper.title: Beyond Isolated Dots: Benchmarking Structured Table Construction as Deep Knowledge Extraction

author.affiliation: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: With the emergence of large language models (LLMs), there is an expectation that they can effectively extract structured information from complex, real-world documents. However, most LLMs generate paragraph-style answers that are chaotic, disorganized, and untraceable. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Arranged and Organized Extraction Benchmark (AOE), a new bilingual benchmark featuring long-form documents (171k tokens on average) designed to systematically evaluate the ability of LLMs to comprehend fragmented information and reconstruct it into an organized table. Unlike conventional text-to-table tasks, which rely on fixed schema and narrow domains, AOE includes 12 carefully designed tasks across four diverse domains, requiring models to generate context-specific schema tailored to varied input queries. In our experiments, we evaluated 12 open-source and proprietary LLMs. Even the most advanced models struggle significantly.

paper.title: Explainable End-to-End Argument Mining with Toulmin-Structured Explanations

author.affiliation: King's College London, University of London

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have advanced argument mining (AM), yet most approaches treat component classification, relation identification, and explanation generation as separate tasks, limiting coherence and explainability. We propose the first explainable end-to-end AM framework grounded in Toulmin’s theory, jointly predicting argument components, argumentative relations, and structured explanations in a single generation step. This unified formulation encourages LLMs to produce internally consistent argument graphs and reasoning traces aligned with their predictions. Further, we introduce five explainability criteria tailored to AM and grounded in Toulmin’s theory: completeness, correctness, faithfulness, soundness, usefulness, and develop a unified evaluation protocol combining structural metrics, neural similarity, LLM-based judgment, human evaluation and qualitative analysis. Extensive evaluation on several LLMs shows that our approach achieves competitive performance while substantially improving explainability, generating Toulmin-based explanations that are complete, grounded and faithful, uncovering reasoning errors not captured by standard AM metrics, and being consistently preferred in usefulness evaluations.

paper.title: WebWorld: Web-Simulated World Model
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise as planners across web, spatial, and embodied domains. However, existing agents often handle information seeking, spatial grounding, and action planning as separate capabilities, limiting their ability to solve long-horizon compositional tasks. To address these challenges, we present **WebWorld**, a web-simulated world model for long-horizon reasoning over web evidence, scene observations, and action plans. WebWorld maintains structured intermediate states across heterogeneous modalities and verifies them through schema-guided hierarchical planning. The framework introduces a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that coordinates website, scene, and motion experts via multi-modal self-attention. To support training and evaluation, we develop WebWorld-CoT-55K, a large-scale dataset that integrates heterogeneous modalities into schema-guided reasoning traces, and **WebWorldBench**, a curated benchmark for evaluating long-horizon compositional tasks. Training combines cold-start supervised fine-tuning with offline reinforcement learning based on structural, semantic, and planning rewards; inference uses test-time scaling to aggregate multiple reasoning trajectories. Experiments on WebWorldBench show that WebWorld improves the overall score by up to 8.4% over strong LLM-agent baselines, with gains in outdoor reasoning, geolocation, and travel planning, while still leaving substantial room for progress toward human-level performance.

paper.title: DramaAgent: Agentic Storytelling Video Generation

author.affiliation: University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston

paper.abstract: Recent diffusion and autoregressive video generators have substantially improved short-form synthesis, yet composing multiple independently generated clips into a coherent audiovisual story remains challenging. Character identities may drift across scenes, narrative events can become inconsistent, and dialogue or sound may not align with the evolving visual context. We present **DramaAgent**, a hierarchical, agentic, and model-agnostic framework for multi-scene long-horizon audiovisual story generation. Rather than modifying the underlying video backbone, DramaAgent introduces a stateful control layer that combines hierarchical story planning, persistent character conditioning, scene-wise generation, and reflection-guided targeted repair. The framework maintains reusable story and character states across scenes, diagnoses failures along identity, semantic, temporal, and audio-visual dimensions, and maps each diagnosed failure to a corresponding localized repair operation. Experiments on 50 narrative scripts across five video-generation backbones show consistent improvements in semantic alignment, character consistency, narrative fidelity, and scene-level audio-visual compatibility. Controlled same-backbone comparisons further show that these gains cannot be explained solely by stronger generators or additional sampling. Our results suggest that persistent state, failure diagnosis, and targeted repair provide a practical control paradigm for coherent multi-scene audiovisual generation.

paper.title: You Can Create Words Rather Than Just Detect Them: Towards A New Paradigm of Chinese Neologisms
paper.abstract: Lexical evolution is universal across languages, yet the mechanisms driving neologism formation vary substantially from one language to another. In Chinese, this variation is particularly reflected in the productivity of compounding, where morphemes are combined through word-formation relations to create interpretable lexical forms. This morphological productivity implies that the Chinese lexicon can be viewed not only as a set of attested words, but also as a dynamically latent space with potential neologisms to be realized. However, this perspective still remains underexplored in computation, as current approaches are largely reactive, focusing on detecting attested words from corpora. This raises a question about word-formation itself: which morpheme combinations do the rules license beyond those that corpora already attest? Motivated by this, we propose a proactive creation paradigm for Chinese neologism research. We introduce a three-stage pipeline: KG-Based Candidate Generation, Morphological Discarding, and LLM-Based Filtering. We then probe the candidates with three complementary signals: expert judgment, model perplexity, and corpus attestation. The three signals agree: accepted candidates sit close to real words and clearly apart from rejected combinations. The pipeline yields 18,662 candidates with definitions, examples, and formation metadata, released as material for follow-up work, such as lexical gaps and lexical change. Overall, this study substantiates a proactive creation paradigm for Chinese neologism research, and uses it to characterize what Chinese word-formation rules license beyond what dictionaries have already recorded.

paper.title: From Construction to Injection: Edit-Based Fingerprints for Large Language Models

author.affiliation: Hasso Plattner Institute and University of Potsdam

paper.abstract: Reliable model fingerprints are essential for protecting large language models (LLMs) against unauthorized redistribution and commercial misuse. In black-box deployment, verification is hindered by defensive filtering of suspected fingerprint queries, as well as by downstream model modifications that may weaken embedded ownership evidence. These risks require fingerprints to be robust in both construction and injection. For construction, prior paradigms face an imperceptibility trade-off: natural-language fingerprints may be accidentally activated, whereas garbled fingerprints are statistically exposed and easier to filter. For injection, existing methods struggle to preserve persistent trigger–target behaviors under model modification. We propose an end-to-end injected fingerprinting framework to address these challenges. Code-mixing Fingerprints (CF) use lowest-perplexity code-mixing under a high-complexity constraint to mitigate this two-sided imperceptibility trade-off. Multi-Candidate Editing (MCEdit) constructs structurally redundant, margin-separated trigger–target mappings to enable graceful degradation under model modification. Extensive evaluations on imperceptibility, detectability, and harmlessness demonstrate robust ownership verification with negligible impact on utility.

paper.title: Is a Picture Worth a Thousand Words? Adaptive Multimodal Fact-Checking with Visual Evidence Necessity
paper.abstract: Automated fact-checking is a crucial task that supports a responsible information ecosystem. While recent research has progressed from text-only to multimodal fact-checking, a prevailing assumption is that incorporating visual evidence universally improves verification accuracy. In this work, we challenge this assumption and show that the indiscriminate use of visual evidence can reduce accuracy. Building on this finding, we propose AMuFC, a modular fact-checking framework that employs two collaborative vision-language models with distinct roles to enable the adaptive use of visual evidence. Experimental results on three datasets, including WebFC, introduced in this study, demonstrate the effectiveness of adaptive visual evidence use in fact-checking.

paper.title: When Token Supervision Fails: Segment-Level On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
paper.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) for long-horizon language agents fails even when the teacher remains sequence-informative: in a failing Qwen3 configuration, the teacher still separates good from bad rollouts (sequence AUROC \approx 0.75), yet the local token-gradient alignment \alpha_{\mathrm{diag}} decays from 0.71 to 0.09 and standard OPD recovers only 1.3% of the teacher–student gap. We restrict our claims to two coupled mechanisms, jointly termed CHOP (Counterfactual Hierarchical On-Policy distillation): (i) a per-state reliability gate routing between per-token reverse Kullback–Leibler matching and per-segment sliced-Wasserstein matching, and (ii) a counterfactual total-variation gate activating privileged information (PI) only when the PI changes the teacher’s distribution. The scope is explicit: CHOP targets low-reliability, long-horizon traces where token-local support matching plateaus; in short-horizon or high-reliability regimes Top-K local-support matching (LSM) is already sufficient and CHOP’s segment branch is rarely activated. CHOP recovers 31.7% of the anisotropic-Qwen3 gap (vs. 1.3%/14.5%/24.7% for OPD/Top-K LSM/Li et al. 2026); on SWE-bench Verified under a fixed OpenHands harness, CHOP-deployable prevents the OPD-induced regression (6.5\%\!\to\!13.2\%, matched to off-the-shelf 11.8%, not a significant gain over off-the-shelf) and oracle PI reveals further headroom (14.2%, 95% CI [11.4,17.3]); on AIME 2024 at a 60K-token stress cap (a diagnostic horizon, not a deployment target), CHOP holds 44.9 vs. 42.8 for Top-K LSM (p=0.032), while standard OPD collapses to 28.4.
