Compute-matched, leakage, and PI-removed-teacher controls attribute the gain to supervision-object routing rather than extra compute or PI contamination.

paper.title: Private Evaluation Protocol: Contamination-Resistant Black-Box Evaluation via Public-Slice Surrogates
paper.abstract: Existing paradigms for black-box LLM evaluation by independent third parties share a structural weakness: the testing benchmark must reach the model being evaluated, enabling model developers to game future evaluations through logging or retraining. Ideally, rigorous evaluation would grant evaluators direct access to the model so testing can occur without exposing benchmark contents. However, proprietary black-box models cannot be released to external evaluators, creating a fundamental barrier to independent evaluation. To address this gap, we propose the Private Evaluation Protocol (PEP), a surrogate-based framework for independent evaluation of black-box models without sending the private benchmark to the model developer. PEP releases a small public slice of a held-out benchmark, queries the target model only on that slice, and trains a surrogate from the resulting responses, balancing fidelity to the target model against leakage of the private remainder over a tunable revelation budget. Across six benchmarks, composite leakage scores reliably predict behavioral exposure (r=0.788), and fine-tuned surrogates reach 0.85–0.90 agreement on template-heavy datasets while plateauing below 0.73 on reasoning-heavy datasets. The optimal revelation budget is dataset-dependent, and PEP estimates black-box performance with 5.88 percentage-point MAE, showing the feasibility of private surrogate-based evaluation for structured tasks while protecting the privacy of the held-out benchmark.

paper.title: Llm agent memory: a survey from a unified representation–management perspective

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face significant challenges in sustaining long-term memory for agentic applications due to limited context windows. To address this limitation, many work has proposed diverse memory mechanisms to support long-term, multi-turn interactions, leveraging different approaches tailored to distinct memory storage objects, such as KV caches. In this survey, we present a unified taxonomy that organizes memory systems for long-context scenarios by decoupling memory abstractions from model-specific inference and training methods. We categorize LLM memory into three primary paradigms: natural language tokens, intermediate representations and parameters. For each paradigm, we organize existing methods by three management stages, including memory construction, update, and query, so that long-context memory mechanisms can be described in a consistent way across system designs, with their implementation choices and constraints made explicit. Finally, we outline key research directions for long-context memory system design.

paper.title: Emotion Is Not External Knowledge: Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model’s own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.

paper.title: IndicRipple: Measuring Cross-Lingual Ripple Effects of Knowledge Editing in Indic Languages
paper.abstract: Large language models can be updated after training by modifying parameters, conditioning on edit demonstrations, or supplying retrieved evidence. Yet successful factual updates should do more than change one prompt: they should generalize to related questions, transfer across languages, suppress obsolete facts, and preserve unrelated knowledge. This is the problem of measuring cross-lingual ripple effects of factual updates. The existing evaluations on multilingual knowledge injection, however, focus on high-resource languages like English, and it is unknown whether the findings can transfer to Indic languages. In this paper, we present IndicRipple, a controlled evaluation of multilingual factual updating over 500 factual updates across five domains and five languages: English, Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, and Kannada. We compare parametric editing, in-context editing, and retrieval-based correction using ripple-oriented probes for logical generalization, compositionality, subject aliasing, relation specificity, and forgetfulness. Our results show that current factual update mechanisms show limited cross-lingual ripple effects. IKE performs best overall but reaches only 21.07% strict semantic-plus-language accuracy; RAG often recovers the edited fact but fails to answer in the requested language; and ROME/MEMIT are frequently language-compliant without semantically propagating the update. Strict accuracy is consistently higher for English evaluation than for the Indic-language evaluations. These findings show that direct update success overstates progress: multilingual factual updating must be evaluated as stable cross-lingual propagation, not isolated prompt-level overwrite.

paper.title: A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models

author.affiliation: Technische Universität München and Imperial College London

paper.abstract: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.

paper.title: Hallucinate at the Last in Long Response Generation: A Case Study on Long Document Summarization

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced text generation capabilities, including tasks like summarization, often producing coherent and fluent outputs. Despite these advances, hallucinations remain a critical challenge. While prior studies primarily focus on detecting or mitigating hallucinations, little attention has been paid to where hallucinations occur within long generated outputs. In this work, we investigate where hallucinations occur in LLM-based long response generation, using long document summarization as a key case study. Focusing on the challenging setting of long context-aware long response generation, we find a consistent and concerning phenomenon: hallucinations tend to concentrate disproportionately in the latter parts of the generated long response. To understand this bias, we explore potential contributing factors related to the dynamics of attention and decoding over long sequences. Furthermore, we investigate methods to mitigate this positional hallucination, aiming to improve faithfulness specifically in the concluding segments of long outputs.

paper.title: What’s Worth Asking? Evaluating Preference Elicitation in Transactional Agents
paper.abstract: Transactional agents must act on underspecified requests. "Book me a flight from Chicago to San Francisco" omits budget, timing, stop tolerance, and airline loyalty, any of which can change the best option by hundreds of dollars. The challenge is identifying, without a user-specific prior, which unstated attribute preference is most likely to change the recommendation.We introduce ELICITBENCH, a benchmark of 1,387 travel and housing scenarios pairing real search-result pages (SERPs) with transaction-grounded preference profiles. Each scenario partitions attributes into stated and hidden preferences. An ex-post analytical oracle assigns question-value labels based on the normalized reduction in market-conditioned recommendation regret. Agents are evaluated by task success, question count, and net utility under a super-linear patience cost.ELICITBENCH reveals that plausible questions are often not decision-relevant: on Gemini 2.5 Flash and Claude Sonnet 4.5, unguided agents ask natural follow-up questions with little downstream value. SERP-aware prompting raises net utility from 0.073 to 0.306 and task success from 21.7% to 57.6% on Gemini, and net utility from 0.221 to 0.346 on Sonnet while asking fewer questions. The selection of items is a second bottleneck: with every preference stated, agents still pick the wrong item in about 11% of the scenarios.

paper.title: The Same Answer Every Time: Auditing Small Medical LLM Agents
paper.abstract: We investigate how small open-weight language models make decisions in medical tasks and whether their failures also occur in other settings. We evaluated nine models on wearable fatigue and intensive-care tasks, where they chose among six recommendations, including continued monitoring. We then extended testing to a non-medical tool router and subsets of the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard and JSONSchemaBench. We introduce the Minimum Viable Audit (MVA) to examine which actions models choose, whether their responses contain usable decisions, and whether they copy prompt content. Comparisons across tasks help establish where these behaviors recur. Under the baseline intensive-care prompt, MedGemma chose continued monitoring in all 450 attempts, achieving 33.3% accuracy. On the router, it used all six tools and answered 144 of 150 requests correctly. Meditron-7B produced unusable responses and copied prompt content across intensive-care monitoring and the non-medical evaluations at both four-bit and eight-bit quantization. MedGemma’s results motivate checking the medical instructions. Meditron’s recurring failures warrant checking the model configuration and how outputs are generated. Differences between tasks and mismatches between medical prompts and scoring rules limit conclusions about the causes of these failures. We recommend reporting selected actions, invalid and copied responses, and results for each prompt condition alongside accuracy.

paper.title: CRAFT: A Unified Counterfactual Reasoning Framework for Tabular Question Answering and Fact Verification
paper.abstract: Table reasoning remains challenging for large language models (LLMs), particularly in tasks that require multi-step inference over long and structured tables. Existing approaches predominantly rely on single-direction reasoning, which limits their ability to explore alternative hypotheses across tasks. In this work, we propose CRAFT, a unified Counterfactual Reasoning Framework that reformulates Tabular question answering and fact verification into a general bidirectional verification process. Our method explicitly constructs both declarative statements and their counterfactual variants. Evidence is then extracted from reasoning along both the original and counterfactual paths, and integrated via a weighted mechanism to arrive at the final answer. Experimental results show that our approach consistently surpasses representative baselines on table reasoning datasets such as WikiTQ and TabFact, achieving especially large improvements on complex question answering. Our framework also significantly mitigates performance gaps between different backbone LLMs. This indicates that counterfactual reasoning effectively overcomes the limitations of single-direction inference, guiding LLMs toward more discerning reasoning and establishing a more principled paradigm for structured reasoning tasks.

paper.title: Multidimensional Consistency Improves Reasoning in Language Models
paper.abstract: While Large language models (LLMs) have proved able to address some complex reasoning tasks, we also know that they are highly sensitive to input variation, which can lead to different solution paths and final answers. Answer consistency across input variations can thus be taken as a sign of stronger confidence. Leveraging this aspect, we introduce a framework where models are systematically pushed to diversify solution paths towards a final answer, thereby testing them for answer consistency across multiple input variations. Focusing on math problems, we induce variations in (i) order of shots in prompt, (ii) problem phrasing, and (iii) languages used. Experiments on a wide range of open-source LLMs of various sizes show that reasoning consistency differs by variation dimension, and that by aggregating consistency across dimensions, our framework enhances mathematical reasoning performance on monolingual datasets GSM8K and MATH500, and the multilingual dataset MGSM. We also discuss the different efficacy of the types of variations induced and how they could be further leveraged in future work.

paper.title: CriticGen: Generation-Aware Evaluation as Actionable Feedback

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: Current evaluation methods for large language models are coarse-grained and decoupled from generation, producing generic explanations that fail to provide actionable feedback for model improvement. We propose CriticGen, a fine-grained, generation-aware evaluation framework that turns evaluation into actionable control for answer improvement. CriticGen first generates sample-specific evaluation dimensions and scoring criteria, then uses the induced rubric to jointly produce a score, a reason, an executable refinement suggestion, and a refined answer. Experiments show that fine-grained evaluation should be both instance-specific and actionable. CriticGen improves human-rated rubric relevance/coverage from 3.33/4.03 to 3.97/4.24. On the score-consensus-filtered RefineData test set, the best CriticGen variant reaches 0.9556/0.9560 Pearson/Spearman agreement with the reference scores and improves reason/suggestion F1 to 0.7554/0.7900. Independent validation provides additional support: on 180 human-scored instances, CriticGen-Qwen2.5-7B obtains higher observed score correlations than GPT-5, with 0.8868/0.8969 Pearson/Spearman versus 0.8542/0.8615. Crucially, its feedback translates into substantial answer improvement, raising accuracy from 45.36% to 91.26% on 5,000 examples with reliable gold answers, with 47.30% of answers corrected from Wrong\rightarrowRight and only 1.40% degraded from Right\rightarrowWrong.

paper.title: LLM-Generated Social-Desirability Ratings for Forced-Choice Questionnaire Construction: A Preregistered Downstream Validation
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly produce evaluative judgments, but rating-level human–model agreement does not establish whether they can replace human inputs in a downstream task. Using HEXACO personality items as a case study, we conduct a preregistered three-stage validation of whether LLM-generated social-desirability ratings can serve as inputs to forced-choice scale construction, a psychometric task that requires costly human ratings. In Stage I, three LLMs served as raters of item-level social desirability for sentence- and adjective-format items, with human ratings serving as references. In Stage II, human- and LLM-based ratings were entered into the same constrained optimization procedure. In Stage III, 400 participants completed the resulting forms, and latent trait estimates were compared using graded Thurstonian item response theory. LLM ratings showed strong item-level correspondence with human ratings (sentence: r = 0.942–0.963; adjective: r = 0.979–0.980), but optimized forms showed partial item overlap and sparse exact pair overlap. Despite these design differences, LLM-based forms produced latent trait estimates that closely matched those from human-based forms (mean r = 0.815 for sentence items and 0.768 for adjective items). These results support the conditional use of LLM-generated ratings as scalable construction inputs while showing why downstream validation is necessary.

paper.title: What Changes in Hidden States When Model Merging Hurts Task Performance?
paper.abstract: Model merging is a practical way to combine several fine-tuned models, but merged models can lose performance relative to their task-specific counterparts. Task accuracy shows the degradation, but not how merging changes the model’s internal representations. We study this question through hidden-state distortion, which measures the difference between a merged model’s hidden states and those of the corresponding task-specific reference model on the same examples. Across two model families, six tasks, and three merge methods, we find that the distortion is highly anisotropic: much of the merged-reference change is concentrated in a small number of directions. Removing distortion components along dominant directions often improves accuracy more than removing those along unrelated directions. When we jointly fit a single distortion basis across tasks for each model family, this removal still improves accuracy, suggesting that the tasks share some useful distortion structure. In addition, the distortion score provides a label-free criterion for choosing among candidate task-arithmetic merge scales, matching supervised selection for both model families.

paper.title: STRIDE: Structural Reasoning for In-context Demonstration Extraction in Multi-hop Question Answering

author.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong

paper.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) for multi-hop question answering (MHQA) depends critically on the choice of demonstrations. Yet most existing methods prioritize semantic similarity, even though semantically similar examples may follow different reasoning paths and therefore be poor demonstrations for the target query. We present STRIDE (STructural Reasoning for In-context Demonstration Extraction), a structure-centric framework for multi-hop QA. STRIDE first infers the latent reasoning structure of a query. It then performs positive–contrastive structural routing, selecting structurally compatible demonstrations as positives and semantically plausible but structurally mismatched examples as contrastives. Finally, it constructs structural prompts that expose compact, role-consistent reasoning traces over supporting evidence. Together, it turns demonstration retrieval from semantic matching into structure-aware problem-solving guidance. Empirical results show that STRIDE consistently improves downstream QA performance across settings.

paper.title: ArtHopQA: Diagnosing Hidden-Chain Recovery in Artwork Question Answering

author.affiliation: Nara Institute of Science and Technology
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
CyberAgent, Inc. and Nara Institute of Science and Technology
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan

paper.abstract: Many artwork questions begin with vision but cannot be answered by visual recognition alone. A model may need to connect an artwork to its creator, depicted subject, collection, or location, and then follow multiple facts to reach the answer. We introduce ArtHopQA, a multimodal multi-hop question answering benchmark for artwork understanding, containing 4,885 image-grounded questions paired with supporting fact chains. Experiments with open and API large vision-language models show a large gap: even the strongest open model reaches only 36.87% accuracy when given the image and title, while gold-path performance reaches 97.77% to 99.80% when the supporting fact chain is provided. Text-only language models exhibit a similar gap, showing that the difficulty is not confined to visual input. Further analysis reveals high-prior geographic guesses, inconsistent answers under image-title conflict, and limited recovery of intermediate entities even when final answers are correct.

paper.title: Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention for Conversational LLMs
paper.abstract: Large language models often lose track of persistent instructions and relevant information as multi-turn conversations grow. We study this cumulative contextual decay through three related failure modes: attention pollution, dilution, and drift. We propose **REA** (Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention), a context-management framework that assigns different persistence and representation policies to instructions and episodic interactions. Instructional Memory retains identified global constraints in a dedicated prefix. Episodic Memory preserves user inputs and compresses model replies, while heuristic retrieval selects raw text, compressed representations, or omission for each historical turn. On Long-MT-Bench+, REA improves the judge score from 6.32 to 7.36 on a 10-point scale, a 16.5% relative gain over the Vanilla baseline, and reduces average latency by 2.91×. Additional evaluations show aggregate gains on three backbones spanning 1.7B–7B parameters and on Chinese and English role-playing tasks. These results support role-aware context management as a practical approach to maintaining conversational continuity and instruction adherence.

paper.title: AtomicCheck: Learning Structured Reasoning for Fact Verification via Protocol-Guided Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Fact verification is a critical primitive for ensuring the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs). While frontier LLMs are effective verifiers, their repeated long-context inference incurs substantial costs; meanwhile, existing specialized verifiers face a fundamental dilemma: label-only models suffer from black-box opacity, while free-form rationale generators, whether trained by distillation or explanation-oriented RL objectives, can produce fluent but not structurally checkable explanations. In this work, we propose AtomicCheck a Protocol-Guided Policy Optimization framework that trains specialized verifiers to produce protocol-guided, locally checkable traces, moving beyond opaque label-only predictions and free-form rationales. Rather than cloning teacher traces or optimizing unstructured explanations, AtomicCheck uses RL to make the verification protocol itself part of the policy objective. To preserve semantic integrity during atomic decomposition, we introduce a Contrastive Decomposition Reward that compares decomposed reasoning with a same-backbone holistic counterfactual and penalizes decompositions that reduce verification accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AtomicCheck outperforms existing specialized verifiers and approaches strong frontier LLMs while producing structured traces that expose local checks behind the final decision.

paper.title: KoMMERCE: A Korean Multimodal and Multitask Evaluation Benchmark for Reliable Conversational E-commerce Agents

author.affiliation: Hankuk University of Foreign Studies and Korea Electronics Technology Institute
Korea Electronics Technology Institute and Korea Electronics technology Institute

paper.abstract: E-commerce conversations are increasingly multimodal, yet end-to-end response scores cannot localize which dialogue competence failed, and no public benchmark evaluates finegrained multimodal dialogue understanding for Korean commercial agents. We present KoMMERCE, a Korean multimodal fashion-domain benchmark that coordinates nine fine-grained dialogue understanding tasks on the same conversations: sentiment, intent, and strategy classification;image and text knowledge retrieval;dialogue state tracking; span detection; coreference resolution; and the first formulation of cross-modal dialogue relation extraction. The corpus contains 15,293 dyadic role-play dialogues under two-stage quality control. Baselines on six frontier multimodal LLMs reveal task-conditional patterns that should inform deployment choices: no model wins all nine tasks, and context length affects accuracy differently from one task to another.

paper.title: KoEVD: A Korean Benchmark for Metadata-Conditioned Multi-Stage LLM Safety Evaluation
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) safety benchmarks often evaluate input risk, response selection, generation, and tool use separately, making comparisons across tasks difficult. We introduce KoEVD (Korean Ethical Violation Dataset), which links five evaluation and analysis tasks through annotated Korean source utterances: input-risk judgment, candidate-response selection, generation safety, response-strategy analysis, and non-executable mock-tool selection. The tasks share source IDs, with task-specific subsets and candidate sampling where required. Built through an approximately 3.5-year human-governed, AI-assisted process, KoEVD contains 13,552 curated user utterances and 71,395 linked response candidates. Across 12 open-weight and commercial models, observed task profiles differ, and aggregate scores obscure variation across severity, explicitness, utterance type, and topic. In matched generation and mock-tool-selection cases, responses classified as safe coexist with unsafe mock-tool choices; pooled unsafe-call rates are 9.73% and 9.31% for the classifier-safe and classifier-unsafe groups, respectively, with framing-specific differences. These diagnostic measurements do not establish real-world safety. KoEVD supports detailed Korean safety analysis through contextual annotations and source-linked comparisons.

paper.title: ConceptWeave: Concept-Driven Prompting through Adaptive Semantic Infilling

author.affiliation: Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.

paper.abstract: Conventional prompting and prompt-based finetuning offer only weak semantic structure, leaving models to derive task-specific reasoning from limited cues. Existing techniques, such as using demonstrations, chain-of-thought prompting, or retrieval augmentation, can improve performance, but often at the cost of longer, more redundant prompts, higher inference overhead, and reliance on external knowledge sources. We present ConceptWeave, a novel concept-centric prompt-based finetuning approach built on adaptive semantic infilling. Instead of depending on external resources, it extracts concise, task-relevant concepts directly from a small portion of downstream data and organizes them into a dynamically evolving hierarchical memory. During fine-tuning, ConceptWeave identifies informative spans in the input through semantic alignment and augments them with corresponding concept representations, enabling fine-grained, localized conditioning of the model. As training progresses, the concepts are continuously refined and structured into a hierarchy that supports efficient retrieval while preserving semantic richness and scalability. We validate ConceptWeave across a range of NLP tasks, including misinformation detection, question answering, sentiment analysis, and hate speech classification, where it consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent state-of-the-art methods.

paper.title: CulturALL: Benchmarking Multilingual and Multicultural Competence of LLMs on Grounded Tasks

author.affiliation: University of Turku and ELLIS Institute Finland
Southern University of Science and Technology
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now deployed worldwide, inspiring a surge of benchmarks that measure their multilingual and multicultural abilities. However, these benchmarks prioritize generic language understanding or superficial cultural trivia, leaving the evaluation of grounded tasks—where models must reason within real-world, context-rich scenarios—largely unaddressed. To fill this gap, we present CulturALL, a comprehensive and challenging benchmark to assess LLMs’ multilingual and multicultural competence on grounded tasks. CulturALL is built via a human–AI collaborative framework: expert annotators ensure appropriate difficulty and factual accuracy, while LLMs lighten the manual workload. By incorporating diverse sources, CulturALL ensures comprehensive scenario coverage. Each item is carefully designed to present a high level of difficulty, making CulturALL challenging. CulturALL contains 2,610 samples in 14 languages of 51 regions, distributed across 16 topics to capture the full breadth of grounded tasks. The experiments show that the best LLM achieve 44.48% accuracy on CulturALL, underscoring substantial room for improvement.

paper.title: Self-Distillation for Multi-Token Prediction
paper.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to scale, inference efficiency has emerged as a critical bottleneck. Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) offers a promising avenue to accelerate LLM inference by predicting multiple future tokens simultaneously. Wherein, DeepSeek MTP has gradually become an indispensable component in industrial LLMs. However, it still faces two challenges: limited accept rates of MTP heads, and difficulties in jointly training multiple MTP heads. To address these challenges, we propose MTP-D, a simple yet effective self-distillation method that substantially boosts MTP head accept rates while maximally preserving main-head performance. We further introduce a looped extension strategy for MTP-D, enabling effective and economical extension to multiple MTP heads and yielding significant additional inference speedup (up to 4.55\times). Beyond these contributions, we conduct systematic experiments across seven benchmarks to explore and validate key insights into distillation strategies and the scalability potential of DeepSeek MTP. Results demonstrate that MTP-D and the grouped extension strategy consistently enhance MTP head performance and inference efficiency, facilitating the practical usage of MTP in LLMs.

paper.title: CLEF: Closed-Loop Error Feedback for Multi-Bit Watermarking in Short LLM-Generated Text

author.affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Huazhong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Multi-bit watermarking for large language models (LLMs) enables richer provenance information, but existing schemes remain unreliable for short texts because they rely on local or pre-specified allocation strategies. To address this limitation, we propose a Closed-Loop Error Feedback (CLEF) Multi-Bit Watermarking framework. By treating the LLM as a noisy channel, CLEF tracks the global feature state of generated tokens and dynamically measures its deviation from an ideal multidimensional target trajectory. The resulting dynamic error vector is then used to modulate the logits of candidate tokens via an inner-product scoring mechanism, biasing generation toward tokens that compensate for underrepresented payload dimensions. This closed-loop control enables robust multi-bit embedding with a simple, fully linear decoding process. Experiments on short-text generation show that CLEF improves bit extraction accuracy and complete message recovery rate over the evaluated multi-bit watermarking baselines. Furthermore, CLEF achieves higher bit extraction accuracy under different text perturbations while maintaining acceptable generation quality across downstream tasks such as text summarization and machine translation.

paper.title: “Do You Truly Love Me?” Benchmarking LLM Capability on Hierarchical Pragmatic Tactic Conversations
paper.abstract: Pragmatic reasoning, including inferring intent, manipulation, and hidden meaning in dialogue, is essential for trustworthy language understanding yet remains underexplored in current large language models (LLMs). We introduce HIPO, a new benchmark designed to assess Hierarchical Pragmatic Tactic in multi-turn Conversations. Inspired by linguistic pragmatics, HIPO operationalizes a hierarchical annotation schema for multi-turn conversations and labels each utterance along one dialogue-level goal and three utterance-level dimensions: communicative intention (why), veracity strategy (how), and illocutionary act (what). To ensure reliable supervision, we design a structured generation pipeline to generate high-quality synthetic dialogues. The benchmark comprises over 4,088 benchmarking utterances with 6,350 contextual utterances across 1,131 dialogues drawn from 31 real-world-inspired scenarios. Benchmarking 22 state-of-the-art LLMs reveals a striking gap: while models achieve higher performance at recognizing surface speech acts(83.3% accuracy), they perform poorly on detecting veracity strategies(32.2%) and speaker intentions(45.1%). These results suggest current LLMs remain challenged by the pragmatic inferences operationalized in HIPO, particularly those involving information manipulation and intended effects beyond literal content. We further show that supervised fine-tuning on additional synthetic data generated by our pipeline can improve performance on HIPO, suggesting a practical path for targeted capability improvement within this benchmark setting.

paper.title: What Makes User Reactions Useful for Fake News Detection?
paper.abstract: Fake news detection is often treated as a content-centered task, yet social media posts are embedded in user reactions that express skepticism, endorsement, correction, ridicule, and affective responses. This paper asks what makes user reactions useful for fake news detection. We study performance according to different dimensions: text only, emotions in comments, and number of available comments. We study this question across Fakeddit and Weibo20 under both standard and temporal splits (in a temporal split, most recent posts are included in the testing split). Robustness of results is measured across two encoder families (BERT-base, RoBERTa-base) and two English emotion taxonomies (dair-ai/emotion, GoEmotions). Across these configurations, comment-only representations outperform post-only baselines in most evaluation regimes, though this gain depends on dataset, split, and number of available comments. Emotion-fine-tuned comment encoders produce a temporal-shift-specific significant benefit compared to non-temporal splits.We compare post-only representations, generic comment representations, emotion-fine-tuned comment representations, and post–reaction fusion models, while varying comment availability, showing that a minimum number of comments is necessary to improve detection of fakes. In addition, we show that fine-tuning comment or reaction-encoders on relevant auxiliary tasks such as emotions has a significant impact on the distribution of embeddings of fake and real posts in their representation space.In light of these findings, we believe that user responses—and their emotional structure for example—should be taken into account when detecting fake news or compiling datasets for this purpose.

paper.title: Safety in Batches? Understanding and Mitigating Safety Failures in Batch Prompting

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Batch prompting is a practical inference strategy for large language models, but its safety implications remain underexplored. We show that the success of batch prompting for utility does not extend to safety: a harmful question that is reliably refused in isolation can elicit a harmful response when embedded in a batch of benign questions. We identify this as a distinct safety failure mode, not reducible to known vulnerabilities such as in-context learning or long-context effects—and analyze its causes from two complementary perspectives: alignment signal weakening and refusal signal dilution. Across widely used open-source and frontier commercial models, batch prompting consistently achieves high attack success rates as a simple black-box attack. We further show that batch-aware preference optimization effectively mitigates the vulnerability. These findings highlight a blind spot in current safety alignment and point to batch-aware alignment as a necessary step toward robust deployment.

paper.title: Positive-Unlabeled Contrastive Retrieval for Graduate Program Recommendation
paper.abstract: Graduate program selection is a high-stakes decision where applicants struggle to identify programs matching their latent academic profiles. We address this as a retrieval problem: given a student profile, rank 531 graduate programs by estimated admission compatibility, i.e., how closely the student’s profile resembles each program’s historical admit pool. Because applicants rarely report rejections, training data consists only of positive labels, making negative supervision unavailable. We propose PURE (Positive-Unlabeled Retrieval Encoder), a positive-unlabeled biencoder with InfoNCE contrastive loss and a gated structural residual that fuses GPA and experience counts with free-text descriptions. With a novel multi-positive MRR protocol that corrects for false negatives, PURE achieves MRR=0.2696, outperforming BM25 (+4.9 points) and GPT-4o-mini (+8.3 points), while remaining statistically indistinguishable from Biencoder + GPT-4o-mini reranking at negligible cost.

paper.title: Does Translation Preserve Character Personality? Quantifying Perceived Character-Personality Consistency Across Languages
paper.abstract: Translation conveys meaning across languages, but does it preserve the personality a character conveys? We introduce an evaluation framework for quantifying how well translation systems maintain perceived character personality, the personality impression a reader forms from a character’s dialogue, described along the five Big Five dimensions; we use these dimensions as descriptive labels for the impression, not as a psychometric measurement of the character. Our framework applies personality predictors to both source and translated utterances, measuring cross-lingual consistency via Spearman rank correlation at the speaker level. We study entertainment subtitle translation, where every utterance is produced by a named character, and compare evaluation conditions that include, shuffle, or withhold the character names. We evaluate five MT systems, including dedicated MT APIs (Google Translate, DeepL) and LLMs (GPT-4o, Qwen3- 32B, Aya-expanse-32B), and additionally report human translation as a reference condition on GAME OF THRONES (English→12 target languages, 11 characters) and ONE PIECE (Japanese→English, 15 characters). Under our evaluation protocol, measured personality consistency varies across systems and language pairs, and high BLEU/COMET translation quality does not reliably imply high personality consistency.

paper.title: Cross-Lingual Semantic Fusion: Towards Universal Sentence Representations via LLMs
paper.abstract: Extracting sentence representations from pretrained large language models (LLMs) is a training-free approach that leverages their inherent semantic understanding. Existing methods primarily rely on prompt engineering to distill core semantics, but the resulting representations often retain language-specific features that hinder semantic tasks. Moreover, these approaches fail to exploit the cross-lingual capabilities of LLMs, remaining confined to monolingual settings. To address these limitations, we propose CLSF, a novel method that actively introduces diverse language perturbations when encoding the same sentence and then fuses the perturbed embeddings, effectively reducing language-specific biases and producing a more universal representation. CLSF is plug-and-play and can be integrated with existing prompt-based methods. Experiments on Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), multilingual alignment, and various downstream tasks show that CLSF consistently improves performance across different LLMs.

paper.title: CGVR: Contradiction-Guided Visual Reasoning for Mitigating Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently suffer from object hallucination, producing descriptions or answers unsupported by visual evidence, which undermines their reliability in real-world applications. This paper begins with an intriguing phenomenon: prefacing queries with statements explicitly contradicting image content often yields more accurate responses than direct questioning. We term this the Contradictory Prompting Effect (CPE). Priming inputs with assertions opposing reality triggers an intrinsic self-verification mechanism within MLLMs, where conflicting claims compel the model to prioritize visual evidence over linguistic priors. Inspired by this discovery, we propose Contradiction-Guided Visual Reasoning (CGVR), a novel training-free framework for hallucination mitigation. CGVR systematically generates deliberate contradictory captions alongside standard ones. These captions drive a dual-channel inference process, in which conflicting signals enforce rigorous cross-checking against visual evidence. Our work reveals MLLMs’ latent self-verification capability triggered by contradictions and establishes a paradigm for lightweight, reliable multimodal reasoning. Extensive evaluations on POPE and MME benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed CGVR significantly mitigates hallucinations across diverse MLLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/dhr1698/CGVR.

paper.title: KBS: A Korean Benchmark Suite for Foundation Model Evaluation
paper.abstract: We present a Korean Benchmark Suite (KBS) comprising Ko-ARC, Ko-GSM8K, Ko-EQ-Bench, Ko-WinoGrande, Ko-LAMBADA, and Ko-IFEval, covering six capabilities across 9,396 items. The suite combines review, localization, direct Korean construction, and redesign for Korean, avoiding a translation-only approach to benchmark adaptation. We evaluate Korean-developed models, multilingual open models, and closed API models under protocols that account for model access, prompt format, and scoring differences. Results show that Korean benchmark scores depend on task construction, scoring rules, prompting, and model post-training. These findings suggest that Korean evaluation should report both final scores and the settings used to obtain them.

paper.title: Constructing Disambiguated Knowledge Bases from Large Language Models at Scale

author.affiliation: VNU University of Engineering and Technology

paper.abstract: Automated Knowledge Base Construction (AKBC) is a core NLP task, and recent work proposes generating knowledge bases directly from large language models (LLMs), treating the model itself as the knowledge source. However, LLMs natively possess no representation of entities, leading to duplicate entries as well as conflations.We propose DisamKB, a methodology for constructing disambiguated KBs directly from LLMs. DisamKB incorporates on-the-fly disambiguation of entities, relations and classes, and is meticulously designed to satisfy both scalability and disambiguation accuracy. We analyze the central design decisions and characterize the trade-offs between accuracy, scale, and cost. We execute DisamKB at scale, obtaining a materialized KB containing over 1M disambiguated entities and 38.4M triples. This represents the first million-scale LLM-native KB with explicit internal canonicalization of entities, relations, and classes, a significant departure from prior Wikimedia-centric works. DisamKB is anonymously available at https://gptkb.org/.

paper.title: JanusPO: Asymmetric Clip and KL for Entropy-Stable Group Policy Optimization in Tool-Augmented LLM Reasoning

author.affiliation: Fujian University of Technology and Fujian University of Technology

paper.abstract: Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO, DAPO, ARPO) has become the dominant recipe for RL fine-tuning of reasoning LLMs, yet in the resource-constrained regime most practitioners train in (a single GPU, small batches) it consistently suffers from rapid entropy collapse that kills exploration, together with sparse credit assignment in long rollouts, which is most extreme under multi-turn tool use but already present in long single-turn chain-of-thought. We address both failure modes with JANUSPO, a drop-in GRPO modification that introduces asymmetric PPO clipping \epsilon_{+}<\epsilon_{-} to tolerate larger downward than upward updates, pairs it with an asymmetric KL schedule \beta_{pos}<\beta_{neg} that doubles as a free entropy regulator without any explicit upper bound, and redistributes the terminal reward through a turn-weighted decomposition w_{t}(n) that generalises naturally from single-turn CoT to multi-turn rollouts. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct / GSM8K, JANUSPO improves from 74.8% to 84.3\pm0.2% (mean\pmstd over 2 seeds) across 14 controlled ablations, and the same recipe lifts 7B from 85.3% to 93.6% with no hyper-parameter retuning. On multi-turn DeepSearch (103 GAIA + 100 HLE), SFT-warmup-then-JANUSPO is the only RL recipe whose paired comparison against SFT survives best@8 outlier verification, achieving strict dominance on all four reward and F1 columns while a matched-init GRPO baseline’s apparent F1 wins collapse to 0%. Beyond this main result, we document a systematic negative finding: SFT warm-up is a necessary precondition for GRPO-style multi-turn RL on format-unaware base models.

paper.title: Explainable Multimodal Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Dependency-guided Large Language Model

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Multimodal aspect-based sentiment analysis (MABSA) aims to identify aspect-level sentiments by jointly modeling textual and visual information, which is essential for fine-grained opinion understanding in social media. Existing approaches mainly rely on discriminative classification with complex multimodal fusion, yet lacking explicit sentiment explainability. In this paper, we reformulate MABSA as a generative and explainable task, proposing a unified framework that simultaneously predicts aspect-level sentiment and generates natural language explanations. Based on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), our approach employs a prompt-based generative paradigm, jointly producing sentiment and explanation. To further enhance aspect-oriented reasoning capabilities, we propose a dependency-syntax-guided sentiment cue strategy. This strategy prunes and textualizes the aspect-centered dependency syntax tree, guiding the model to distinguish different sentiment aspects and enhancing its explainability. To enable explainability, we use MLLMs to construct new datasets with sentiment explanations to fine-tune. Experiments show that our approach not only achieves consistent gains in sentiment classification accuracy, but also produces faithful, aspect-grounded explanations.

paper.title: HorizonBench: Evaluating Ideation Agents on Future Scientific Discoveries
paper.abstract: As ideation agents become more capable, evaluating them poses an increasing challenge. LLM-as-a-judge approaches are brittle and gameable, while human evaluation is expensive and hard to scale. To address this, we introduce HorizonBench, an evaluation methodology leveraging future scientific discoveries. HorizonBench uses published papers as ground truth for ideation quality. Specifically, ideation agents pretraining and context retrieval data are strictly constrained to pre-publication knowledge, and scored on how well their predicted ideas align with subsequently published work. Using HorizonBench, we conduct the first unified comparison of five published ideation agents across multiple frontier model backbones. We verify that our soft recall metric captures meaningful ideation quality aligned to human judgement via a user study with 51 domain experts. We then uncover a surprising finding: a naïve baseline that receives only the research goal as an input consistently matches or outperforms all existing agents that require retrieval or multi-step reasoning, highlighting the importance of the research goal for ideation. Based on this result, we develop OSCAR, an ideation agent that distils retrieved papers into insights and explicitly reinforces the research goal in each step of the pipeline. OSCAR outperforms all evaluated agents on HorizonBench. We publish the code and an online version of HorizonBench.

paper.title: A Framework for Evaluating AI-Generated Creativity: Human–LLM Agreement in Evaluating AI-Generated Stories
paper.abstract: Creative text is inherently subjective: any opinion can be equally valid, and there is no objective ground truth. The only way to quantify such subjectivity is to model the crowd of opinions that produces it. Large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge has emerged as a scalable substitute for human raters, but whether an LLM can stand in for the human crowd on AI creativity remains unexplored. We develop a decomposition framework (four main components, 11 sub-components) and a three-step rating procedure, applied identically to human raters and to different LLM judging conditions on AI-generated stories. Humans rate AI creativity with the same subjectivity that creativity research documents for human-authored creative work. Across three structural comparisons (disagreement on the same story including ranking; revision from impressionistic to reflective; sub-component weighting of the final rating), no LLM reproduces all three human patterns. We frame the contribution as a methodological framework plus a quantification of where LLM judges currently fall short of the human ratings in our study. We release all stories, ratings, and code at https://github.com/ku-nlp/creativity-evaluation-artifact.

paper.title: GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation

author.affiliation: Aleph Alpha Research and Institute for Computational Linguistics, Heidelberg University, Ruprecht-Karls-Universität Heidelberg
Institute for Computational Linguistics, Heidelberg University, Ruprecht-Karls-Universität Heidelberg

paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

paper.title: Structuring the Unstructured: A Systematic Review of Text-to-Structure Generation with a Universal Evaluation Framework

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Alibaba Group and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: The evolution of AI systems toward agentic operation and context-aware retrieval necessitates transforming unstructured text into structured formats like tables, knowledge graphs, and charts. While such conversions enable critical applications from summarization to data mining, current research lacks a comprehensive synthesis of methodologies, datasets, and metrics. This systematic review examines text-to-structure techniques and the encountered challenges, evaluates current datasets and assessment criteria, and outlines potential directions for future research. We also introduce a universal evaluation framework for structured outputs, establishing text-to-structure as foundational infrastructure for next-generation AI systems.

paper.title: A2M: Trace-Optimized Agent Hijacking in the MCP Ecosystem

author.affiliation: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology and Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) rely on semantic matching to select tools from third-party servers, exposing a semantic supply-chain risk through attacker-controlled metadata and outputs. We introduce A2M (Attraction-to-Manipulation), a two-stage black-box framework for hijacking MCP agents. The Attraction phase optimizes tool metadata to increase invocation probability; the Manipulation phase uses execution traces to refine adversarial tool returns that steer agents toward attacker-desired outcomes. On LiveMCPBench, direct attacks optimized and evaluated on GLM-4.6 achieve a macro-average malicious tool invocation rate of 93.6% across four scenarios, increase weighted token costs to 32.4\times the benign baseline under Cognitive Denial of Service, and attain a mean attack success rate of 74.4% across Information Exfiltration, Environment Integrity Compromise, and Reasoning Derailment. Transfer to four other models without re-optimization yields corresponding macro-averages of 63.6%, 2.7\times, and 24.5%. These findings motivate stronger tool vetting and runtime isolation in MCP ecosystems. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Lilaizhen/A2M.

paper.title: All Verdicts are Not Equal: Rethinking LLM Judge Reliability
paper.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge is the standard paradigm for NLP evaluation, yet its systemic reliability remains poorly understood despite being widely treated as a deterministic ground truth. We present a comprehensive reliability audit, stress-testing six frontier models across four benchmarks, five prompt formats, two presentation orders, three sampling temperatures, and ten repetitions per condition. Our empirical analysis reveals severe vulnerabilities: verdicts change across identical replications at temperature zero, position-order swaps flip the majority of verdicts on challenging tasks, and the most deterministic judge achieves perfect consistency by trivially repeating incorrect verdicts, agreeing with ground truth only 51% of the time. To formalize these multi-faceted failure modes, we introduce the trustworthy verdict rate (T), a unified metric capturing the joint probability that an evaluation is reproducible, order-invariant, and accurate. Using T , we derive a theoretical upper bound on accuracy imposed by position bias and show that reliability is item-specific rather than model-level. Finally, we demonstrate that shifting from pairwise win-rate to holistic rubric scoring improves trustworthiness more than any single-format prompting intervention, offering an actionable framework for robust NLP evaluation.

paper.title: MedHal: A Synthetic Dataset for Medical Hallucination Detection

author.affiliation: Mila - Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute and École Polytechnique de Montréal, Université de Montréal
École Polytechnique de Montréal, Université de Montréal

paper.abstract: Hallucination, the generation of non factual content by AI systems, poses a serious risk in medical contexts, where errors can directly affect patient outcomes. We present MedHal, a novel large-scale dataset specifically designed to assess capabilities and train models on the task of hallucination detection in medical texts. Current hallucination detection methods face significant limitations when applied to specialized domains like medicine, where they can have disastrous consequences. MedHal addresses this issue by incorporating diverse medical text sources and tasks covering both intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations, and by providing a substantial volume of data samples suitable for training medical hallucination detection models. We demonstrate MedHal’s utility by training and evaluating a baseline medical hallucination detection model, showing improvements over general-purpose hallucination detection approaches. This resource enables more efficient evaluation and training of medical text generation systems while reducing reliance on costly expert review, potentially accelerating the development of medical AI research.

paper.title: Structure Tax: How Structured Output affects LLMs Performance
paper.abstract: Deploying large language models in production often requires constraining outputs to structured formats such as JSON or XML, and prior work treats the resulting accuracy loss as an inherent "structure tax". We re-examine this claim by evaluating a battery of models, datasets and schemas, measuring task accuracy, confidence calibration, and hidden-state geometry. The tax turns out to depend on schema design rather than on structure per se: reasoning-first field ordering matches or exceeds free-form accuracy, while answer-first ordering causes steep drops, particularly in smaller models. Format sensitivity scales inversely with a task’s own structural constraints, and schemas that preserve reasoning order also improve calibration with CKA showing greater separability between correct and incorrect representations in middle transformer layers. Our findings indicate that properly designed structured formats can match or exceed free-form performance, reframing the critical question from ’whether to structure’ to ’how to structure’ for optimal reasoning preservation.

paper.title: Grounded or Guessing? LVLM Confidence Estimation via Blind-Image Contrastive Ranking

author.affiliation: Henry Ford Health System and Michigan State University
Michigan State University and Ghamut Corporation

paper.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) suffer from visual ungroundedness: they can produce a fluent, confident, and even correct response driven entirely by language priors, with the image contributing nothing to the prediction. Existing confidence estimation methods cannot detect this, as they observe model behavior under normal inference with no mechanism to determine whether a prediction was shaped by the image or by text alone. We introduce BICR (Blind-Image Contrastive Ranking), a model-agnostic confidence estimation framework. The LVLM stays entirely frozen; instead, we extract its hidden states twice per sample, once with the real image-question pair and once with the image blacked out while the question is held fixed. A small, separate probe is then trained on the real-image hidden state, regularized by a ranking loss that penalizes higher confidence on the blacked-out view, teaching it to treat visual grounding as a signal of reliability. At inference only the single real-image pass is used, so BICR adds zero cost beyond a standard single-view probe. Evaluated across five modern LVLMs and seven baselines on a benchmark covering visual question answering, object hallucination detection, medical imaging, and financial document understanding, BICR achieves the best cross-LVLM average on both calibration and discrimination simultaneously, with statistically significant discrimination gains robust to cluster-aware analysis, at 4–18× fewer parameters than the strongest probing baseline.

paper.title: Exploring Cross-Scenario Generality of Agentic Memory Systems: Diagnostics and a Strong Baseline
paper.abstract: LLM agents accumulate interaction histories that exceed their context windows, motivating extensive research on memory systems. Yet most existing designs are tailored to a single scenario (such as multi-session chat or a specific trajectory format), offering little evidence that they generalize across the heterogeneous trajectories encountered in deployment. We evaluate twelve baselines spanning specialized memory systems, long-context models, and an unindexed search agent across five scenarios: single-turn QA, multi-session chat, agentic-trajectory QA, memory stress tests, and long-horizon agentic tasks. Notably, DCI-Lite, an unindexed baseline that searches raw text via grep and bounded reads, is among the strongest existing baselines. This suggests that memory performance depends partly on granting the agent active control over retrieval rather than coupling a static store to a single retrieval route. We instantiate this diagnostic insight in **AutoMEM**, a strong baseline that exposes both raw-text and indexed memory views through an agent-controlled interface. Across the evaluated systems, AutoMEM achieves the best mean cross-scenario rank.

paper.title: Forgetting Only What Matters: Layer-Selective Unlearning toward Robust LLMs
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or otherwise undesirable training content, creating privacy, safety, and regulatory concerns. Machine unlearning offers a practical alternative to full retraining, but many existing methods apply broad or fixed parameter updates that can degrade utility and remain brittle under deployment changes such as post-training quantization, where forgotten knowledge may partially re-emerge.We propose Forgetting Only What Matters via Unlearning Layers (FOM-UL), a layer-level unlearning framework that selects transformer layers using a forget-to-retain significance score. This score identifies layers with high influence on the forget set and low sensitivity to the retain set, allowing FOM-UL to concentrate updates where they are most effective while leaving most of the model unchanged. This targeted update strategy improves the forgetting-utility trade-off and provides an empirical path toward quantization-resilient unlearning by reducing the chance that small, diffuse updates are erased by low-bit rounding.Across TOFU, KnowUnDo, and MUSE-style evaluations, FOM-UL reduces residual memorization compared with strong GA, NPO, KLD, SURE, ReLearn, and LUNAR-based baselines while preserving retain-set utility close to the vanilla model. Under 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization, FOM-UL maintains a favorable forgetting-utility trade-off, combining competitive memorization suppression with stronger retained utility. Overall, FOM-UL provides an efficient unlearning strategy that improves targeted forgetting, utility preservation, and deployment robustness without claiming formal guarantees of erasure.

paper.title: A Pre-Training Analogue of Grokking in Language Models: Tracing Delayed Grammatical Generalization

author.affiliation: Amazon and University of Massachusetts, Lowell

paper.abstract: Grokking, the phenomenon in which neural networks generalize long after fitting their training data, has been studied in supervised settings on many epochs. LLM pre-training instead involves next-token prediction over an unlabeled corpus, with limited data repetition and no explicit train/validation split. To address this, we propose an exposure-based framework that enables the study of grokking-like dynamics during LLM pre-training. We ground our evaluation in BLiMP minimal pairs, which provide controlled grammatical contrasts. For every BLiMP minimal pair, we identify a critical phrase, the smallest continuous span that captures the grammatical contrast and the phenomenon-relevant context. Examples whose critical phrase appears in the pre-training window are assigned to the proxy-train split; the remaining examples are assigned to the proxy-validation split. Across five grammatical phenomena, we observe delayed generalization. Analyzing pre-training checkpoints before and after generalization shows that grammatical concept vectors become more predictive of grammatical acceptability and occupy a higher-dimensional subspace after generalization. We also find that attention from the critical token to the relevant context token is concentrated in a small number of heads.

paper.title: GEAR: Training-Free Rule Distillation for Advanced and Efficient Tool-Augmented Reasoning
paper.abstract: Improving tool use in large reasoning models (LRMs) typically demands expensive test-time compute, training resources unavailable to API-only practitioners, or expensive iterative rollouts with execution feedback required by training-free context-engineering methods, all incompatible with resource-constrained deployment. We introduce **GEAR**, a training-free framework that extracts compositional rules from tool-use failures via single-pass meta-reasoning and distills them into inference prompts. We hypothesize that combining explicit rules with examples outperforms either alone. Across 78 API domains, **GEAR**+2-shot outperforms 3-shot by 24.9% on Qwen3-30B, validating our complementarity hypothesis. On Qwen3-4B, **GEAR** exceeds LoRA SFT by 24.3% and RAG-3-shot by 38.5%, while **GEAR**+2-shot beats the state-of-the-art context-engineering method ACE by 38.8% at 4.1\times lower cost. Remarkably, Qwen3-30B with **GEAR**+2-shot nearly doubles zero-shot accuracy while remaining under 1 s latency, demonstrating rollout-free adaptation for resource-constrained deployment.

paper.title: HARPA: A Testability-Driven, Literature-Grounded Framework for Research Ideation

author.affiliation: University of Arizona and Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
Department of Informatics, University of Zurich, University of Zurich and Koblenz University
Department of Informatics, University of Zurich, University of Zurich

paper.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have accelerated automated scientific discovery (ASD), but existing ideation tools still struggle to generate hypotheses that are both testable, literature-grounded, and adaptive to prior experimental outcomes. We developed HARPA to address these challenges by following a human-inspired ideation workflow that mines literature trends, explores hypothesis design spaces, and converges on precise, testable hypotheses by pinpointing research gaps and justifying design choices. Human evaluations show that HARPA-generated hypothesis-driven research proposals performs comparably to a strong baseline system, AI-researcher, in novelty and overall quality, while showing a positive trend in feasibility (+0.78, p<0.05, bootstrap) and a significant gain in groundedness (+0.85, p<0.01, bootstrap) on a 10-point Likert scale. When evaluated with the ASD agent CodeScientist, HARPA produced more successful executions (20 vs. 11 out of 40) and fewer failures (16 vs. 21 out of 40) indicating that expert feasibility judgments track execution success. HARPA also learns a reward model that scores hypotheses based on prior experimental outcomes, achieving approx. a 28% absolute gain over HARPA’s untrained baseline scorer.

paper.title: Retrieve the Logic, Not the Topic: Taxonomic Strategy RAG for Cross-Domain Persuasion Agents
paper.abstract: Foundation-model agents in multi-step, open-ended environments frequently suffer from compounding errors, where early mistakes contaminate long-horizon trajectories. While Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) succeeds in deterministic domains with external validators (CITATION), agents in subjective, non-deterministic tasks such as persuasion experience problem drift and sycophantic conformity. Focusing on subjective argumentation, we identify semantic leakage in standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a reproducible trigger for these failures: standard RAG prioritizes vocabulary overlap over logical structure.To mitigate this leakage, we introduce Taxonomic Strategy RAG (TS-RAG), a systems intervention that routes strategy retrieval through a discrete categorical bottleneck to decouple argumentative structure from topical content. Zero-shot, cross-domain evaluations on r/ChangeMyView show that TS-RAG improves the transfer of abstract argumentative logic where standard semantic retrieval degrades (+14.5 win-rate points over an unaugmented persuader for Gemini Flash 3.0, p<0.05). In asymmetric deployments that mix lightweight and frontier models, TS-RAG raises the win rate of a lightweight persuader against a stronger opponent (70.5% \rightarrow 78.5%, p<0.05) and reduces rounds to consensus when the persuader is already dominant. Finally, we introduce trace-level diagnostics via a turn-by-turn Debate State Representation (DSR), and show that strict stance-holding constraints on the opponent are necessary to prevent evaluation collapse caused by default agentic sycophancy.

paper.title: Fast Listwise Passage Reranking via Semantic Tokens
paper.abstract: Listwise passage reranking often achieves strong ranking performance, but it incurs substantial computational cost. We propose FLASH, an efficient listwise reranking framework based on semantic token compression and single-step listwise scoring. FLASH represents each query–passage pair with a small set of query-aware semantic tokens and jointly scores all candidates in a single decoder step, enabling query-conditioned joint scoring without expensive token-level listwise processing. We further introduce multi-cardinality training, which allows a single model to support different semantic-token budgets at inference time. We also propose FLASH-LITE, a lightweight variant with offline passage encoding for low-cost online inference. Across TREC and BEIR benchmarks, FLASH improves average ranking effectiveness at comparable online latency and slightly lower FLOPs, while FLASH-Lite substantially reduces query-time cost with a modest effectiveness trade-off. FLASH-LITE enables offline passage encoding, substantially reducing online query-time cost while maintaining competitive reranking performance. Code is provided in the supplementary material.

paper.title: TeleSWEBench: A Commit-Driven Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Powered Software Engineering in Telecommunications
paper.abstract: With the telecommunications field embracing zero-touch management alongside novel O-RAN and AI-RAN frameworks, contemporary telecom networks now function as immensely intricate and heavily softwarized codebases. While automated software engineering (ASE) tools and Software Engineering (SWE) Agents hold the potential to alleviate the critical code generation bottleneck in this domain, their ability to navigate and modify specialized, mathematically rigorous wireless stacks like srsRAN 5G remains unverified. General-purpose coding benchmarks fail to capture the stateful logic and strict requirements of telecommunications, leaving a critical evaluation gap. In this paper, we introduce TeleSWEBench, the first commit-driven benchmark specifically designed to measure an agent’s performance in the telecom domain. We mine real developer commits from the srsRAN 5G repository and distill them into structured test cases across three difficulty tiers (Easy, Medium, and Difficult). Our benchmark consists of 734 questions that are accompanied by executable unit tests. To avoid the rigidity of test cases, we further propose a hierarchical LLM-as-a-Judge framework called TeleJudge that scores agent outputs at the file level and aggregates verdicts holistically. This follows an evaluation based on context and semantic similarity in parallel to a standard unit test-based evaluation. Using this benchmark, we evaluate AIDER, OpenHands, and the Claude Code frameworks, powered by state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs, including Qwen, GPT-OSS, Gemma 4, Kimi, GLM, and Qwencoder 2.5. Our two-stage evaluation reveals that models suffer from a lack of both localization accuracy and functional correctness, with the strongest ASE tools achieving up to 25% of shippable changes.

paper.title: Reasoning-Based Personalized Generation for Sparse Users

author.affiliation: University of Georgia and Vanderbilt University

paper.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) personalization holds great promise for tailoring responses by leveraging personal context and history. However, real-world users usually possess sparse interaction histories with limited personal context, such as cold-start users in social platforms and newly registered customers in online E-commerce platforms, compromising the LLM-based personalized generation. To address this challenge, we introduce GraSPer (Graph-based Sparse Personalized Reasoning), a novel framework for enhancing personalized text generation under sparse context. GraSPer first augments user context by predicting items that the user would likely interact with in the future. With reasoning alignment, it then generates texts for these interactions to enrich the augmented context. In the end, it generates personalized outputs conditioned on both the real and synthetic histories, ensuring alignment with user style and preferences. Extensive experiments on three benchmark personalized generation datasets show that GraSPer achieves significant performance gain, substantially improving personalization in sparse user context settings.

paper.title: Identifying User-Inference-Dependent Out-of-Character Behavior in LLM-Based Role-Playing Agents

author.affiliation: Nagoya Institute of Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology and CyberAgent, Inc.

paper.abstract: For the practical deployment of the Role-Playing Agents with Large Language Models, prior work has mainly focused on suppressing out-of-character behavior relative to explicitly provided character information such as personas. However, as shown in psychological research, out-of-character behavior can arise not only from contradictions with explicit information but also from mismatches with character images implicitly inferred by users. Modeling user-inference-dependent out-of-character behavior is a challenging task, because it is unclear what kinds of inferences users make from existing information. To tackle this problem, we construct a dataset of 480 dialogue scenarios and collect 2,152 descriptions from users familiar with those titles. Using cases that annotators judged inappropriate despite the absence of contradiction with existing settings, we derive a 12-category typology, organized into general, title-specific, and individual-specific groups. We also conduct an exploratory evaluation of category-guided feedback, finding no consistent overall advantage over standard self-refinement but possible benefits for some characters. Our shareable code and dataset are at https://github.com/CyberAgentAILab/User-Inference-OOC.

paper.title: The Error Is the Signal: Misconception Discovery via Step-Error Annotation Clustering
paper.abstract: Discovering student misconceptions is a key challenge in intelligent tutoring systems, where identifying recurring error-producing patterns can support targeted feedback and adaptive practice. In settings without a predefined misconception taxonomy, clustering is a natural approach for discovering such patterns at scale. Yet clustering is only as good as its representation: full student records contain problem wording, numerical context, and solution-specific details that embeddings can conflate with the student’s error, obscuring the misconception behind the wrong answer. We construct an LLM step-error-annotation-first pipeline that generates step-error annotations, embeds them with or without problem and student response text, and clusters the resulting representations. On MalruleLib, a 101-class misconception benchmark, clustering step-error annotations alone improves clustering accuracy by 0.22 and normalized mutual information by 0.05 on average over clustering the problem and student response, consistent with annotations capturing recurring error patterns more effectively. On Eedi and unlabeled MalAlgoQA, annotation-based representations show higher average held-out clustering accuracy and internal cluster separation, respectively, than their unannotated baselines. To help experts interpret these clusters, the pipeline then generates candidate misconception descriptors and coherence scores for human triage. Overall, these findings show that input representation substantially affects clustering results and that step-error annotations often improve clustering quality.

paper.title: LLM-as-RNN: Feedback-Driven Memory Rewriting for Online Learning and Sequential Prediction
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are strong sequence predictors, but standard context accumulation offers no explicit mechanism for revising the memory carried between predictions. We propose LLM-as-RNN, an inference-time framework for online learning with frozen LLMs through a bounded natural-language memory state. At each timestep, the model predicts from the current observation and its memory, receives feedback, and rewrites the state to correct errors and retain task-relevant patterns without updating model parameters. Implemented as a structured system prompt, this state makes the adaptation process inspectable through human-readable memory traces. We evaluate LLM-as-RNN on sequential prediction benchmarks in healthcare, meteorology, and finance across Llama, Gemma, and GPT-oss model families. Comparisons with static-context and feedback-aligned baselines examine predictive performance, feedback sources, memory budgets, and inference cost.
