Our results demonstrate that feedback-driven memory rewriting supports online error correction and sequential prediction under a fixed memory budget, with performance varying across tasks and backbones.

paper.title: Epistemic Erosion: An Error Class Beyond Hallucination in LLM Text Generation
paper.abstract: Expert writers calibrate their claims with qualifiers such as “likely benign“ in a radiology report, “may constitute“ in a court ruling, and “suggest“ in a scientific paper. We ask whether this calibration survives when Large Language Models (LLMs) summarize and rewrite professional text. We define epistemic erosion as any change in a source’s expressed certainty, including qualified claims that are dropped or introduced without basis. We measure it with the Epistemic Faithfulness Score (EFS), computed by aligning source and output claims one-to-one with rule-based matching and assigning each distortion to one of six types, namely escalation, attenuation, omission, fabrication, scope shift, and severity warp. On clinical notes, mean EFS for 11 open-weight LLMs ranges from 0.415 to 0.493; three of these models are also evaluated on legal and scientific text. Four hosted models (GPT-4o, GPT-5.4, Phi-4, Mistral-Large-3) reach at most 0.483 in any domain. The most frequent detected distortion is omission (66%), in which a qualified claim is dropped entirely; claims that survive tend to shift toward greater certainty. Model scale and medical adaptation bring no consistent gain, seven prompting strategies bring at most modest gains, and ROUGE-L and BERTScore correlate only weakly with EFS (|r| \approx 0.1).

paper.title: The bias is in the generator: locating medical chain-of-thought subgroup gaps upstream of the verifier
paper.abstract: Verifier-guided best-of-N decoding has two stages: a generator samples candidate chains of thought, and a verifier selects among them. A subgroup disparity may already be present in the generator’s candidates or be amplified during selection. We separate the two stages using adversarial demographic counterfactuals of medical exam questions. On HuatuoGPT-o1-8B, a substantial race accuracy gap is already present in a single sampled response, before verifier selection. Across seven generators, only Gemma-3-27B-it under Skywork-RM shows significant verifier-induced amplification after multiple-testing correction. Even an oracle selector leaves a residual gap on every medical generator analyzed, showing that correct answers are less often available for one subgroup. Counterfactually paired low-rank adaptation (LoRA) of the generator reduces the single-sample gap on two medical models, although on HuatuoGPT-o1-8B the reduction does not persist after self-judge selection. Single-variant controls indicate that the single-sample reduction is not explained by additional training steps alone. A short fairness instruction modestly reduces the single-sample gap, and a direct preference optimization (DPO) variant of the paired training also reduces it and, on HuatuoGPT-o1-8B, keeps race mention near its baseline rate. For the medical generators studied, candidate generation rather than inference-time selection is the primary locus for mitigating this gap.

paper.title: Dgrammar: Efficient Constrained Decoding for DLMs
paper.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) decode several tokens per step. However, the grammar-constrained decoders evaluated here, IG-CD and LAVE, verify candidate tokens sequentially within each denoising step and treat every violation as a rejection, a lookahead verification, or a fallback to autoregressive decoding. We observe that a violation is local to the first token the parser cannot consume, so the rest of the parallel step can be kept. We propose Dgrammar, a training-free decoder that repairs that frontier token in place under the same forward-pass logits, paired with a grammar-gated backoff schedule for the unmask batch size, asynchronous mask construction, and a bounded grammar-guided tail. On JSONSchemaBench medium with LLaDA-8B, Dgrammar improves schema validity by 8.6 percentage points over the strongest DLM baseline while reducing mean latency by 5.8x and eliminating timeouts. Validity and latency gains also hold on the other JSB splits and on Dream-7B, and experiments with a SMILES grammar demonstrate cross-grammar transfer.

paper.title: CircuitPile: A Data Synthesis Framework for Enhancing Multimodal LLMs’ Perception on Circuit Schematics
paper.abstract: In recent years, multimodal large language models have achieved substantial progress, yet their performance remains limited in specialized domains such as circuit diagram understanding. A key bottleneck lies in the lack of diverse and large-scale training data tailored to the structural characteristics of circuit diagrams, together with the high cost of expert annotation. To address this challenge, we propose CircuitPile, a systematic data synthesis framework for circuit visual-language modeling. CircuitPile integrates heterogeneous circuit resources from multiple sources and constructs standardized label spaces and multi-granularity visual representations. Based on this framework, we build 738K domain-specific pre-training samples and 100K task-oriented instruction-tuning samples for the pre-training and supervised fine-tuning stages, respectively. Furthermore, to systematically evaluate fundamental visually grounded circuit perception, we introduce CircuitPerception-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 2,700 multiple-choice samples across three dimensions: component recognition, spatial understanding, and quantitative reasoning. CircuitPerception-Bench focuses on fundamental visually grounded perception and complements external benchmarks such as AMS Benchmark. Experimental results show that multimodal models trained with CircuitPile achieve significant performance gains on the internal benchmark and demonstrate favorable transferability on the external public AMS Benchmark. For example, applying CircuitPile-based SFT to Qwen3-VL-8B improves the scores on CircuitPerception-Bench and AMS Benchmark from 0.5759 and 0.5067 to 0.7703 and 0.5988, respectively.

paper.title: Do Correctness Probes Transfer? A Cross-Family Study of LLM Hidden States
paper.abstract: Linear probes on language-model hidden states can predict output correctness, but it remains unclear whether they capture transferable correctness representations. We study out-of-distribution correctness-probe transfer across seven datasets, four task families, and three open-weight LLMs: Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B, with all findings validated across five random seeds. Within-family transfer is consistently stronger than cross-family transfer (gap 0.075 AUC), with code generation showing the clearest pattern across MBPP-test, MBPP-train, and HumanEval. We further find that probe weight directions are nearly orthogonal across most dataset pairs despite strong predictive transfer, suggesting that probes do not encode a single canonical correctness direction. Comparing probes to logprob confidence baselines, we find probe advantage is concentrated in in-domain and within-family transfer cells. We also identify a layer-selection confound where early-layer shortcuts can appear transferable in-domain but fail cross-source. Overall, correctness probes transfer selectively rather than universally, making them most useful in-domain and within task families.

paper.title: SWE-Adept: An LLM-Based Agentic Framework for Deep Codebase Analysis and Structured Issue Resolution
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong performance on self-contained programming tasks. However, they still struggle with repository-level software engineering (SWE), which demands (1) deep codebase navigation with effective context management for accurate localization, and (2) systematic approaches for iterative, test-driven code modification to resolve issues. To address these challenges, we propose SWE-Adept, an LLM-based two-agent framework where a localization agent identifies issue-relevant code locations and a resolution agent implements the corresponding fixes. For issue localization, we introduce agent-directed depth-first search that selectively traverses code dependencies. This minimizes issue-irrelevant content in the agent’s context window and improves localization accuracy. For issue resolution, we employ adaptive planning and structured problem solving. We equip the agent with specialized tools for progress tracking and Git-based version control. These tools interface with a shared working memory that stores code-state checkpoints indexed by execution steps, facilitating precise checkpoint retrieval. This design enables reliable agent-driven version-control operations for systematic issue resolution, including branching to explore alternative solutions and reverting failed edits. Experiments on SWE-Bench Lite and SWE-Bench Pro demonstrate that SWE-Adept consistently outperforms prior approaches in both issue localization and resolution, improving the end-to-end resolve rate by up to 4.3%.

paper.title: VTBench: Evaluating Visual Tokenizers for Autoregressive Image Generation

author.affiliation: Rice University and University of Rochester

paper.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models have recently shown strong performance in image generation, where a key component is the visual tokenizer (VT) that maps continuous pixels into discrete tokens. The quality of the VT largely determines the upper bound of AR model performance. However, existing discrete VTs significantly lag behind continuous variational autoencoders (VAEs), leading to degraded reconstructions and poor preservation of fine details and text. Current benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end generation quality, making it difficult to isolate VT performance. We introduce VTBench, a comprehensive benchmark for systematic evaluation of visual tokenizers across three core tasks: image reconstruction, detail preservation, and text preservation. Evaluating state-of-the-art VTs with multiple metrics, we find that continuous VAEs consistently outperform discrete VTs, especially in retaining spatial structure and semantic details. Discrete VTs often produce distorted reconstructions and fail to preserve fine textures and text. We release VTBench publicly to facilitate future research on robust, general-purpose visual tokenizers.

paper.title: User Feedback to Actionable Insights: A Fine-grained Multilabel Approach for Classifying App Reviews
paper.abstract: The rapid proliferation of mobile applications has resulted in a vast volume of user-generated reviews, which often contain critical insights into bugs, feature demands, and overall user satisfaction. Efficiently organizing and interpreting this feedback is essential for developers seeking to enhance app quality and user experience. In this study, we propose a fine-grained, multilabel classification schema for app reviews, structured as a two-level taxonomy. The first level categorizes reviews into three primary classes: Bug Report, Feature Request, and App Satisfaction Feedback. The second level further refines these categories into subtypes addressing specific concerns such as performance, usability and privacy. To automate this classification, we fine-tune several state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), including LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral, Qwen, on a manually annotated dataset spanning 10 diverse application domains. Among these, LLaMA 3.1 achieved the highest performance, with weighted F1 scores of 0.90 and 0.79 at the first and second taxonomy levels, respectively. To assess scalability, we applied the fine-tuned LLaMA 3.1 model to label an additional 10,000 unlabeled reviews, creating a silver-standard corpus. This taxonomy-driven approach enables more nuanced analysis of user feedback, supporting targeted app improvements and fostering enhanced user satisfaction.

paper.title: Beyond Idealized Patients: Evaluating LLMs under Challenging Patient Behaviors in Medical Consultations
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for medical consultation and health information support, where safety depends not only on medical knowledge but also on robust responses to unclear, inconsistent, or misleading patient input. However, most existing medical LLM evaluations assume idealized and well-posed patient questions, limiting their realism. We study challenging patient behaviors that commonly arise in real medical consultations and complicate safe clinical reasoning. We define four clinically grounded categories of such behaviors: information contradiction, factual inaccuracy, self-diagnosis, and care resistance. For each behavior, we specify concrete failure criteria that capture unsafe responses. Building on four existing medical dialogue datasets, we introduce CPB-Bench (Challenging Patient Behaviors Benchmark), a bilingual (English and Chinese) benchmark of multi-turn dialogues annotated for these behaviors. We find that although models perform well overall, they exhibit consistent behavior-specific failures, especially when handling contradictory or medically implausible patient information. We further evaluate four intervention strategies and find inconsistent improvements, with some interventions introducing unnecessary corrections. We release the dataset and code.

paper.title: Latent Prediction Needs Alignment: A Controlled Study of Joint-Embedding Predictive Vision–Language Learning
paper.abstract: Predictive vision–language learning aims to learn semantic representations by predicting latent targets rather than reconstructing pixels or generating text. We ask whether latent prediction alone induces the global image–text geometry required for zero-shot matching, and how the location of alignment pressure changes this outcome. In a controlled joint-embedding predictive model family with matched training and evaluation protocols, non-contrastive latent prediction retains information recoverable by supervised adapters and token-level probes but does not form a usable zero-shot image–text space under pooled cosine scoring. A target-contrastive design improves matching, but remains weaker than the directly aligned variant. Our results show that latent prediction is underconstrained at the global embedding level in this setting. Direct global alignment supplies the constraint that makes predictive representations usable for zero-shot scoring. With only a modest direct global alignment loss, latent prediction becomes competitive with matched CLIP and SigLIP baselines and improves several language-sensitive diagnostics.

paper.title: SaFeR-ToolKit: Structured Reasoning via Virtual Tool Calling for Multimodal Safety

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Huazhong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Vision–language models remain susceptible to multimodal jailbreaks and over-refusal because safety hinges on both visual evidence and user intent, while many alignment pipelines supervise only the final response. To address this, we present SaFeR-ToolKit, which formalizes safety decision-making as an inspectable protocol: during offline data synthesis, a planner specifies a persona, a **Perception**→**Reasoning**→**Decision** tool set, and a constrained transition graph, while a responder emits a typed key–value tool trace before the final answer. To learn this protocol, we train a single policy with a three-stage curriculum (SFT→DPO→GRPO), where GRPO directly supervises tool usage beyond answer-level feedback. We contribute (**I**) the first tool-based safety reasoning dataset of 30,654 training entries (SFT 6k, DPO 18.6k, GRPO 6k) plus 1k held-out evaluation, and (**II**) experiments on Qwen2.5-VL showing large gains in Safety/Helpfulness/Reasoning Rigor on 3B (29.39/45.04/4.98 → 84.40/71.13/78.87) and 7B (53.21/52.92/19.26 → 86.34/80.79/85.34), while preserving general capabilities (3B: 58.67 → 59.21; 7B: 66.39 → 66.81). Code: [https://github.com/Duebassx/SafeR_Toolkit](https://github.com/Duebassx/SafeR_Toolkit).

paper.title: Improving LLM-Based Entity Detection with Annotation Guidelines
paper.abstract: In this work, we investigate whether detailed, dataset-specific annotation guidelines can replace or augment annotated few-shot exemplars for prompt-based entity detection. To this end, we propose an in-context learning framework that conditions the LLM on a guideline document, task instructions, and optional demonstrations, enabling single-pass, primarily zero-shot nested entity detection. We evaluate multiple instructional aspects from the comprehensive ACE 2005 annotation guidelines, using three guideline-compliant datasets as benchmarks and GPT-5 variants for inference. Based on extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that detailed, dataset-specific instructions, especially those governing mention boundaries, consistently and robustly improve performance, even in conjunction with established few-shot methods. Indeed, even under zero-shot constraints, our guideline approach outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot methods on ACE-2005, achieving up to 81.2 percent F1 without relying on existing labeled datasets. Our findings present detailed annotation guidelines as a promising resource for improving instruction-based information extraction.

paper.title: Do not be greedy, Think Twice: Sampling and Selection for Document-level Information Extraction
paper.abstract: Document-level Information Extraction (DocIE) aims to produce an output template with the entities, relations, and events of interest occurring in the given document. Standard practices include prompting decoder-only LLMs using greedy decoding to avoid output variability. Rather than treating this variability as a limitation, we show that sampling can produce substantially better solutions than greedy decoding, especially when using reasoning models. We thus propose ThinkTwice, a sampling and selection framework in which the LLM generates multiple candidate templates for a given document, and a selection module chooses the most suitable one. We introduce both an unsupervised method that exploits agreement across generated outputs, and a supervised selection method using reward models trained on labeled DocIE data. To address the scarcity of golden reasoning trajectories for DocIE, we propose a rejection-sampling-based method to generate silver training data that pairs output templates with reasoning traces. Our experiments show the validity of unsupervised and supervised ThinkTwice, consistently outperforming greedy baselines and the supervised state-of-the-art.

paper.title: RL-ARC: Calibrating Large Reasoning Models via Reasoning-guided Uncertainty
paper.abstract: Language models (LMs) are commonly trained with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to enhance their reasoning capabilities. However, since RLVR does not explicitly account for calibration during training, it can lead to severe calibration degradation, including overconfidence. Recent calibration-aware training methods for LMs, which incorporate objectives for uncertainty estimation into training, improve calibration but still exhibit overconfidence under distribution shift, while sacrificing reasoning performance. To this end, we propose RL-ARC, a calibration-aware training framework that jointly leverages reasoning confidence and answer confidence. Specifically, RL-ARC leverages reasoning confidence as an auxiliary signal for calibrating answer confidence, applying it as reasoning-guided regularization for correct cases and as an overconfidence penalty for incorrect cases. Comprehensive results across ID and OOD settings show that, beyond improving calibration, RL-ARC enables reasoning models to adaptively estimate confidence based on the given question without substantially sacrificing reasoning performance, thereby highlighting the importance of reasoning confidence for training reliable reasoning models.

paper.title: HeRE: A Novel Benchmark for Hebrew Relation Extraction via LLM-Guided Denoising of Knowledge Graph Alignments

author.affiliation: Bar-Ilan University, Bar-Ilan University and JCT Lev Academic Center

paper.abstract: While LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in English Relation Extraction (RE) tasks, a significant gap remains in assessing their RE performance in low-resource languages, due to a lack of standardized benchmarks. Creating native, language-specific annotated RE benchmarks is expensive and requires human expertise, while relying on translation yields suboptimal, inaccurate datasets that introduce English-centric biases. To tackle this, we propose a scalable, language-agnostic methodology to create RE data by denoising naturally occurring yet noisy alignments of knowledge bases and corresponding texts. We define a proper alignment via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, where a relation triplet is entailed by an input text. We empirically assess five denoising strategies and demonstrate that multilingual models outperform language-specific models in the few-shot LLM setting, while Hebrew-specific encoders remain competitive under NLI fine-tuning and are strongest in the label-free cross-training setting. We further find that prompting in the native language achieves performance on par with or slightly exceeding English prompts, confirming that the pipeline operates naturally in the target language. The best open-weights model, Gemma-4-31B-it (F1=0.915), matches the best API model, GPT-5.4 (0.921), and reaches F1=0.844 on a fully held-out, dual-annotated test set. Applying the optimized pipeline, we release HeRE: a novel, massive, 1.5-million-instance silver dataset for Hebrew RE, designed to support data-intensive experimentation and model fine-tuning. HeRE bridges a critical gap in standard Hebrew RE evaluation, while providing the NLP community with a reproducible, language-agnostic pipeline for RE dataset construction in other low-resource settings.

paper.title: Query-Conditioned Graph Retrieval for Contextualized LLM Reasoning in Personalized Wearable Data

author.affiliation: Donald Bren School of Information and Computer Sciences, University of California, Irvine

paper.abstract: The growing prevalence of multi-sensor wearable devices generates vast amounts of long-term, multimodal time-series data, posing significant challenges for context-aware Large Language Models (LLMs). Current LLM-based health analysis methods typically rely on manually curated context, which becomes impractical with increasing data volume and sensor diversity. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Wearable As Graph (WAG), a novel framework that automates context retrieval for LLMs using personalized knowledge graphs. WAG constructs knowledge graphs mapping relationships between wearable modalities and incorporates user-specific data. We develop a data-driven retrieval pipeline that leverages both global (long-term) and local (short-term) relationships within metrics to identify the most relevant nodes for user queries. We evaluate WAG on a benchmark of over 10k data-associated queries created from multiple wearable datasets. WAG consistently delivers the strongest overall performance, while using substantially fewer input tokens than query-window full-context prompting in the diagnostic setting. These gains remain broadly consistent under human evaluation and across a cross-model generator–judge matrix, supporting structured, query-adaptive context retrieval for LLM-driven analysis of wearable data.

paper.title: Policy-Conditioned Constrained Decoding for Column-Level Access Control in Text-to-SQL
paper.abstract: Text-to-SQL is increasingly deployed across trust boundaries between data providers and users. Such deployment must balance three competing requirements: policy compliance, answer coverage, and bounded cost. Existing approaches typically decide refusal based on which columns a query mentions and enforce it stochastically. Whether a query is compliant, however, depends not only on which columns appear but on how they are used, and stochastic enforcement cannot deterministically rule out violations. We formalize this requirement as a column-use policy over semantic use: output, filter condition, and aggregation argument. We integrate the policy by aligning each role with grammar productions tracked by the decoder. The resulting system, PCC-SQL, applies a per-token logits mask that deterministically eliminates single-query column-use violations on the supported SQL fragment in a single decoding pass. Across three benchmarks and three open-source models, PCC-SQL achieves 0% Leakage Rate and Coverage up to 88.7% on Spider-CU, while staying within +10% tokens of direct prompting. We additionally assess semantic alignment with execution accuracy.

paper.title: A Systematic Review of Meta-Reasoning for Large Reasoning Models
paper.abstract: In this paper, we survey recent advances in meta-reasoning for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). Although LRMs have made remarkable progress, they face critical limitations including overthinking on simple queries, under-thinking on complex problems, and ineffective exploration lacking strategic direction. We examine how meta-reasoning addresses these challenges by providing the necessary mechanisms to dynamically regulate and optimize the reasoning process, and propose a framework to categorize existing studies into three core components: the monitor which provides self-perception of the reasoning state, the controller which dictates the meta-policy for regulating actions, and the mechanism which executes the algorithmic mapping between them. By systematically reviewing these developments and foundational challenges, we aim to map the current landscape and identify promising directions for creating more adaptive, efficient, and self-regulating reasoning systems.

paper.title: Domain-Agnostic Neural Topic Modeling with Contextual Token-Level Semantic Graph Representation
paper.abstract: PLM-powered neural topic models depend on general-domain pre-training, leading to degraded topic interpretability on specialized corpora. The root cause is geometric: domain-specific terms unseen during pre-training collapse into an indistinguishable region of the embedding space, and neither domain-specific re-training, word-level graph enrichment, nor parameter-efficient fine-tuning can restructure this space without inheriting the capacity ceiling of the underlying encoder. Our key insight is that a learnable graph layer operating on token-level PLM embeddings can acquire corpus-specific semantic structure that the frozen encoder lacks, because token-level graphs preserve document-local context that word-level representations discard and joint optimization with the topic objective reshapes embedding geometry directly from target-domain evidence. We instantiate this insight as DARTopic, a domain-agnostic framework that constructs token-level semantic graphs from frozen PLM embeddings and jointly trains a GNN encoder with variational topic inference. Across three benchmarks spanning general, biomedical, and legal domains, DARTopic consistently outperforms strong baselines in topic coherence and document clustering without any encoder fine-tuning, while demonstrating robustness to PLM choice and favorable runtime efficiency over fine-tuning-based alternatives.

paper.title: Surfacing Minor Nuances in Subjective Expressions: Initial Evidence for Improved Output Quality in Collaborative Caption Revision
paper.abstract: Creative collaboration benefits when collaborators can absorb the nuances embedded in others’ subjective expressions. We focus on especially difficult-to-notice nuances, which we call **minor nuances**, and provide initial empirical evidence that supporting their communication can improve creative collaboration outcomes. We then propose a commonsense-generation-based method that identifies minor nuances in subjective expressions and presents them as cues for collaborators. We evaluated the proposed method in a collaborative image-caption revision experiment designed to reflect brainstorming. Compared with a baseline in which collaborators freely explained the nuances embedded in their own subjective expressions, our method significantly improved output-quality ratings from human evaluators. These results provide initial evidence suggesting that explicitly sharing minor nuances supports richer creative expression by helping convey fine-grained aspects of senders’ inner states that are difficult to communicate through ordinary explanations.

paper.title: PoliSpace: Political Opinion Prediction using Shared Latent Space
paper.abstract: Modeling and predicting political opinions remains a challenging task for AI systems. We introduce PoliSpace, a framework that embeds individuals and political questions into a shared latent space, where vector alignment directly reflects agreement. Individuals are represented as learnable vectors, and questions are encoded via a contrastively fine-tuned language model with individual-specific affine transformations to capture subjective interpretation. This design yields an embedding space that is robust to question rephrasing and sensitive to negation. Evaluated on real-world voting data from Swiss national elections, PoliSpace achieves an 89.81% F1 score on seen opinion prediction for rephrased questions, outperforming prior embedding-based approaches (66.17% F1). We further introduce retrieval and confidence-aware thresholding mechanisms that reach up to 100% F1 at reduced coverage, demonstrating how the learned embedding space can be leveraged to improve prediction reliability. Ablation studies confirm the importance of both individual-specific interpretation modeling and negation-aware encoder fine-tuning. The learned individual embedding space also exhibits clear clustering by political party affiliation, despite no party-label supervision during training, capturing the underlying ideological structure of the Swiss political landscape.

paper.title: Predicting Mergeability of Language Model Domain Experts

author.affiliation: Amazon and University of Massachusetts, Lowell

paper.abstract: Model merging allows extending an expert model’s capabilities by fusing its weights with another expert. However, task interference has been shown to negatively affect mergeability. To address this, prior work has mainly focused on introducing new merging methods. Despite reducing task interference, the effectiveness of these merging methods is only evident post-merging, requiring a full evaluation of the merged model, which for contemporary LLMs can be expensive. In this work, we study the overlooked predictive power of structural and functional properties of merged experts for mergeability. Our experiments with 8 expert LLMs spanning several programming languages, math, and knowledge show that activation L2 distance and activation cosine similarity emerge as the most important properties for predicting effective merging, contrasting with prior findings on vision models where gradient-based metrics dominated. We further show that task vector L2 distance, a cheaply computed structural metric, provides a mechanistic link between mergeability prediction and training dynamics: it explains why learning rate effects on mergeability are domain-dependent in LLMs, contradicting the universal “higher noise improves merging” principle from vision. This enables a practical intervention where mergeability metrics guide learning rate selection during expert training.

paper.title: RAGCap-Bench: Benchmarking Capabilities of LLMs in Agentic Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems

author.affiliation: national university of singaore, National University of Singapore
The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen); National University of Singapore and National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates key limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs), such as factual errors, outdated knowledge, and hallucinations, by dynamically retrieving external information. Recent work extends this paradigm through agentic RAG systems, where LLMs act as agents to iteratively plan, retrieve, and reason over complex queries. However, these systems still struggle with challenging multi-hop questions, and their intermediate reasoning capabilities remain underexplored. To address this, we propose RAGCap-Bench, a capability-oriented benchmark for fine-grained evaluation of intermediate tasks in agentic RAG workflows. We analyze outputs from state-of-the-art systems to identify common tasks and the core capabilities required for their execution, then construct a taxonomy of typical LLM errors to design targeted evaluation questions. Experiments show that “slow-thinking” models with stronger RAGCap performance achieve better end-to-end results, underscoring the benchmark’s validity and the importance of enhancing these intermediate capabilities.

paper.title: Beyond Retrieval: Deterministic Memory Governance with Pairwise Constraints and Certified Repair for Long-Term Language Agents
paper.abstract: Long-term memory significantly enhances language-model agents but introduces a critical failure mode: retrieval surfaces relevant yet stale, deleted, or mutually inconsistent facts. A query about a current address may retrieve the correct address alongside deleted ones. The answer is present, but the memory set is unsafe. We reframe agent memory as a governed object-selection problem and present MemGov, a substrate-agnostic middleware layer between existing retrieval pipelines and agent context. MemGov wraps retrieved evidence as explicit memory objects, detects must-link and cannot-link constraints, and applies deterministic constraint-aware repair, returning either a certified safe memory set or an auditable obstruction certificate rather than silently passing unsafe combinations. Evaluations on controlled governance scenarios and MemoryAgentBench-style end-to-end tasks, deliberately separating retrieval quality from governance decisions, demonstrate that while raw retrieval recovers answer-bearing evidence successfully, it simultaneously returns detected unsafe memory combinations in 47-51% of cases. The same retrieval substrates governed by MemGov reduce unsafe merges to 0% while preserving answer utility within about 2-4 percentage points, with fully auditable reasoning for all repair and refusal decisions. Additional diagnostics assess eligibility, temporal constraints, and paired answer retention.

paper.title: HDSL: A Hierarchical Domain-Specific Language for Structured 3D Indoor Scene Generation and Localized Editing with LLM Agents

author.affiliation: ETHZ - ETH Zurich, EPFL and University of Zurich

paper.abstract: Text-driven indoor scene generation and editing require an intermediate representation that language models can both produce and revise. Existing LLM-based systems often rely on scene graphs or global constraint lists, which are compact but underspecify local geometry and make instruction-based edits difficult to localize. We frame the task as structured program generation and local program repair, and propose the Hierarchical Descriptive Scene Language (HDSL), an XML/CSS-style domain-specific language in which rooms, regions, objects, and support surfaces form a tree with parent-relative local coordinates. Our pipeline generates HDSL subtrees recursively with bounded verification, grounds non-virtual nodes through multimodal asset retrieval, and applies force-directed layout optimization to repair boundary and collision errors. For editing, Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves the relevant subtree, rewrites only that local context, and merges the result back through a deterministic three-way merge. In our reproduced benchmark, HDSL improves average object coverage, text-scene alignment, and generation time over full text-to-scene baselines while remaining competitive with layout-only reproductions on geometry metrics. On thirty paired editing instructions, HRAG reduces token use by 67.6% and runtime by 68.1%, and cuts non-target removals by 87.5% over full-scene rewriting; attribute ablations confirm that local coordinates and virtual/leaf flags are necessary for valid, locality-preserving edits.

paper.title: Training LLMs Beyond Next Token Prediction - Filling the Mutual Information Gap

author.affiliation: Department of computer science and informational engineering, National Taiwan University

paper.abstract: Autoregressive language models are usually trained with next-token prediction under a fixed left-to-right target order. This paper studies target-token organization as a training-time design choice across arithmetic reasoning, multi-label text classification, and text generation. Controlled order studies show that the default NTP order can be far from the best-performing tested organization, while fixed hand-crafted orders such as reverse order do not generalize across tasks. To address this, Max(MI(S; t)) is introduced as a deterministic mutual-information-based heuristic that prioritizes information-rich target tokens. For fixed-length outputs, it constructs task-specific prediction orders; for open-vocabulary text generation, the same principle is applied through lightweight prefix augmentation. Experiments with GPT-style models and pretrained Llama/Qwen variants show that Max(MI(S; t)) often improves over standard NTP and simple baselines such as reverse order, TF-IDF, and conditional-probability selection, without changing model architecture or autoregressive decoding.

paper.title: Structural vs Cultural Reasoning: Reliability Limits of LLM-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Evaluation
paper.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation in multilingual cultural reasoning, yet its reliability for culturally grounded judgments remains poorly understood. We present a human-aligned validation study using the CRaFT framework across Arabic, Bengali, and Spanish, evaluating six judge models, including five open-weight models and GPT-4.1, against paired human annotations across two structurally observable dimensions (Answer Consistency and Explanation Consistency) and three culturally interpretive dimensions (Cultural Fluency, Linguistic Adaptation, and Deviation). Our results reveal a consistent reliability divide: automated judges align substantially better with humans on structural dimensions than on culturally interpretive ones requiring sociocultural reasoning. Reliability further varies across languages, judge architectures, and response-generation models, with several failures reflecting systematic calibration limits rather than prompt underspecification alone. These findings suggest that current automated evaluators are best treated as complementary diagnostic tools rather than replacements for human judgment in culturally sensitive multilingual settings.

paper.title: Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied for clinical decision support, and medical question answering provides an effective testbed for evaluating this capability. In particular, medical multiple-choice questions (MCQs) reflect a core challenge in clinical decision-making: plausible options often share substantial overlapping evidence, while only a few decisive factors distinguish the correct option from other incorrect ones. However, existing retrieval-based and reasoning-oriented methods mainly focus on supplying broadly relevant knowledge or eliciting reasoning paths, rather than identifying the compact differential evidence that separates confusing alternatives. In this work, we present a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs. Our method extracts option-specific pieces of differential evidence and organizes them into concise evidence prompts for answer selection. This design better aligns external knowledge with differential reasoning while reducing irrelevant context. Experiments show consistent accuracy gains over strong baselines. Ablation studies further show that our framework outperforms both directly using retrieved evidence chunks and closed-source LLM-generated general hints, and that its improvements are not solely explained by answer-proximal guidance, but are consistent with differential evidence serving as a compact aid for reasoning over competing alternatives. Our findings also offer insights for medical reasoning and other decision-making settings with multiple possible choices.

paper.title: The Expense of Seeing: Attaining Trustworthy Multimodal Reasoning Within the Monolithic Paradigm

author.affiliation: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, Delhi

paper.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is often framed as enabling unified multimodal understanding, but rests on an under-examined assumption: that current VLMs faithfully synthesise multimodal data. We argue they often do not, and that this gap reflects a trustworthiness problem in the dominant Vision Encoder-Projector-LLM paradigm. Rather than extracting grounded knowledge from visual inputs, state-of-the-art models frequently exhibit functional blindness, exploiting strong language priors to bypass severe visual representation bottlenecks. We challenge the conventional methodology of multimodal evaluation, which relies on data ablation or new dataset creation and therefore conflates dataset biases with architectural incapacity. We propose an information-theoretic departure: the *Modality Translation Protocol*, which preserves a sample’s semantic payload while translating its modality rather than ablating it. From this, we derive three metrics—the Toll (*ToS*), Curse (*CoS*), and Fallacy (*FoS*) of Seeing—culminating in the *Semantic Sufficiency Criterion (SSC)*, a single condition that detects, quantifies, and localises multimodal failures to the visual encoder or the projection head. We further hypothesise a *Divergence Law of Multimodal Scaling*: as language backbones grow, the penalty of the visual bottleneck may widen rather than close. Examining the closest-matching existing benchmarks, motivates our central call: the construction, through *Semantic Equivalence Engineering*, of a large, diverse dataset whose modalities are isomorphic by construction. We frame this not as an experiment awaiting compute, but as a mission for the community: to move beyond "multimodal gain" and build the substrate on which faithful multimodal architectures can be designed.

paper.title: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction from Structured Metadata and Climate Science Publications
paper.abstract: The rapid expansion of scientific literature far outpaces the speed of manual curation, creating a fundamental bottleneck in extracting structured knowledge from scientific texts. To address this, we introduce an agentic, ontology-guided framework for knowledge graph (KG) construction. Our framework utilizes specialized agents for document understanding, information extraction, ontology conformance, and entity linking. First, an LLM extracts factual knowledge in the form of triples with explicit textual evidence from research papers. Then the triplets undergo a multistage verification process to ground the triplets in the ontology. By enforcing schema constraints and requiring evidence in the form of text fragments, we ensure the data is both semantically consistent and traceable. In an agreement study over 1,000 extracted triplets, Gemini-2.5-flash achieves Cohen’s \kappa scores of 0.640–0.700 against three human annotators, matching the human–human agreement range of 0.616–0.689. We applied this framework to 2,000 scientific publications and construct a novel, ontology-grounded KG for climate science with 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations; of the 23,327 triplets that the publications contribute after validation, 98.96% are judged correct. The pipeline code and KG is publicly available.

paper.title: Sampling via Decision-Flow: Training-Free Extraction of Improved Latent Reasoning Paths in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: A central question in LLM reasoning is whether reinforcement learning (RL) instills genuinely new capabilities or merely reshapes how existing knowledge is expressed during inference. Building on the distribution-sharpening hypothesis, which holds that RL reallocates probability mass toward high-reward trajectories already latent in base models, we ask: can we unlock those latent paths without costly RL fine-tuning? We present Decision-Flow Sampling (DF-Sample), a training-free, data-free inference-time framework that constructs a hierarchical reasoning tree, scores terminal nodes for quality, and back-propagates utilities to inform each intermediate branching decision. Unlike conventional sampling strategies that make purely local step-wise choices, DF-Sample performs explicit global trajectory evaluation before committing to a path, recovering high-quality but low-probability reasoning chains that standard decoding overlooks. On GPQA, DF-Sample achieves 45.6% accuracy, surpassing power sampling (38.9%) and GRPO (39.9%), showing that a training-free method can outperform a trained one. Across three models and four benchmarks, DF-Sample consistently outperforms baselines, indicating substantial latent reasoning potential in pretrained base models.

paper.title: Does Fairness Survive Model Adaptation in Legal Judgment Prediction?
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP), raising concerns about demographic bias inherited from pre-training corpora and historical legal records. We investigate how fairness robustness changes under model adaptation in LJP through a controlled counterfactual evaluation across gender, ethnicity, and intersectional demographic groups. Using 23 demographic variants over encoder-based models and generative LLMs, we evaluate demographic sensitivity, counterfactual instability, and bias propagation under zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned settings. Experiments show that model adaptation substantially affects fairness. Fine-tuning often improves predictive performance while simultaneously increasing demographic sensitivity and propagating biased supervision signals into downstream judicial predictions, whereas few-shot prompting generally produces smaller propagation effects. We further show that legal-domain specialization does not reliably guarantee fairness: legal-domain encoders span both highly robust and highly sensitive behavior after fine-tuning, and a legal-domain LLM is highly sensitive under few-shot prompting yet comparatively robust after fine-tuning under counterfactual perturbation.

paper.title: Activation-Efficient Fine-Tuning via Sequence-Compressed Low-Rank Subspaces

author.affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Broad Institute

paper.abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has become the standard approach for adapting large language models (LLMs). However, despite reducing trainable parameter counts, many PEFT methods remain memory-bound by token-level activation intermediates that scale linearly with sequence length, limiting their practicality for long-context and on-device adaptation. Unlike prior memory-efficient PEFT approaches that preserve token-level adapter activations, LARS (Low-memory Activation-Rank Subspace) reduces the sequence-length scaling of stored adapter activation intermediates from O(BSRL) to O(BRL) by performing adaptation within a sequence-level low-rank subspace. Through pooled feature extraction, low-rank subspace modulations, and residual projection, LARS reduces the overall memory footprint by 23% on GPUs and 47.8% on CPUs relative to LoRA at S = 1024, with relative savings increasing with context length. Experiments across reasoning, understanding, long-context, retrieval, and token-level tasks show that LARS maintains competitive performance relative to LoRA while substantially improving memory efficiency. Beyond GPUs, LARS also reduces average CPU power and energy consumption per optimization step by 22.43% and 22.06%, respectively. These results demonstrate that activation-efficient adaptation provides a practical path toward resource-constrained and on-device fine-tuning of LLMs.

paper.title: Detect Before You Disambiguate: Perturbation-Based Input Ambiguity Detection in LLMs

author.affiliation: Arizona State University and Arizona State University

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often answer ambiguous inputs as if they had a single intended meaning. This is problematic because input ambiguity is an upstream source of uncertainty: when a prompt admits multiple valid interpretations, the key question is whether the model should answer directly at all. Existing input uncertainty methods often rely on LLM-generated statements or clarifications, but such transformations may already disambiguate the input before the ambiguity is measured. We propose a label-preserving perturbation framework for input ambiguity detection in which perturbations remain close to the original input while preserving its label. We instantiate this principle with two detectors: a black-box rule-based perturbation library and a white-box importance-guided method using model-internal signals. Experiments across four datasets in open-domain, conversational, and visual QA show that our methods outperform output-side uncertainty baselines and LLM-paraphrase-based perturbation baselines. Our results highlight the importance of detecting ambiguity before attempting to disambiguate it. Our code is available here.

paper.title: Diverse Reasoning Paths Matter: Symbolic Equivalence Augmentation for Enhancing RL Exploration

author.affiliation: Arizona State University and Arizona State University

paper.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. However, the role of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data in enabling effective downstream RL remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate a key hypothesis: the diversity of reasoning steps in chain-of-thought (CoT) during SFT is a critical enabler of RLVR performance. To test this hypothesis, we introduce EquivAug, a data augmentation framework that uses symbolic equivalence transformations to generate diverse yet provably correct reasoning paths. By converting CoT solutions into formal symbolic representations, applying equivalence transformations, and reconstructing natural-language explanations, EquivAug produces training data that differs in reasoning steps rather than surface-level lexical variation. Experiments on GSM8K and FOLIO across model scales demonstrate that EquivAug consistently achieves the highest reasoning path diversity after SFT and the strongest accuracy after GRPO. Our results establish that CoT diversity during SFT is positively correlated with downstream RLVR performance.

paper.title: Information-Theoretic Design of Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
paper.abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based activation steering is a lightweight approach for modifying the behavior of large language models (LLMs) by adding small vectors to hidden states during inference. However, designing effective steering interventions remains challenging. In this work, we develop an information-theoretic framework for analyzing SAE activations through empirical feature-firing distributions. The central object of the framework is the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between such firing distributions, which quantifies how far a generated or intervened state deviates from a dataset-induced target distribution. Based on an analytic divergence response for virtually shifted states, we construct steering vectors toward the target firing distribution. The same divergence can also be used to monitor deviation from another empirical distribution, such as a general valid-language distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the steering in a question-mode generation task study. We further use teacher-forced pulse experiments to show that local interventions induce structured downstream JSD responses in later layers, and apply the framework to a safety-related target–contrast response setting for feature analysis.

paper.title: An Empirical Study of Position Bias in Visualized Text Retrieval

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: Visualized text retrieval, which renders text into images and retrieves them with vision-language models, has been proposed to avoid lossy text parsing and compress long contexts. We ask whether it also bypasses a known flaw of text retrieval: position bias, the tendency to overweight a passage’s beginning. Rendering 1D text into a 2D image may change the bias in two respects: its shape, which position is favored, and its magnitude, how strongly performance varies across positions. We test this by rendering the PosIR benchmark as controlled plain text images and comparing eight visual retrievers with four text retrievers on identical instances. We find that (1) position bias persists, with all visual retrievers exhibiting measurable bias (macro PSI 0.061–0.168); (2) its shape is transformed: seven of eight visual retrievers favor the middle of the page in an inverted-U pattern, contrasting with both the primacy bias of text retrievers and the lost-in-the-middle effect of LLMs with long contexts; (3) its magnitude is sensitive to rendering settings, as taller images amplify PSI and can even reverse positional preference, while font size has a similarly large effect; and (4) under matched backbones, visual retrievers exhibit lower position bias than their text counterparts on longer documents, but this advantage vanishes beyond the pixel budget and at document scale. Visualized text retrieval therefore does not eliminate position bias; it transforms a familiar 1D textual bias into a more complex 2D spatial bias.

paper.title: A Geometric Perspective on Stabilizing Value Conflict Resolution
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle to navigate user requests that contain complex value conflicts, as direct scalar rewards are often ill-equipped to handle these scenarios. To address this challenge, we investigate how chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can help improve performance in this domain. Geometrically, we show that CoT correlates with further smoothing the model’s loss landscape in its sharpest direction, helping resolve the optimization instability of traditional scalar rewards. In terms of performance, we demonstrate via relevant downstream benchmarks that CoT may increase capability, demonstrating that value conflict-focused CoT has the potential to be an effective mechanism for better moral reasoning. To capitalize on this potential, we create a new value conflict-focused CoT design that correlates with further smoothing the sharpest direction of the loss landscape and further increases moral reasoning performance. This finding shows that explicitly modifying and improving the design of reasoning dynamics offers a promising avenue for advancing pluralistic alignment in LLMs.

paper.title: Do LLMs Have Social Sense? Evaluating Alignment of Conversation Understanding and Reasoning
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong instruction-following and reasoning abilities, yet struggle with the socially nuanced understanding humans handle naturally. Humans rely on social sense to interpret intentions, emotions, and relationships in context. We investigate whether and to what extent LLMs exhibit similar abilities when reasoning about social interactions. We propose a structured approach that decomposes social interactions into three aspects and prompts LLMs to generate aspect-based summaries capturing complementary signals. We evaluate these summaries and resulting reasoning within a unified framework across three dimensions, analyzing both LLM–human alignment and the quality of LLM-generated social explanations. Our results show that LLMs achieve moderate agreement with humans and with one another as evaluators and capture some socially nuanced information across aspects, but struggle with interaction-level dynamics shaped by situational norms. Across four downstream CSS tasks, aspect summaries improve aggregate prediction performance across three model families, though effects vary by task. Complementary rationale analysis shows that summaries substantially alter expressed reasoning. Finally, we introduce a benchmark dataset with gold-standard annotations to support systematic study of social understanding and situated reasoning in LLMs.

paper.title: Encoded but Not Express: Probing Subtle Speech-Conditioned Emotion in Large Audio Language Models
paper.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) exhibit strong speech understanding ability, yet it remains unclear whether they meaningfully utilize subtle speech-conditioned emotional cues beyond coarse acted emotions. In this work, we investigate whether the evaluated LALMs exhibit measurable sensitivity to fine-grained emotional variation in speech through controlled perturbation experiments, fine-grained emotion elicitation tasks, and representation geometry analysis. Our results show that vocal delivery variations systematically influence both model behavior and hidden representations, indicating that the evaluated LALMs already encode non-trivial speech-conditioned affective information. However, models struggle under emotionally ambiguous settings, particularly for semantically related fine-grained emotions. Representation analysis further suggests that subtle emotional structure is partially preserved despite weak downstream utilization. Overall, our findings suggest that the evaluated LALMs do not completely ignore subtle speech emotion cues, but instead utilize them inconsistently under ambiguous affective conditions

paper.title: See Every Block Once: Variance-Reduced Post-Training for Masked Diffusion Language Models
paper.abstract: Policy gradient methods are widely used to align large language model outputs with human preferences, but the log-likelihoods they require cannot be directly computed in Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs). MDLM post-training therefore relies on a surrogate objective based on the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and recent work estimates a blockwise variant of this objective via Monte Carlo methods to support blockwise generation. However, existing estimation schemes randomly sample the block index, leading to unstable estimation. In this work, we propose a full-block estimator that evaluates every block exactly once and averages the results. We theoretically show that the proposed estimator remains unbiased while eliminating the between-group variance arising from block selection, thereby always achieving lower variance than the baseline for the same sample size. In experiments on five benchmarks spanning mathematics, planning, and coding, our method achieves the highest accuracy on four benchmarks and outperforms the random block sampling baseline by an average of 12.79 points.

paper.title: Amortizing Self-Correction for Continual Embodied Adaptation
paper.abstract: Language model (LM)-powered agents have shown promise in addressing complex embodied tasks by leveraging the commonsense world knowledge of pre-trained models in interactive physical environments. Yet, real-world deployment requires agents to continually adapt to a stream of tasks, where neither large-scale expert supervision nor reliable external feedback is consistently available. In this paper, we present ASC, a framework for efficient continual embodied task adaptation through amortizing self-correction. Specifically, ASC trains the policy under two objectives: a standard CoT reasoning objective distilled from stronger experts, and a reflexive reasoning objective that internalizes self-correction by correcting initial rationales generated by a previously learned policy. This dual optimization allows the agent to adapt more efficiently through forward knowledge transfer over time, ultimately fostering robust CoT reasoning at inference without requiring explicit reflection. Furthermore, we introduce rationale-wise test-time scaling that dynamically adjusts the depth of CoT reasoning based on the model’s confidence in actions inferred from its own rationales. Through experiments on VirtualHome and ALFWorld, we demonstrate performance superiority over other LM-based planning and continual task adaptation approaches, while achieving strong efficiency in computation, data usage.

paper.title: Back to Basics, Powered by Data: Character-Level Transformers for Robust Chinese Machine-Generated Text Detection

author.affiliation: Tsinghua University and Wuhan Ripple Effect Technology Co., Ltd.
Huazhong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Machine-generated text detection remains difficult in Chinese, where systematic benchmarks and large paired corpora are still scarce. We revisit this problem with a compact 4-layer character-level Transformer, trained on a 363.4-million-character Chinese detection corpus, to our knowledge the largest AI-human paired Chinese resource for this task. The resulting data-centric pipeline attains strong scores on Chinese benchmarks and, for the independently trained English variant, state-of-the-art RAID leaderboard numbers that remain stable under 11 RAID adversarial attack types. Ablations expose a double-edged sword role for punctuation: it eases optimization yet encourages overfitting to surface cues; symbol cleaning shifts the model toward deeper syntactic and discourse patterns and improves generalization. Minimal architecture plus rich supervision thus yields compact detectors suitable as a document-level authorship authenticity screen before downstream Chinese text processing; on a laptop RTX 3070 Ti we measure 5.90 x 10^5 tokens/s at under 100 MB VRAM. We present GiantMelon-ZH (Chinese) and GiantMelon-EN (English for RAID): same backbone, disjoint training corpora, transparent data descriptions.

paper.title: PULSE-CARE: A Measurement-Validity Audit of Simulated-Patient Clinical Agent Evaluation
paper.abstract: Simulated-patient benchmarks are widely used to evaluate clinical AI agents, yet the patient simulator itself can alter the evidence available to the agent and therefore the conclusions drawn from the benchmark. We introduce PULSE-CARE, a measurement-validity audit for simulated-patient clinical-agent evaluation that quantifies sensitivity to patient simulator behavior, agent architecture, simulator backbone, scorer choice, and demographic framing. Across 24 synthetic longitudinal cases, four dynamic simulator variants, three agent models, and two architectures, the mean per-case score range across simulators is 0.25 (95% CI: 0.21-0.29), and escalation decisions differ across simulator conditions for 60% of agent-case pairs. A 392-trajectory repeated-sampling analysis shows that simulator effects persist after pooling repeated draws, while also revealing substantial within-policy stochastic variation. Nominal model rank reversals occur in 17% of comparisons but disappear under a 0.05 practical-difference margin. Demographic counterfactuals change escalation in 26% of matched pairs, essentially the same rate as the same-input repeated-sampling control, providing no evidence of a demographic effect in this audit. PULSE-CARE combines simulator-sensitivity metrics, EFI composite indices, Patient Simulator Cards, and an Audit Report template to make the measurement conditions behind simulated-patient benchmark results explicit. Our results show that clinical-agent performance reported from a single patient simulator should be interpreted as conditional on the simulator and evaluation pipeline used to obtain it.

paper.title: DensePath REINFORCE: Lightweight Policy Improvement from SFT-Induced Token-Level Reward Signals
paper.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is typically viewed as behavior cloning on expert demonstrations. Recent methods recover richer supervision from demonstrations through self-play preference synthesis or bilevel inverse reinforcement learning, yet these require additional optimization stages or separately trained reward models. Motivated by the connection between SFT and inverse soft-Q learning, we propose Dense-Path REINFORCE (DPR), a lightweight post-SFT policy-improvement method that extracts a dense reward signal directly from the SFT training trajectory. We construct a token-level reward from the log-probability gap between the final SFT policy and an intermediate checkpoint, capturing the incremental likelihood gain acquired during training while mitigating the length and early-EOS biases inherent in raw log-probability rewards. DPR reuses the same demonstrations and prompts as SFT, requires no preference data, no external teacher, and no separately trained reward model. Across four pretrained backbones and four instruction-following evaluations, DPR obtains 55.2-66.8% win rates over SFT, improves MT-Bench by 0.22-0.46 points, and matches or exceeds the best demonstration-only baseline in 15 of 16 settings.

paper.title: Not All Tokens Are Equally Important: Auditing and Compressing Redundancy in LLM Reasoning

author.affiliation: Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Chain-of-thought traces drive strong LLM accuracy but dominate inference cost: output length sets both monetary cost and decoding latency. We ask which tokens in a reasoning trace actually carry the answer. A token-level analysis of the model’s own next-token distribution identifies three redundancies - discourse-element removal, tokenizer-aware abbreviation, and substitution of prose causal connectives with an arrow "X -> Y". All three leave the predictive distribution close to the original under Jensen-Shannon divergence and preserve the greedy next token in the vast majority of prefixes. We instantiate the analysis as CONCISON, a single training-free system prompt that operationalises the three rules and protects numeric, equation, and code tokens verbatim. Across 18 models from six families (2B-120B) and five reasoning benchmarks, CONCISON cuts output tokens by 24-62% on strong models at -1.1pp average accuracy, outperforms token-budget prompting in a single decoding call, and matches trained routers on the accuracy-cost frontier without any training, model pool, or extra infrastructure.

paper.title: ICCU: In-Context Continual Unlearning via Pattern-Induced Refusal Rules
paper.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific data from trained language models. In real-world deployments, unlearning requests often arrive sequentially, which challenges existing fine-tuning-based methods: fine-tuning each request is costly, accumulates utility loss, and may cause cross-request interference. To address these issues, we propose ICCU (In-Context Continual Unlearning), an in-context continual unlearning framework that induces readable refusal rules from unlearning datasets and applies them at inference time either as a filter or via the system prompt, without modifying model parameters. Because rules are accumulated as an order-independent union, ICCU is compositional and free of cross-request interference, and the original forget-set data can be discarded after rule induction. Extensive experiments show that ICCU effectively suppresses target knowledge while preserving utility, scales across long sequences of requests, and remains robust to paraphrased, cross-lingual, and adversarially framed queries. Our code is available at https://github.com/rhpan/ICCU.

paper.title: PerQ: Efficient Evaluation of Multilingual Text Platform-Adaptation Quality
paper.abstract: Since no metrics are available to evaluate specific aspects of a text, such as its personalization quality or quality of adaptation to a specific form, researchers often rely solely on large language models to evaluate such texts. Due to internal biases of individual language models, it is recommended to use multiple of them for combined evaluation, which directly increases costs of such evaluation. In this paper, a computationally efficient method (called PerQ) for evaluation of personalization quality (in terms of platform adaptation) of a given text (generated by a language model) is introduced, which is based on predicting the LLM judgments (i.e., a kind of metric distillation). A case study of comparison of generation capabilities of large and small language models shows the usability of the proposed metric in research, effectively reducing the waste of resources.

paper.title: BrainMoE: A Brain-Inspired Modular Mixture-of-Experts Model for Multimodal Reasoning

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Reliable cross-modal reasoning requires Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLMs) with interpretable and controllable computation. However, existing models rely on data-driven architectures that entangle multimodal processing, obscuring the functional processes underlying their outputs. Inspired by the human brain’s specialized and dynamically collaborative networks, we propose **BrainMoE**, a multimodal MoE model with six sensory and cognitive experts: Language, Logic, Social, World Knowledge, Vision, and Auditory. To support flexible sensory–cognitive coordination, we incorporates a layer-wise adaptive router that dynamically determines which experts are activated at each layer based on task-processing demands. Experiments on text, image, and audio reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that BrainMoE outperforms strong baselines by 1.59 and 2.2 points on text-only and multimodal benchmarks, while matching competitive external multimodal models. Routing and ablation analyses demonstrate clear expert specialization and causally important module-level contributions. Experiments on the cognitive benchmark further show that adaptive-routing BrainMoE aligns more closely with human behavioral patterns than baselines and static routing methods.

paper.title: DALSA: Difficulty-Aware Long-to-Short LLM Reasoning with Model Merging

author.affiliation: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Recent advances in large language models(LLMs) have given rise to large reasoning models that achieve strong performance through explicit multi-step reasoning. However, models often generate long reasoning chains even for simple inputs. We present Difficulty-Aware Long-to-Short LLM Reasoning with Model Merging (DALSA), an inference-time framework that adaptively controls reasoning depth based on input difficulty. DALSA integrates (i) representation-based difficulty estimation, which predicts a soft failure-rate score from the prompt hidden state, and (ii) difficulty-aware model merging, which uses a quantile remapped score to modulate the interpolation coefficient between short- and long-reasoning models. DALSA trains a lightweight probe while keeping both LLMs frozen. On mathematical benchmarks with the evaluated Qwen pairs, the accuracy–length trade-off depends on scale: at 7B, DALSA preserves static ACM-TA average accuracy (66.60% vs. 66.61%) while reducing average response length by 22.35%; at 1.5B, it improves average accuracy from 56.75% to 58.24% with a 2.27% length in- crease. Additional merging baselines, routing-threshold and merge-range sweeps, and component ablations show sensitivity to the operating configuration. Domain-matched commonsense and Llama-family diagnostics do not establish broader efficiency gains, limiting the primary empirical claim to the evaluated Qwen mathematical setting.

paper.title: From Preferences to Scores: Semi-Supervised Multi-Trait Essay Scoring with LLM Pairwise Preferences and Few Human Anchors
paper.abstract: Multi-trait automated essay scoring (AES) provides trait-level scores as feedback but requires costly annotations across multiple traits to train accurate scoring models. To alleviate this annotation burden, we propose MTPAS (Multi-Trait Preference-to-Absolute Scoring), a semi-supervised framework that learns relative score orderings from LLM-generated pairwise preferences and calibrates them to absolute rubric scales using a small set of human-scored anchor essays in an end-to-end manner. To this end, MTPAS jointly optimizes three objectives: a Bradley–Terry pairwise preference loss, a regression loss on the anchor essays, and a Sinkhorn divergence-based distribution regularizer. The model adopts a bifactor architecture that decomposes essay representations into a shared general factor and trait-specific residuals, improving robustness against noisy LLM-generated preferences. We further introduce pairwise rubric compression, which reformulates the original score-level rubrics into concise comparative criteria, reducing the inference cost of collecting LLM preferences. On ASAP and ASAP++, MTPAS achieves 91.4% of the fully supervised SoTA performance with only 30 anchor essays per prompt and further narrows the gap with 200 anchors. Under the same anchor budget, MTPAS outperforms conventional multi-trait AES baselines at every anchor size investigated in this study.

paper.title: Orthogonal Style Injection: Mechanistic Persona Steering for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Subtitle Translation

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Patna and National Institute of Technology Silchar,

paper.abstract: In conversational and cinematic subtitle translation, large language models often exhibit stylistic collapse, defaulting to neutral registers that flatten character-specific personas. Prompt-based attempts to recover style frequently introduce instruction drift and semantic degradation. We propose Orthogonal Style Injection (OSI), a parameter-efficient, inference-time intervention that removes global stylistic bias through orthogonal projection at an intermediate layer and injects a character-specific style vector derived solely from English source dialogue. We evaluate OSI for English-to-Bengali, Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, French, German, and Italian subtitle translation, spanning 11 typologically diverse target languages. Results show that zero-shot stylistic transfer depends strongly on pretraining alignment. Llama-3.1-8B yields gains in several European languages but degrades on Indic languages, whereas Qwen-2.5-7B transfers style more robustly across Indic and East Asian languages. To probe sociolinguistic mechanisms, we curate a parallel English-Bengali cinematic dataset as a focused morphological stress test. Automatic metrics and human evaluation show that OSI enables meaningful honorific and register shifts while largely preserving semantic fidelity, revealing a dataset-dependent trade-off between stylistic fidelity and translation quality in highly colloquial, morphologically constrained settings.

meta.booktitle: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 2: Short Papers)

paper.title: An Empirical Study of On-Device Translation for Real-Time Live-Stream Chat on Mobile Devices
paper.abstract: Despite its efficiency, there has been little research on the practical aspects required for real-world deployment of on-device AI models, such as the device’s CPU utilization and thermal conditions. In this paper, through extensive experiments, we investigate two key issues that must be addressed to deploy on-device models in real-world services: (i) the selection of on-device models and the resource consumption of each model, and (ii) the capability and potential of on-device models for domain adaptation. To this end, we focus on a task of translating live-stream chat messages and manually construct LiveChatBench, a benchmark consisting of 1,000 Korean–English parallel sentence pairs. Experiments on five mobile devices demonstrate that, although serving a large and heterogeneous user base requires careful consideration of highly constrained deployment settings and model selection, the proposed approach nevertheless achieves performance comparable to commercial models such as GPT-5.1 on the well-targeted task. The code, trained models, and LiveChatBench will be made publicly available at our GitHub.

paper.title: ImmunoFOMO: Are Language Models missing what oncologists see?
paper.abstract: Language model (LM) capabilities have rapidly advanced over the past decade, driving their adoption across fields, including biomedical research. While domain-specific pretrained language models (PLMs) have long supported biomedical NLP, recent focus has shifted to medical large language models (LLMs) and their language understanding capabilities. In this paper, we investigate this capability by probing the medical conceptual alignment of various LMs against clinical expertise for identifying hallmarks of immunotherapy in breast cancer abstracts. Our results show a clear trade-off: LLMs achieve stronger performance and higher consistency on high-level concepts, whereas PLMs are more reliable for fine-grained, low-level concept identification. We find that hallucinations are the primary factor limiting LLM performance in these settings; once mitigated, LLMs surpass PLMs across all tiers of biomedical concepts. Despite this, PLMs remain competitive, particularly in closely aligning with medical expert judgments on detailed conceptual distinctions.

paper.title: Constructive Comment Extraction from Japanese YouTube Shorts: A Dataset and Empirical Study

author.affiliation: Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
CyberAgent, Inc. and Nara Institute of Science and Technology
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan

paper.abstract: Identifying constructive comments from user-generated content is important for improving information discovery and discussion quality on platforms such as YouTube. However, existing resources focus predominantly on English news comments, leaving short-form video platforms underexplored despite their distinct characteristics: comments are shorter, more reactive, and not well captured by popularity signals. In this work, we introduce the first Japanese YouTube Shorts dataset for constructive comment extraction, featuring multi-annotator labels that preserve naturally occurring disagreement. We also develop a real-time system that surfaces constructive comments from a noisy comment stream, evaluated in a preliminary user study. To train under noisy annotation conditions, we combine self-training with high-confidence pseudo-labels and active learning. Experiments show that iterative data expansion improves performance, while our compact task-specific model achieves the highest PR-AUC point estimate among the evaluated systems. These findings demonstrate the value of dataset construction and targeted training for constructive comment extraction in realistic settings.
